headline: US Commerce expands anti-circumvention inquiry into aluminium containers made with Chinese foil
summary_text: The U.S. Department of Commerce has expanded its anti-circumvention enforcement by launching new inquiries into disposable aluminium containers, pans, trays and lids assembled in Indonesia and Malaysia using Chinese-origin aluminium foil. The country-wide investigations, initiated on August 6, 2026, are the latest step in Commerce's efforts to examine whether Chinese products are being routed through third countries to avoid U.S. antidumping and countervailing duties. The inquiries were launched after the Aluminum Foil Container Manufacturers Association (AFCMA), together with member companies Reynolds Consumer Products, Durable Packaging International and D&W Fine Pack, filed circumvention allegations on July 1. After reviewing supplemental information submitted by the petitioners, Commerce concluded that the requests met regulatory requirements and opened formal investigations covering the entire trade flow from Indonesia and Malaysia, rather than limiting the probe to individual companies. ... The latest inquiry follows a series of trade actions that began with the original case against Chinese aluminium container producers. In 2024, Commerce launched material injury investigations into Chinese disposable aluminium container manufacturers. By March 2025, the agency had imposed antidumping duties of 287.8 per cent on unspecified Chinese entities and rates of 193.9 per cent on more than 20 named companies. After the orders took effect, Commerce opened its first anti-circumvention inquiry in July 2025, covering disposable aluminium containers finished in Thailand and Vietnam using Chinese aluminium foil. Another circumvention inquiry followed in February 2026. The latest investigations into Indonesia and Malaysia suggest production has continued shifting to new manufacturing locations as Commerce broadened its enforcement efforts. Industry representatives say the latest move was expected. AFCMA's counsel, John Herrmann, said last year that the association would encourage Commerce to apply anti-circumvention rules aggressively to deter importers "considering hopping to additional third countries like Indonesia, Malaysia, and Taiwan" - closely reflecting the agency's latest action. ... According to industry reporting, AFCMA alleges that facilities in Indonesia and Malaysia carry out limited processing, including assembling, stamping and rebranding disposable aluminium containers, while relying on Chinese-sourced aluminium jumbo rolls, intellectual property and container-forming equipment. Under U.S. anti-circumvention law, Commerce considers factors such as investment levels, research and development activity, and the proportion of value added in the third country to determine whether the manufacturing process is substantial enough to fall outside the scope of the original trade orders. Commerce has also indicated that duties could be applied retroactively to shipments that entered the United States before the inquiries were formally announced. AFCMA has urged the agency to use this provision to discourage importers from accelerating shipments or relocating production before investigations begin. ... Commerce will obtain U.S. Customs and Border Protection import data within five days to identify companies for further review. Liquidation of relevant entries will remain suspended, while cash deposit rates will be applied as though the products were already covered by the 2024 trade orders. Preliminary determinations are expected within 150 days of publication, with final rulings due within 300 days, placing a decision around the middle of 2027. The inquiries also form part of broader concerns over Chinese aluminium products entering the US through third-country transshipment. The Aluminum Association has separately raised concerns that Chinese aluminium sheet is being routed into the United States through Mexican beverage-can and beer producers. The latest action also comes during a period of heightened volatility in global aluminium markets, with prices reacting to renewed Middle East shipping disruptions and naval activity affecting international supply chains.

headline: EU Industrial Heat Auction Secures Major €1bn Boost
summary_text: # EU Sets €1bn Industrial Heat Auction Terms, Brussels Last updated: 27 September 2026 6:41 pm Alaa AbuJaser - The European Commission published final IF26 Heat Auction terms on 24 September. - The €1bn programme will be financed from EU Emissions Trading System revenues. - Electrification, direct renewable heat and nuclear technologies are eligible. - Successful EU industrial heat auction projects can receive fixed-premium support for up to five years. - Bidding is planned to open in December 2026 and close in February 2027. Brussels, 27 September, (Brussels Morning Newspaper) – The European Commission has set the final terms for a €1 billion EU industrial heat auction aimed at cutting emissions from the heat used in European manufacturing. Published on 24 September, the IF26 Heat Auction rules cover projects using electrification, direct renewable heat and, for the first time in the scheme, nuclear technologies. ... The auction will be financed through revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System and implemented under the Innovation Fund. It is open to projects of all sizes and industrial sectors across the European Economic Area. Successful bidders will receive a fixed-premium subsidy proportional to each tonne of direct CO₂ emissions avoided, with payments available for a maximum of five years. Eligible electrification technologies include heat pumps, thermal storage, plasma torches and electric boilers. Direct renewable heat from solar thermal and geothermal sources can also qualify. Nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors, have been added for the first time. ... The latest auction widens eligibility to include some projects producing industrial heat above 80°C. The previous auction covered projects producing heat above 100°C. The Commission has also introduced further incentives for flexibility measures that can reduce pressure on the electricity system, particularly during periods of high demand. Process heat is used across industries including chemicals, steel, cement, pulp and paper, and food and beverages. The Commission says these processes remain largely dependent on fossil fuels and account for three-quarters of industrial emissions. ... Kurt Vandenberghe, Director-General of the Commission’s Directorate-General for Climate Action, called the auction a “crucial stepping stone” towards implementation of the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank. ... The IF26 round follows the first industrial heat auction, which received 85 bids. Sixty-five projects were selected for grant preparation, seeking nearly €400 million in support. Both auctions are pilots for the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank, which is intended to provide €100 billion in funding for industrial decarbonisation. ... The Commission’s current timetable lists national applicant information webinars throughout October 2026. The call for proposals is then planned to open in December 2026 and close in February 2027. The auction is not yet open, and the Commission has not published exact opening and closing dates. The official call for proposals and its accompanying documents will set the definitive requirements applicants must follow. Member states can also add national funding through the Auction-as-a-Service mechanism, allowing additional qualifying projects in participating countries to receive support.

headline: HUBS4BUILD project launched to develop Circularity Hubs for a Bio-based and Resilient Built Environment - Greenovate! Europe
summary_text: The Horizon Europe project HUBS4BUILD is launching its mission to demonstrate, deploy, and upscale circular solutions, by establishing a network of permanent and replicable regional Circularity Hubs that integrate the circular bioeconomy and circular construction value chains. The built environment is responsible for approximately 40% of the EU’s energy consumption and 36% of its GHG emissions, and the current linear construction sector is characterised by siloed operations with little communication between stakeholders, from material suppliers to end-of-life managers. Circular alternatives struggle to compete in this market for several reasons, such as inconsistent EU-wide standards, insufficient financial incentives, and the relatively low cost of virgin materials. The absence of economically viable technologies for processing diverse waste streams and the higher labour costs associated with deconstruction, are also limiting their adoption at large scale. ... The project will deliver a data-driven, bankable, and replicable blueprint for regional transformation, empowering communities to turn local underutilised resources into high-value, low-carbon assets for a climate-neutral and resilient built environment. To achieve this, HUBS4BUILD will co-design 13 Hubs in 13 countries, involving 500 local quadruple helix stakeholders to ensure solutions are context-specific and socially accepted. The project will innovate and validate a portfolio of 9 bio-based construction products (e.g. insulation from textile waste, panels from construction and demolition waste), deploying these solutions in 13 diverse operational environments via Public-Private-People-Partnerships. In doing so, the project aims to valorise around 700 tonnes of local waste and train 200 local professionals. HUBS4BUILD will also deliver a Bankable Twinning Methodology and foster a Replicators Network, in collaboration with the Circular Regions and Cities Initiative and other key initiatives, to ensure widespread adoption. To promote the emergence of systemic solutions, the project model will encourage collaboration among stakeholders through transition brokers. Each of the 13 Circularity Hubs has a specific role and will act as the central orchestrator for its regional network, connecting farmers, waste collectors, processors, architects, and policymakers. The four lead hubs in Greece, Spain, the Netherlands, and Romania are the project’s epicentres of innovation, aiming to demonstrate integrated value chains in real operational environments. They will generate the primary data on technical performance, economic viability, and social acceptance, serving as “lighthouses” for the rest of the consortium. The five replication hubs in Austria, Cyprus, Hungary, Ukraine, and Serbia will serve as “test-beds” for adaptability and robustness of the project methodology, ensuring that it can be applied beyond the conditions of the original demonstration hubs. The two scaling hubs in Umeå (Sweden) and Greater Rostock (Germany) will develop strategies for the systemic uptake and scaling of the project’s most successful solutions. These hubs will focus on governance, policy integration, and business model innovation to accelerate region-wide transformation. To strengthen future replication opportunities, the two transfer hubs in Bulgaria and the Western Balkans will promote capacity building, stakeholder mobilisation, policy development, and business case adaptation, preparing the ground for future investment and implementation of circular bio-based solutions in high potential regions. By facilitating structured dialogue, co-creating governance frameworks, and developing shared business models within the Circularity Hubs, the project will enable a lasting systemic shift, in line with the EU Bioeconomy Strategy’s call for stronger regional governance. The HUBS4BUILD project started in September 2026 and will run for 4 years. The consortium connects 39 partners from 13 countries and is coordinated by the University of Thessaly (Greece), with scientific coordination by CluBE (Greece). You can keep up with project progress on the project LinkedIn page. The International Energy Agency estimates that electric vehicles, heat pumps and electric industrial processes are already competitive across a much larger share of demand than is currently electrified. The calculation uses today's technology costs, energy prices and financing conditions and represents economic potential rather than a forecast or an adopted target. Europe could increase electricity's share of final energy consumption by almost 15 percentage points if it fully deployed technologies that are already cost-competitive under today's economic conditions, the International Energy Agency estimates in its new report on electrification. The result is among the highest of the regions examined and reflects the potential for electric vehicles, heat pumps and some industrial processes to replace fuels without relying on technologies that are not yet commercially available. The calculation is neither a forecast for the coming years nor a target European countries have committed to achieve. The IEA holds technology costs, energy prices and financing conditions at the levels used in its analysis and asks how much current demand could be competitively electrified if all already economic applications were adopted. The nearly 15 percentage points therefore describe techno-economic potential rather than the trajectory the Agency considers most likely. ... 1. The IEA estimates competitive electrification potential in Europe at almost 15 percentage points above the current level. 2. Globally, around half of residential fuel consumption, half of oil-based road transport and almost 40% of fossil-fuelled low- and medium-temperature industrial heat could be competitively electrified under today's conditions. 3. If all existing cost-competitive potential were exploited, the global electrification rate would rise from 23% in 2025 to around 33%. 4. Potential differs by region according to economic structure, climate, fuel and electricity prices, equipment costs and access to finance. 5. Upfront investment, grid capacity and electricity prices remain important barriers even where electric technologies are competitive over their operating lifetime. One explanation for the large potential is the much higher efficiency of electric technologies. In an internal-combustion engine, much of the energy contained in fuel is lost as heat, while an electric motor converts a much larger share of the energy it receives into movement. In buildings, a heat pump can provide three to five units of heat for each unit of electricity it consumes, whereas a gas boiler cannot deliver more useful heat than the chemical energy contained in its fuel. Those differences change the economic comparison. Electricity can cost more than gas or petrol for ... unit of final energy purchased, but electric equipment can use that energy far more efficiently. The IEA estimates on a global average that USD 100 spent on electricity can power an electric car around three times further than USD 100 spent on gasoline for an internal-combustion vehicle. The same logic applies to building heating. Using the average prices and efficiencies in the report, USD 100 of electricity used in a heat pump can provide about 42 days of heating compared with around 30 days from the same spending on fuel for a gas boiler. Actual results vary significantly between countries according to climate, tariffs, taxes, equipment costs and financing conditions. In industry, electrification is already competitive for many applications requiring low- and medium-temperature heat and for mechanical energy. The IEA estimates that almost 40% of current fossil-fuel use for these industrial applications could be replaced competitively, although processes requiring very high temperatures remain harder to electrify. Transport offers another large source of potential. Electricity still represents only a small part of transport energy consumption because the total vehicle fleet changes much more slowly than new-car sales. Nevertheless, the report estimates that around half of current oil-based road transport could be competitively electrified if available technologies were deployed at scale. The IEA finds wide regional differences. The calculated increase is around five percentage points in the Middle East but reaches almost 15 percentage points in Europe and India. These differences reflect industrial structure, vehicle ownership, average temperatures, fuel prices, equipment costs and access to capital. Europe already starts from a higher electrification level than many regions. In the European Union, electricity accounts for around one quarter of final energy consumption and the policy objective discussed for 2030 is around 32%. Those figures should not be mechanically overlaid on the IEA estimate for the broader European region because the geographical and methodological definitions are not identical. A favourable economic case does not mean investment happens automatically. A household still has to finance the upfront price of an electric car or heat pump, while a company must pay to replace industrial equipment before receiving lower operating costs. Interest rates, access to credit and energy-price stability can materially change the calculation. Infrastructure is another constraint. Faster electrification shifts part of demand away from oil and gas and towards the electricity system, potentially requiring significant investment in generation, grids, connections, storage and flexibility. The IEA warns that the benefits of electric technologies cannot be realised at scale if infrastructure does not expand quickly enough. ... to 2035 in which electricity's ... 35%. ... and should not be ... It does not say that the increase will occur, when it will happen or that the investment required will automatically be delivered.

headline: Commission publishes terms and conditions for €1 billion industrial heat decarbonisation auction - Climate Action
summary_text: On 24 September 2026, the Commission published the final Terms and Conditions (T&Cs) for its second Europe-wide auction for projects decarbonising industrial process heat (IF26 Heat Auction). Today, these processes are largely powered by fossil fuels and represent three-quarters of industrial emissions. The auction has a planned budget of €1 billion coming from EU Emissions Trading System revenues and is expected to open to bidders in early December 2026. Successful bidders will receive a fixed premium subsidy that is linked to its CO 2 emissions reductions for up to five years. Announced in the Clean Industrial Deal the auction will boost investment in homegrown clean energy solutions, strengthening resilience, and reducing energy prices. It follows the successful selection of 65 projects at the first auction, IF25. Both auctions function as pilots for the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank (IDB), that aims to provide €100 billion in funding for industrial decarbonisation. The IF26 Heat Auction will support innovative technologies to decarbonise process heat from three main categories: electrified technologies such as heat pumps, thermal storages, plasma torches, and electric boilers; direct renewable heat from solar, thermal, or geothermal sources; and, for the first time, nuclear technologies such as small modular reactors. Process heat refers to the energy used to generate high temperatures for manufacturing activities in sectors such as chemicals, pulp & paper, steel, food & beverage, or cement. The second auction expands eligibility to include projects producing industrial heat above 80ºC, where previously only projects producing above 100ºC were included. It also provides further incentives to implement flexibility solutions which reduce pressure on the electricity system. The final T&Cs were prepared following public consultations with industry and stakeholders. The auction may also be topped up by Member State contributions via Auction-as-a-Service, an approach that has already proven successful in previous auctions under the European Hydrogen Bank. ... - Fixed premium subsidy: Successful bidders will receive a fixed premium subsidy that is linked and proportional to each tonne of direct CO 2 emissions abated for a maximum period of five years. - Wide scope: The IF26 Heat Auction is open to projects of all sizes from every industrial sector across the European Economic Area. - Focus: It serves projects that use continuous industrial processes but also incentivises flexibility solutions to avoid electricity consumption in peak hours or technologies which don’t require electricity. ... This auction targets one of the biggest sources of EU industrial CO 2 emissions: process heating. This refers to the heat used to transform raw materials into products; from melting plastics and metals to driving chemical reactions. Today, these processes are largely powered by fossil fuels and represent three-quarters of industrial emissions. All industrial sectors have such processes and can take part in the heat auction. The IF26 Heat Auction aims to close the cost gap between direct renewable heat, nuclear heat or electrification solutions, and fossil fuel-based alternatives. By de-risking these innovative projects, it not only enhances the competitiveness of clean industries in Europe, but also reduces greenhouse gas emissions, boosts energy independence and security, makes energy prices more affordable, and brings our continent closer to achieving its climate neutrality goals by 2050. With this auction, the Commission continues to deliver on the Clean Industrial Deal and gains important insights for the implementation of the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank. ... The Innovation Fund is one of the world’s largest funding programmes for commercialising and deploying innovative low-carbon and net-zero technologies. Financed by revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System, it helps businesses invest in clean energy and bring market-ready solutions to scale – driving industrial decarbonisation and strengthening European competitiveness. The Fund has already allocated around €12 billion to around 200 innovative projects across the European Economic Area. IF25 and IF26 are implemented under the Innovation Fund. > Kurt Vandenberghe, Director-General, Directorate-General for Climate Action, said: > > “ This auction is a crucial stepping stone toward the implementation of the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank. It opens the door to scaling investments in industrial electrification technologies driving industrial decarbonisation. I call on industry leaders to join us in tapping into the vast potential for cost-effective emission reductions through electrification and prepare their bids for the auction that will open in early December.”

summary_text: After the summer break, the policy agenda is back in full swing. As institutions return to Brussels and policymakers turn their attention to the months ahead, several key files are moving forward. Additionally, we explain how the proposed new Public Procurement Act could affect European industry. ... On 9 September, the European Commission unveiled its proposal for a new Public Procurement Act, which signals a shift in how governments across the EU buy goods and services. The proposal would overhaul the EU’s 2014 public procurement rules, replacing them with a single, directly applicable Regulation designed to strengthen European industrial competitiveness, accelerate the clean-tech transition, and build more resilient supply chains. Drawing on the recommendations of the Draghi and Letta reports as well as the priorities of the Clean Industrial Deal, the Commission wants to use one of the EU’s most powerful economic levers: public spending. With public procurement representing around 15% of EU GDP, the Commission sees government purchasing as far more than a question of getting the lowest price. The new approach would place greater emphasis on European manufacturing, decarbonisation, resilience and economic security: using public contracts to help scale strategic industries and strengthen Europe’s position in the global clean-tech race. ... The proposal seeks to cut red tape and make public procurement more flexible and business friendly. Instead of relying on rigid tender formats, energy and utility buyers would have greater freedom to choose how they engage with suppliers: they could run single-round tenders with room for negotiation or create dynamic supplier pools that companies can join at any time to compete for regular contracts. At the same time, utilities facing direct market competition can secure fast-track exemptions to bypass procurement rules altogether. For major infrastructure and first-of-a-kind clean energy projects, a new “innovation procedure” allows public bodies and utilities to fund, test, and buy emerging technologies directly from industry partners. ... The proposal would make best price-quality ratio the standard for awarding contracts, moving beyond lowest-price tenders. At least 30% of award points would go to quality criteria such as life-cycle costs, circularity and greenhouse-gas impacts. Industrial tenders would also promote recycled materials, remanufacturing and product-as-a-service models. The Act would further allow the Commission to set mandatory green procurement criteria for clean industrial products regulated under the Ecodesign Regulation, the Net-Zero Industry Act, the Batteries Regulation, and the Critical Raw Materials Act. ... The Public Procurement Act proposal introduces a European preference mechanism allowing public buyers to favour EU and eligible third-country suppliers. Buyers could restrict tenders to these suppliers, reject bids with less than 50% EU or covered content, or award additional points for higher European content. For critical energy and transport infrastructure, buyers would also have to strengthen resilience and security of supply through measures such as multi-source procurement, supply-chain traceability and EU-based stockpiling, reducing reliance on single-country suppliers. ... The proposal now moves to the European Parliament and the Council of the EU. Member States will be weighing the budget impact of mandatory 30% quality criteria on regional and municipal bodies, while industry groups will look for further clarity on how European preference will work with existing trade treaties. In the One Europe, one Market Roadmap, formal agreement is targeted for Q4 2027. The text would favour greater European content in strategic supply chains, introduce tighter rules for foreign investment and public support, and prevent Natura 2000 sites from being designated as industrial acceleration areas. headline: Europe's Green Building Rules: The Case for Hemp - The European Business Review
summary_text: The European Commission published new guidance this year putting “whole-life carbon” at the centre of EU building policy — a shift from measuring only the energy a building uses once occupied to counting the carbon cost of the materials that went into it, and the waste created when it eventually comes down. It’s the kind of document that reads as procedural. That is, according to Evgeny Skigin, an industrial hemp entrepreneur with more than 20 years of experience, until you understand what it actually changes. What it changes, he argues, is which materials get specified in the first place. ... The Commission’s own figures explain the stakes. About half of all EU greenhouse gas emissions are linked to the building stock, and the sector generates the largest waste stream in Europe. For years, Skigin notes, “green building” has mostly meant operational efficiency — insulation, windows, heating systems — which measures only the energy used after a building opens. It says nothing about the carbon locked into concrete and steel before a single occupant moves in. Whole-life carbon accounting closes that gap by measuring emissions across a building’s entire life cycle: design, construction, use, renovation, and demolition. The guidance leans towards reusing existing buildings and reducing demand for new material — both of which eventually raise the same question every builder has to answer, in Skigin’s view: what should that material actually be? ... Skigin’s answer draws on the material he has spent nearly two decades working with. Hemp fibre and hemp hurd — the woody core of the plant — go into insulation and, mixed with a lime binder, into hempcrete. The case for it under whole-life accounting is straightforward, he says: the plant absorbs carbon as it grows, and much of that carbon stays locked into the walls for the building’s life, in direct contrast to concrete and steel, which emit carbon in production before construction even begins. Skigin is careful not to overstate the connection. The Commission’s guidance doesn’t name bio-based materials specifically. But the accounting logic, he argues, does the work regardless: once embodied carbon is what’s being measured, a material that sequesters carbon during growth stops being a niche choice and becomes a rational one on the numbers. Part of what makes hemp a strong candidate, in his telling, is how little it demands to grow. “It’s basically a weed,” he says. “It doesn’t need pesticides or herbicides. It doesn’t require a lot of water. It has a very deep root system. It can grow in Finland and it can grow in Thailand.” From a single crop, he notes, come fibre for textiles, hurds for construction, and seed with a strong protein and fat profile — “textiles, housing, and food” from one plant. ... None of that means hempcrete shows up on job sites next year, and Skigin is blunt about why. “No builder understands what hemp is, no architect understands what it is, and the client in the end also doesn’t quite understand it,” he says. “Even if he wants it, he’ll still go with the safe option.” His own venture had to fly builders to the Netherlands to learn the technique before a single wall could go up correctly — the unglamorous cost, he says, of introducing a new material into a chain built around the old ones. What changes with guidance like this, in his view, is the incentive on the demand side. Once whole-life carbon becomes what gets measured — and eventually regulated — buyers start asking for exactly the properties a bio-based material already has. It’s a variation on an argument Skigin has made for years about hemp’s path to scale: no industry, he says, “has ever succeeded without government support. Not the internet, not oil, not trains, not cars.” Materials, in his reasoning, are no exception. He points to the Netherlands, where his venture built what he describes as the world’s only prefabricated hemp building production line, and where government subsidies and grants have begun closing the cost gap with traditional materials — including supplying materials for a museum project in Eindhoven. “That has now changed in the Netherlands,” he says. “It should really be EU-wide.” Whole-life carbon accounting, in Skigin’s reading, is the tool that finally makes hemp’s case in numbers a finance department has to take seriously, rather than a sustainability slide a builder can set aside. Europe just decided to count all the carbon in its buildings, not only the part on the electricity bill. What gets built next, he argues, depends on which materials are ready when that accounting starts to bite.

Moeve has launched construction of the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley in Palos de la Frontera, Huelva, a project the company is presenting as the largest of its kind in Europe and which aims to put Spain in a leading position in the development of this new energy industry. The first phase, called 'Onuba', will initially have 300 MW of electrolysis capacity, with the option of adding a further 105 MW, and will involve a total investment of more than 1 billion euros, including the associated infrastructure and a photovoltaic plant for self-consumption. During the development, construction and commissioning phases, Moeve estimates that the project will create more than 8,000 direct jobs, as well as indirect and induced employment across the entire value chain, and will support the activity of more than 400 small and medium-sized enterprises and local self-employed workers. "Once again, we are turning ambition into a tangible reality," said Moeve's chief executive, Maarten Wetselaar, quoted in a statement. "Today we are turning the page on green hydrogen pilot projects and moving into the chapter of large-scale construction." In comments to 'Euronews', Wetselaar argued that 'Onuba' can help strengthen Spain's role in the European energy transition and reduce dependence on external suppliers. "We need European energy that is decarbonised and produced by us, and that is exactly what this project delivers," he explained. ... The company expects the facility to be able to produce around 45,000 tonnes of renewable hydrogen a year, avoiding some 250,000 tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually. The hydrogen will be used to support more sustainable production of fuels for road, air and maritime transport, as well as contributing to the decarbonisation of other industries. ... Fair and Competitive ... For Moeve, the conditions in Spain, and especially in Andalusia, offer a clear advantage for the development of green hydrogen. The company highlights the availability of solar and wind power, the land required for large renewable facilities and conditions that allow renewable electricity to be generated at competitive costs. "Spain has abundant solar energy, very good wind energy and space to build large renewable parks," Wetselaar noted. In his view, given that renewable electricity accounts for a large share of the cost of producing green hydrogen, the availability of renewable resources could turn the country into one of Europe's main producers. The 'Onuba' project is led by Moeve, which owns 51% of the venture. Hy24 and Cofides jointly hold 29%, while Enagás Renovable and Alter Enersun control the remaining 20%. The project has been recognised by the European Union as a Project of Common Interest and has received 304 million euros in funding from the Spanish government through the Recovery, Transformation and Resilience Plan, financed by the European Union via NextGenerationEU. ... 'Onuba' is the first phase of the Andalusian Green Hydrogen Valley, which Moeve plans to develop up to a total electrolysis capacity of 2 GW at its energy parks in Palos de la Frontera and San Roque, in the province of Cádiz. The company also plans to connect production in Huelva with other European industrial hubs through pipeline and maritime transport solutions. "We want to scale up this plant and connect Huelva with other industrial centres in Europe," Wetselaar said. The development of hydrogen forms part of a broader transformation of Moeve's facilities in Andalusia. The company plans to invest a total of 2.4 billion euros in energy transition projects in the region, including 'Onuba' and a second-generation biofuels plant that will produce sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel. For Wetselaar, the roll-out of these projects could have effects that go beyond energy output. "If Spain scales up, we are talking about thousands of jobs, a significant impact on GDP and, of course, political clout," he said. In his opinion, the ability to produce and export renewable energy could reshape Spain's energy relationship with the rest of Europe.

headline: Europe Phasing Out Gas Boilers… LG Corp. Secures Contract for Entire ‘Integrated Solution’ Beyond Heat Pumps [Report] - EDAILY
summary_text: [IFA2026] Construction Site for a New 102-Unit Apartment Complex in the Netherlands ThermaV and OSO to Supply Buffer Tank Packages LG Corp. Provides Comprehensive Support from Design and Installation to After-Sales Service Expanding HVAC B2B Business in Line with Europe’s Transition Away from Natural Gas JAEMIN SONG 2026-09-10 10:00:04 [Leidscherk (Netherlands) = E-Daily Reporter JAEMIN SONG ] A newly constructed apartment complex with 102 units in Leidscherk, located about a 20-minute drive from Rotterdam, Netherlands. Climbing onto the roof of the building, which is currently under construction, I saw LGELECTRONICS’ “Therma V” air-source heat pump outdoor units densely lined up at regular intervals. Installed at a rate of one per household, these heat pumps provide heating and hot water for each unit without the need for gas boilers. ... “In the Netherlands, the use of gas boilers is prohibited in new buildings. Heat pumps, geothermal systems, and district heating are the alternatives, but heat pumps are often chosen for their cost-effectiveness.” Kim Seong-bin, Team Leader of the ES Business PD Team at LGELECTRONICS Benelux, explained this on site. As the Netherlands implements policies to reduce gas usage—particularly in new buildings—heat pumps are rapidly replacing traditional boilers. The ThermaV, installed on the rooftop, is an air-source heat pump that extracts heat from the outside air to provide indoor heating, cooling, and hot water. Equipped with LGELECTRONICS’ high-efficiency inverter scroll compressor, it produces approximately 4 to 5 times more thermal energy than the amount of electrical energy consumed. According to LGELECTRONICS, this can reduce energy consumption by about 40–60% compared to fossil fuel boilers. Although the outdoor units are concentrated in one area, noise and vibration were also taken into consideration. Team Leader Kim explained, “Since they are installed on the rooftop, noise sensitivity is relatively low, and vibration-dampening pads are installed beneath each unit to reduce vibration.” On-site, we could indeed confirm the presence of these vibration-dampening pads beneath each outdoor unit. ... LG Corp., which Used to Sell Only Heat Pumps, Now Offers a ‘Bundle’ Including Buffer Tanks The significance of this project became even clearer once we went inside the building, rather than just looking at the ThermaV units themselves. Each unit was equipped with a stainless steel buffer tank from OSO, a Norwegian hot water solutions company acquired by LGELECTRONICS last year. This marks the first instance of a heat pump and buffer tank being designed as a single package and supplied to a large-scale new construction site. The buffer tank stores the heating water heated by the heat pump and supplies it when needed. When the buffer tank holds a sufficient supply of heating water, it helps reduce “short cycling”—where the heat pump turns on and off at short intervals—thereby lowering the load on the unit, minimizing energy waste, and extending its service life. ... Previously, construction companies or installers often sourced heat pumps and buffer tanks from different manufacturers and installed them separately. At this site, however, LGELECTRONICS designed the heat pump and buffer tank—including their capacity, piping, and controls—as a single integrated system. Robin Klaus, ES Business Leader at LGELECTRONICS Benelux, said on-site, “Other companies often purchase parts from multiple suppliers and assemble them into a single product,” adding, “When problems arise, they end up arguing over who is responsible.” He continued, “Since we manufacture most of the components ourselves, we can manage the entire package,” emphasizing, “Our ability to provide a complete package is our greatest advantage.” The installation process has also been simplified. Klaus explained that for this project, LG Corp.’s engineering team pre-designed the configuration—including the piping and valves required for installation—and the installation method, enabling the on-site installation contractor to implement it exactly as planned. ... “Who do I call if it breaks down?”… LG Corp. handles all after-sales service Another distinguishing feature of the integrated solution is after-sales service. If the heat pump and buffer tank are manufactured by different companies, you first have to determine which product is at fault when a malfunction occurs. It can take time to determine where the responsibility lies between the companies. Team Leader Kim said, “If the heat pump is from LG Corp. but the buffer tank is from another brand, the installer has to call multiple companies, and there are often disputes over who is at fault.” He added, “Now that we provide a comprehensive warranty for the entire package, both installers and customers are highly satisfied.” ... This project is also significant in that it demonstrates how LGELECTRONICS’ strategy to expand its HVAC business—pursued since the acquisition of OSO—has translated into actual on-site contracts. While the company has already supplied package products to small-scale renovation sites, this marks the first time such a system has been implemented on a large scale in a new residential complex with over 100 units. Team Leader Kim said, “There have been many sites in the past where we installed one, ten, or twenty units,” adding, “This is the first time we’ve installed over 100 units at a new construction site, making it a significant large-scale reference project.” Building on this success, LGELECTRONICS plans to expand its integrated HVAC solutions business in Europe—moving beyond standalone heat pumps to include heating, cooling, hot water, and thermal storage and control. The company has already supplied heat pumps to more than 100,000 households across five Southern European countries, including France and Spain, and is expanding its business reach to a 1,500-unit residential complex in North Macedonia, as well as to Germany and the United Kingdom. Robin Klaus, the business leader, said, “European customers’ needs are shifting from simple heating devices to integrated solutions that encompass heating, cooling, hot water, and thermal storage and control,” adding, “We will expand into new markets by combining heat pumps with various hot water solutions.”

headline: SolarPower Europe Lifts 2026 EU Solar Forecast After H1 Growth
summary_text: Solar delivers when Europe needs it most, but SolarPower Europe’s mid-year market update warns that the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 solar target ... - Europe’s solar market showed more resilience than expected in H1 2026, despite a challenging policy environment, according to SolarPower Europe - The association has raised its 2026 forecast, but says a lot depends on policy and market conditions - Utility-scale solar is gaining a larger role, while rooftop deployment faces growing pressure from weaker residential demand Europe’s solar market showed unexpected resilience in H1 2026, but SolarPower Europe says the improvement was driven more by the energy crisis than by stronger policy support, which is the need of the hour. In its EU Solar Market Update: 2026 Mid-Year Analysis, SolarPower Europe says the bloc installed nearly 33.8 GW of solar PV capacity, up about 1.9% year on year (YoY). This was slightly higher than the 33.2 GW reported in H1 2025. The increase was mainly due to external factors driven by renewed energy security concerns and higher fossil-fuel prices due to the Middle East conflict. ... The five largest markets – Germany, Spain, France, Italy and Poland – accounted for about three-quarters of H1 installations. Poland recorded the strongest growth among the five, with installations up 39% YoY, while Italy grew 10% and France 5%. Germany and Spain, on the other hand, were down 4% and 6%, respectively, although the report notes that these figures could be revised as more project registrations are reported. ... Based on the data available now, SolarPower Europe expects 68.1 GW of solar capacity to be added in 2026, an increase of 6.6 GW over 61.5 GW it projected in December 2025. The updated guidance is still 2.1% below the revised 2025 record of 69.6 GW, up from the 65.1 GW it reported earlier. The revision mainly reflects a revised installation figure of 13.4 GW for Spain, up from 9.2 GW reported earlier ( ). The report's low and high scenarios for 2026 range from 62 GW to 74.1 GW, depending on market and policy conditions. ... The report authors expect utility-scale projects to account for 56% of new EU solar capacity in 2026, compared with 44% for rooftop systems, down from 45% in 2025. SolarPower Europe blames the projected decline in rooftop solar on weakening residential demand in several markets as support schemes become less attractive or more uncertain. Commercial and industrial (C&I) solar has proved more resilient, with companies continuing to invest to reduce electricity costs and hedge against future price volatility. ... Schmela stated, “H1 2026 has once again demonstrated that higher fossil fuel prices strengthen the business case for solar. But the fact that market resilience has been supported by another external energy shock rather than stronger policy and regulatory frameworks remains a warning sign for the sector’s long-term growth prospects.” The expansion of solar in Europe is increasingly constrained by negative electricity prices, grid bottlenecks and insufficient battery storage. While storage could help absorb excess midday generation and enable further solar deployment, regulatory barriers, limited grid capacity, and a lack of clear business models are slowing its development. ... The report highlights that solar's role in Europe is expanding beyond decarbonization. From March 1 to August 31, the EU’s solar PV generation totaled 282 TWh, which SolarPower Europe estimates avoided about €30 billion in gas import costs for power generation. Solar also became the EU’s largest source of electricity in June, supplying a record 25% of generation. It provided more than 20% of the EU’s electricity in May, June, and July. The timing was important, the association remarks. Heatwaves increased demand for air conditioning, while high river temperatures and low water levels constrained some nuclear and hydropower generation. Solar therefore produced strongly as demand rose and some conventional generation came under pressure. However, Europe is adding solar faster than it is adding the flexibility needed to use it effectively. Without flexibility resources and with grid connection constraints, the market is seeing negative electricity prices, declining solar capture rates, and rising curtailment. These in turn increasingly affect project revenues. Walburga Hemetsberger, CEO of SolarPower Europe, stressed, “ Europe should not need an energy crisis to make the case for solar, and it should certainly not weaken the conditions for solar investment in the middle of one. Policymakers must now focus on the fundamentals: grids, storage, flexibility and stable investment frameworks.” Increasing storage deployment will increase the value of solar and reduce reliance on fossil fuel generation outside solar hours. SolarPower Europe expects EU battery storage installations to reach 52 GWh in 2026, up about 44% from 36 GWh in 2025. SolarPower Europe argues that the current policy environment does not provide enough certainty to sustain the investment needed for the next phase of solar growth. The association maintains that the EU is likely to miss its 750 GW solar target for 2030 by a ‘significant margin’ under current market and policy conditions. “Our assessment therefore remains unchanged: under current market and policy conditions, the EU is not on track to meet its 2030 solar target,” says SolarPower Europe.

headline: S&P Global Eurozone Construction PMI®: Steeper Fall In New Orders Drives Sharper Decline - ConstructUK
summary_text: - New orders contract at fastest pace since April - Employment falls again as outlook remains pessimistic - Cost pressures continue to soften Construction firms in the eurozone saw the pace of decline in total activity accelerate in August amid a sharper contraction in new business. New order intakes decreased at the quickest rate in four months, while all three monitored sub-sectors saw sustained falls in activity midway through the third quarter. At the same time, there were sharp reductions in both employment and purchasing, and cost inflation remained historically marked despite easing to a six-month low. The S&P Global Eurozone Construction PMI Total Activity Index — a seasonally adjusted index tracking monthly changes in total industry activity — posted 43.0 in August, down from 44.3 in July to signal a stronger contraction in construction activity midway through the third quarter. Total activity has now decreased consistently for 52 months. The steeper fall in construction activity reflected an accelerated decline in France that was the most pronounced since May 2020, while Italian firms saw the fastest contraction for four years. German companies meanwhile bucked the downward index level trend to register its softest reduction in 2026 to date. By sector, housing activity decreased at the sharpest rate , followed closely by commercial construction. Civil engineering activity saw the softest decrease of the three, but one that was still solid overall. In line with the picture for total construction activity, the rate of decline in new orders gathered pace during August. New business was down markedly and at the strongest rate since April. New orders fell notably sharply in France, while there was a renewed and solid drop in Italy. Construction orders in Germany declined at a softer rate than that seen in July, but at one that was still substantial. Employment moderated for the seventh month in a row in August, with the rate of job shedding the most prominent in four months. Steeper reduction in workforce numbers were recorded in France and Germany, while staffing levels in Italy rose for the second successive month. Eurozone constructors decreased their usage of subcontractors again, and at a marked rate. As a result, the availability of subcontractors rose, though the rate of increase was only modest. ... Higher cost burdens continued to weigh on the construction sector. The rate of input cost inflation eased further from April’s peak to reach a six-month low, but remained well above the series average. The rise in input costs in Italy slowed on the month, contrasting with a slight acceleration in input cost inflation in both Germany and France. In line with this trend, the rise in subcontractor rates was the softest since February. At the same time, construction firms also scaled back their purchasing activity during August. Input buying has fallen continuously on a monthly basis since June 2022. The latest reduction was unchanged from July. French and German firms saw softer decreases in input buying, contrasting with the sharpest fall in purchasing activity since January 2023 in Italy. While demand for inputs fell, constructions firms continued to face a further lengthening of suppliers’ delivery times, the thirteenth in as many months. Lead times lengthened solidly, though the latest deterioration was the softest since February. Eurozone construction companies gave a downbeat assessment regarding the prospects for activity growth over the coming year. The degree of pessimism was unchanged from July’s three-month record. French companies posted the most pessimistic outlook, posting the weakest level of sentiment since April. German firms also posted a markedly downbeat outlook. Firms in Italy meanwhile registered the most positive outlook for six months. Usamah Bhatti, Economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said, “August data revealed a sharper downturn in construction activity, largely in response to a steeper deterioration in demand conditions. New business intakes fell at the quickest pace in four months, with the decline broad-based across the monitored nations. Moreover, the three sub-sectors of construction also remained firmly in contraction territory, again led by housing. “Weakness across the sector weighed on the outlook for activity, with firms signalling pessimism regarding the year ahead. According to panel members, headwinds to activity stemmed from inflationary concerns and the war in the Middle East. Companies will take heart from the fact that overall cost inflation trended downwards again to reach a six-month low, however.”

headline: Energy crises are driving a renovation revolution – Energy in Demand – Sustainable Energy – Rod Janssen
summary_text: High energy prices have sparked new interest in energy-related renovations and non-fossil heating systems. This post by Desislava Rusinova and Marco Weissler of the European Central Bank argues that such investments cushion the impact of energy shocks on the building and construction sector. The analysis shows that while energy shocks initially hurt the construction sector, they also spur investment in heat pumps, insulation, solar panels and other efficiency measures that reduce fossil fuel dependence and strengthen long-term resilience. ... When energy prices skyrocket, that often comes as a heavy blow to the real estate and construction sector. Construction and building maintenance costs rise, and mortgages often become harder to arrange and come with higher rates. But for many people, it’s also a moment to rethink, renovate and invest in energy efficiency. So while energy shocks may slow new construction, they can simultaneously drive a wave of renovation activity. We argue that the energy price surges in 2022 and 2026 have been driving demand for investment in energy efficiency. The recent wave of renovation has also been supported by declining equipment costs and government subsidies. In the shorter term the additional renovation spending can cushion the negative impact of higher energy prices on housing investment. In the longer term it reduces the dependence of the building sector on fossil fuels, increasing its resilience to energy-driven price and confidence shocks. ... Investment in housing involves not only the construction of new buildings, but also finishing and installation work – so-called specialised construction activities (SCAs). In fact, SCAs represent 75% of construction activity. Energy-related renovations are a large part of SCAs. [1] Electrical, plumbing, heating and air conditioning installations alone accounted for 40% of value added in the five largest euro area countries in 2023. Recently, renovations of existing buildings have been a main driver of the recovery in construction activity. Meanwhile, the construction of new buildings continues to decline – potentially also due to the strong increase in prices for energy-intensive inputs like concrete (Chart 1). [2] ... Efficiency-enhancing renovations comprise a wide range of activities, including the installation of heat pumps, photovoltaic (PV) panels and other heating systems with better energy efficiency, as well as installing or improving building insulation. These activities have become more widespread in recent years. In 2022 PV imports to the euro area increased sharply after the spike in energy prices due to the war in Ukraine. PV imports from China nearly doubled after the energy price hike and have remained high since then (Chart 2, panel a). [3] The decline in their prices since 2023 has likely supported this development. The average price of an imported tonne of PV modules or panels fell by two-thirds – from nearly €5,000 in 2023 to only €1,700 in 2026. More recently, since the beginning of the war in the Middle East, national subsidy programmes have seen additional demand for financing energy-saving measures, e.g. in the Netherlands or the United Kingdom. In Germany, 64,000 households and businesses sought funding between March and May 2026 to renovate their building envelope – 16% more than in the same period a year earlier. The building envelope includes, for instance, insulation and windows. Funding requests for heating investments increased by as much as 40% (Chart 2, panel b). ... Households who have faced higher heating costs or are more exposed to fossil fuels renovate more. Utility costs are a likely driver of such renovations. Recent results of the ECB’s Consumer Expectations Survey (CES) show that when utility costs grew faster, more households opted for energy-efficiency renovations (Chart 3, panel a). [4] In 2024 and 2026, after reported utility costs in the preceding heating season had grown strongly, the share of energy-renovated dwellings increased notably as well. In the period closest to the Ukraine war, between February 2023 and 2024, this share jumped by 10 percentage points. Households facing higher expenditure on utilities in recent heating periods are also more likely to plan energy-efficiency renovations of their property. CES data from February 2026 showed that, besides general repairs, energy-efficiency renovations were the most frequently mentioned type of renovation planned. Such plans were mentioned by 14.5% of CES respondents. [5] Households with high utility costs and relying on fossil fuel-based heating systems much more frequently reported that they plan an efficiency renovation (Chart 3, panel b). In contrast, the probability was lower for households with heating systems that rely on renewable energy sources (e.g. heat pumps or solar collectors), which were not affected by the recent price spikes. [6] ... Beyond cushioning the negative impact of energy price shocks on the building sector, energy-efficiency investments can also make the building sector more resilient to energy price shocks. Following the recent price surges, the share of fossil fuels used for space heating in the euro area declined by 3.5 percentage points between 2023 and 2026 to stand at 56% (Chart 4). Most countries have decreased their reliance on fossil fuels, and those with higher dependence have reduced it by more. Accordingly, households living in energy-renovated housing report lower growth in their utility costs in the subsequent heating season compared with those living in unrenovated homes. [7] This suggests that energy-efficiency renovations allow households to become more resilient to future energy price shocks, simply because they consume less energy. EU policies are aiming to boost this trend. The European Green Deal aims to at least double the annual rate of energy renovations by 2030. [8] One element of this is the extension of the EU Emission Trading System (EU ETS). The EU ETS increases the costs of CO 2 emissions and makes oil and gas more expensive. From 2028, the building sector will also be covered by the EU ETS. And that should further increase the incentives to move away from oil and gas-based heating systems. This has positive implications for monetary policy – both improved energy efficiency and lower reliance on oil and gas heating reduce the impact of oil price fluctuations on inflation. The Commission's blueprint includes significant boosts to energy storage and aims to electrify industrial heating. However, environmental groups and industry associations are already pointing out potential shortcomings and areas demanding greater focus. ... The Action Plan aims to increase the use of electricity across buildings, transport and industry by addressing the cost gap between electricity and fossil fuels. The Commission proposes reforms to allow Member States to reduce network charges for certain consumer groups and lower taxes for energy-intensive industries. It also wants to ensure electricity is not taxed more heavily than gas and accelerate the deployment of smart meters to help consumers manage energy use. A central objective is to reduce the electricity-to-gas price ratio to a maximum of 2.5 for households and 2.0 for industry by 2030. The plan includes measures to expand financing mechanisms and social leasing schemes to reduce upfront costs for electrification technologies, as well as using public procurement to support heat pump deployment and improving energy price transparency. The Commission also aims to improve grid flexibility through reforms to network charging, faster smart meter deployment and greater participation of heat pumps in demand response markets. ... Alongside the electrification target, the Commission has set ambitions to increase EU energy storage capacity from around 55 gigawatts (GW) in 2026 to 200 GW by 2030 and 400 GW by 2040. For the industry, the Commission estimates that around 60% of fuel-based energy demand could be electrified using heat pumps. The Action Plan proposes support through the Industrial Decarbonisation Bank, a second Innovation Fund industrial heat auction, sector-specific electrification roadmaps and investment in grid connections, thermal storage and energy management systems. The plan also includes an EU Waste Heat Initiative, with a target for waste heat recovery to supply 11% of Europe’s heating demand by 2050. This would be supported through district heating and cooling networks and municipal heating plans. The Commission is also proposing measures to strengthen Europe’s heat pump manufacturing base, improve installer skills and establish an Electrification Action Plan Alliance bringing together policymakers, manufacturers and other parts of the value chain. ... Andreas Sieber, head of politics at 350.org, said: “Europe’s electrification push is important, but the level of ambition still falls short of what the climate and energy security crises demand. “The EU now needs a far stronger ... to deepen diplomatic engagement with emerging economies, most notably China, and mobilise credible financial support for developing countries. ... Jozefien Vanbecelaere, policy director at the European Heat Pump Association, said: “This Electrification Action Plan is a game-changer. ... “For the first time it focuses on boosting electrification of demand – and does so via a great line-up of measures, from tackling energy taxation and electricity prices and tapping on heat pumps’ flexibility, to supporting industrial electrification and waste heat recovery. “To ensure it delivers, the European Commission must swiftly convert it into legislation and measures to enact at the national level.” Luka De Bruyckere, acting head of energy transition at ECOS, said: “With its binding electrification target and attention given to cooling, this plan signals that Europe is serious about moving beyond fossil fuels. “It’s encouraging to see this ambition. headline: Bobst India’s view of Indian flexible packaging growth
summary_text: Bobst expects India’s flexible packaging industry to maintain strong growth as rising consumption, inevitably expanding film production and exports drive investment in printing, laminating, coating and metallizing technologies. At the company’s Open House celebrating its 30 years in India, Nilesh Pinto, Zone Business Director, Bobst India, said India’s flexible packaging market has expanded consistently alongside the growth of polyester, BOPP and CPP film production. He explained that India’s per-capita flexible packaging consumption remains significantly below that of developed and other major Asian markets, indicating substantial room for further growth. Per-capita consumption in the US is roughly 10 times India’s, while China’s is about five times higher, he said. “Even a 1% increase in India’s per-capita consumption of flexible packaging would represent a major leap in market size,” he said, highlighting the scale of the opportunity. Industry data from PIRA projected India’s flexible packaging market to grow at 6.7% annually. Pinto added that many anecdotal industry estimates put growth at higher levels, possibly closer to 10 to 12% a year, partly because informal economic activity is not fully captured in official data. India’s flexible packaging capacity could approximately double over the next five years, with a significant portion of new demand coming from tier 2 and tier 3 cities, he said. India is emerging as an important global film manufacturing base, Pinto said. Commissioning a single biaxial film line typically increases production capacity of about 35,000-40,000 tons a year, and several even bigger lines are on order. Recent trade agreements could further support growth in Indian film exports. Global flexible packaging consumption is expected to grow substantially through 2030, with APAC accounting for the majority of the increase. Pinto’s presentation indicated APAC is expected to account for about 70% of the estimated global consumption growth of 8.7 million tons in these years. Adding Africa, the share would rise to about 75% of total global growth. Bobst, which entered the flexible packaging sector in the late 1990s through its acquisition of Schiavi, supplies equipment and technology across the flexible value chain, including gravure and CI flexo printing, lamination, coating, metallizing and labels. Pinto said the breadth of its portfolio allows Bobst to work with customers as a technology partner rather than simply as an equipment supplier. The company has worked with brand owners to develop benchmark processes and packaging structures that have subsequently gained wider use across the industry. ... As the packaging industry moves from its traditional focus on reduce, reuse and recycle towards regulation-driven circularity, Pinto expects that between 2025 and 2030, the key priorities include the use of post-consumer recycled content, paper and fibre substitution, decarbonization, supply-chain resilience and greater use of artificial intelligence in production. Increasingly driven by regulatory requirements, particularly the European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation and the Indian EPR regulations, new structures demonstrate the direction of travel. Mixed laminates for aseptic packaging have already reduced aluminium while increasing renewable content. Bobst has worked with Blue Loop Paper on a paper-based structure with high-barrier performance, while Innovia Films and Toppan have developed recyclable BOPP and polyethylene film structures, respectively. Bobst is also focusing on mono-material structures, compostable and biodegradable films, and paper and fibre-based packaging. Citing a paper structure achieving an oxygen transmission rate of 0.1 using coating and metallizing without plastic, technologies such as Bobst’s FibreCycle, PrimeCycle and EasyCycle are supporting the development of recyclable and lower-impact packaging structures. ... CI flexo printing is gaining market share in India, although Pinto expects flexo and gravure to coexist rather than displace each other. Bobst currently occupies about 35% of India’s CI flexo press market, according to him. The company’s Graphic Positioning System (GPS), combined with Extended Colour Gamut technology, is designed to improve registration and color quality efficiently, while reducing material and ink consumption. Bobst introduced GPS on its CI flexo presses in 2010. Pinto recounted that the technology initially faced scepticism among customers who questioned whether a CI flexo press could produce a saleable, in-register approval sample within 15 meters. The company is also promoting its Flexo Trolley technology for solvent-based lamination. The system replaces the conventional gravure cylinder trolley with flexo technology, reducing solvent consumption by about 50% and adhesive consumption by 20%, Pinto said. The savings stem partly from the higher solid content of adhesives applied using flexo technology, with Indian customers who have adopted the system seeing these savings. Bobst showcased its Multi-Coater laminator, which combines solvent-based gravure, solvent-less, flexo trolley and water-based lamination technologies on one platform. Pinto said the flexibility allows new converters to begin with a basic configuration, and subsequently expand to other lamination technologies. ... Automation is another major area of development. Bobst’s Master 6003 gravure press is designed to enable remote job loading, while reducing manual intervention on the shop floor. Pinto said the operator’s main manual task is changing print cylinders, while ink handling is automated across the fixed set of seven inks using Extended Colour Gamut technology. He explained that limiting production to a seven-ink system can also reduce the requirement for the much larger ink palettes typically used in conventional printing. Bobst is simultaneously expanding its presence in labels through narrow-web machines using UV flexo and UV inks. The technology can process labels, films, paper and board, allowing converters to use one platform across multiple applications. The company’s digital printing can be integrated with flexo printing to give converters a modular or hybrid combination of digital and conventional production. Pinto said the combination of growing domestic consumption, increasing exports, and rapid technological change is creating significant opportunities for Indian flexible packaging converters and for equipment suppliers. Bobst India is keen to provide end-to-end solutions by understanding market needs and their customers’ constraints and pain points.

summary_text: Parason Machinery, a domestic paper machinery manufacturer, is stepping up efforts to minimise India’s dependence on imported paper machines, positioning itself as a key supplier for mills looking to expand or upgrade capacity without relying on foreign equipment. The push comes as India’s paper industry faces structural pressure from rising imports and shifting demand toward packaging-grade paper. India’s paper mills currently import a significant volume of specialised machinery for producing higher-grade writing, printing, and packaging paper, a dependence that raises capital costs and lengthens project timelines for domestic producers. Parason’s expanded manufacturing push aims to offer Indian mills locally built alternatives that can be installed faster and serviced without the delays typical of imported equipment. ... Indian paper mills importing over 30,000 tonnes of finished paper per month, more than 20% of total domestic demand according to the Indian Paper Manufacturers Association, reflects capacity constraints that stem partly from the cost and lead time of importing production machinery. Domestic machinery manufacturing addresses this bottleneck directly, letting mills add capacity in the packaging and kraft paper segments, where demand is currently the industry’s fastest-growing category, without the multi-year wait times associated with importing full paper machine lines from Europe or China. ... India’s paper industry is undergoing a visible shift from writing and printing paper toward packaging-dominated demand, with containerboard, cartonboard, kraft paper, and specialty papers now accounting for a growing share of production and investment. Domestically manufactured machinery tailored to these packaging grades could help Indian mills respond faster to demand shifts than they could relying on imported machine lines built primarily for legacy writing and printing paper production. ... Industry commentary from the Indian Paper Manufacturers Association has flagged that imports from China alone surged 28% to 143,000 tonnes during April-June, consolidating China’s position as India’s largest paper import source. Domestic machinery suppliers like Parason argue that building local manufacturing capability is now urgent, not just to reduce machine import costs but to help Indian paper producers compete on finished-product volumes against cheaper Chinese imports flooding the domestic market. ... Parason is expected to expand its domestic machine production lines further as mills plan capacity additions in the kraft and packaging paper segments, where consumption is projected to grow 6-7% annually, reaching around 30 million tonnes by FY 2026-27. Industry watchers will be tracking whether reduced machinery import dependence translates into faster capacity additions across India’s mid-sized paper mills over the next fiscal year. ... Reducing machinery imports cuts capital costs and installation timelines for Indian paper mills, letting them expand packaging and kraft paper capacity faster to meet fast-growing domestic demand. ... headline: HONCO Machinery Delivers HFQB Slitter Rewinder to Thailand, Strengthening Southeast Asian Presence - Hongke Machinery
summary_text: September 2026 — HONCO Machinery (Hongke Machinery) has successfully delivered an HFQB series slitter rewinder to a customer in Thailand, marking another milestone in the company's expanding footprint across Southeast Asia. The HFQB surface winding slitter rewinder is specifically engineered for applications requiring narrow-width finished rolls, with the ability to slit materials down to 7-10mm widths while maintaining smooth cutting edges and consistent quality. The machine adopts a surface winding structure that ensures precise tension control during narrow-width slitting operations—a critical feature for materials like cigarette paper, baking paper (14gsm), and other lightweight papers that demand exceptional slit quality. Equipped with a Germany Siemens PLC control system and intuitive touch screen interface, the HFQB series delivers multi-function operation including automatic meter stop and tension auto control. The machine is designed for high-speed, intelligent surface winding slitting, making it an ideal solution for paper converting operations that require both efficiency and precision. The HFQB series is part of HONCO's comprehensive slitter rewinder product line, which includes the HFQA series for economical paper slitting, the HFQC series with differential shaft for high-speed applications, and the HFQD series for ultra-high-speed drum-type slitting. The HFQB series accommodates a wide range of materials including 20-500gsm paper (kraft paper, art paper, silicon paper, coated paper, newsprint paper), sticky labels (adhesive paper), various laminates, films with thickness down to 10 microns, and nonwoven materials. The surface-winding structure is particularly well-suited for applications involving larger or heavier finished rolls, delivering excellent roll-build stability and consistent roll hardness. The machine's robust construction features a shaftless unwind system that handles heavy jumbo rolls with ease. The slitting system is designed for precision edge quality, making it suitable for both standard paper grades and more challenging materials like adhesive labels and silicone-coated liners. Honco's three-motor design, standard across the HFQC series and available in select HFQB configurations, enables synchronous control of traction and duplex rewind for consistent web tension and high-quality finished rolls. Prior to shipment, the HFQB slitter rewinder underwent rigorous testing and quality validation to ensure reliable performance and operational stability, including real-material testing to verify slit quality and tension control across the machine's full operating range. The equipment was dispatched in September 2026, ready to support the Thai customer's paper converting and packaging operations. HONCO Machinery, established in Wenzhou, Zhejiang Province, specializes in the production of roll-to-roll slitting machinery and roll-to-sheet cutting machinery for the paper converting, printing, and packaging industries. With over 20 years of experience, CE certification, and exports to 100+ countries and regions with over 1,000 machines installed worldwide, HONCO continues to strengthen its presence in Southeast Asia and beyond.
