headline: Echaar targets short-run opportunity with Flexocompact CI flexo - THE PACKMAN
summary_text: The economics of flexible packaging are changing, particularly at the shorter end of the run-length spectrum. For converters handling short and ultra-short production runs – in some cases as low as around 50 kg – a conventional wide-web press can be more machine than the job actually requires. It is this space that Echaar is targeting with its new Flexocompact Series, a mid- and narrow-web CI flexo press designed for shorter and more diverse production runs. Kirti Panchal, managing director, Echaar Equipments, says the machine has emerged from a requirement the company was already seeing in the market. “Nowadays there are many converters who require ultra-short runs, sometimes even around 50 kg. For such requirements, we believe this can be a better and more economical solution,” he said. The proposition is not limited to flexible packaging converters. The CI configuration gives label converters an opportunity to move into flexible packaging using a press that can address both applications. Panchal also sees potential among rotogravure converters looking to introduce flexo into their production mix. Echaar is offering the Flexocompact Series in both gearless and geared versions – Flexocompact HR 300 GL and Flexocompact HR 200 GD – with print widths of 700 and 880 mm and repeat ranges from 240/280 mm to 650 mm, depending on the configuration. The presses are available in 4, 6 and 8-color configurations. The shorter repeat is significant for short-run work, where plate and cylinder costs can quickly affect job economics. “Minimum repeat also plays a vital role in saving a lot of cost for these plates and cylinders,” Panchal said. Beyond the shorter repeat, the compact web width and machine configuration are aimed at improving the overall economics of short-run production by reducing substrate wastage and optimizing plate and sleeve/cylinder costs, ink and energy consumption, changeover requirements and machine utilization. The new machine adds a mid- and narrow-web option to a portfolio that has so far been largely focused on wide-web CI flexo. Echaar has been building CI flexo presses since 2020, with its current machines covering web widths from 1 to 2 meters and including the Flexo Master, Flexo Delight and Flexo Smart series. Interestingly, CI flexo was not a later addition to the company’s portfolio. “We started with CI only,” Panchal said. The company’s initial three years were spent in technology transfer, followed by the first machine built in 2020. Since then, Echaar has installed eight CI flexo presses, along with two stack presses and one laminator. The installed machines are being used across a fairly broad mix of applications. Flexible packaging laminates account for several installations, while others are producing hygiene products, milk packaging and paper. The presses have also been used for both breathable and non-breathable films, with solutions running at speeds of up to 500 meters per minute. For a machine manufacturer competing in a market that includes both established international suppliers and a growing number of Indian manufacturers, Panchal does not see the expanding competitive landscape as a concern. In fact, he welcomes it. “If you say that some more manufacturers are also coming, I welcome them. The reason I tell you, there is a huge market. India is a huge nation,” he said. His larger point is that India’s machinery industry has already demonstrated its ability to develop sophisticated printing equipment, particularly in rotogravure. He expects a similar evolution in CI flexo, although he acknowledges that the technology demands considerable manufacturing capability and precision. Panchal believes that India has the engineering and manufacturing capability to emerge as an important global source for CI flexo technology. That emphasis on manufacturing also extends to Echaar’s approach to servicing its machines. The company says it manufactures its machines completely in-house and is now also manufacturing the critical CI central impression drums internally. Its service team has been built over the past nine years, while export markets are being supported through dealers expected to provide both sales and service. In the near term, the company appears to be seeing enough demand to continue expanding production. Echaar is currently building five more machines, with another three orders under finalization. For Echaar, the Flexocompact is therefore not simply a smaller version of its existing CI platforms, but an extension of its CI flexo portfolio into a new segment of converters and applications. The company now offers different CI platforms – Flexomaster, Flexodelight, Flexosmart and Flexocompact – addressing different production speeds, web widths, run lengths and application requirements. For Panchal, the direction is clear – the CI flexo opportunity is no longer confined to large-volume flexible packaging. As converters deal with smaller jobs and increasingly varied applications, a more compact CI platform could give flexo a wider role in the production mix.

headline: Innovation push needed for circular flexible packaging - Ester CEO
summary_text: India’s flexible packaging industry needs to move beyond incremental recycling improvements and accelerate investment in technologies that can deliver genuine circularity, Vaibhav Jha, CEO of Ester Industries, said at the 13th Speciality Films & Flexible Packaging Global Summit & Exhibition 2026 in Mumbai. ... Tougher regulations and changing consumer preferences were accelerating the sustainability transition, he said. Citing a McKinsey report, Jha said 40% to 85% of consumers surveyed across markets seek sustainable solutions and are willing to pay a premium. ... Jha linked sustainability to manufacturing sovereignty, arguing geopolitical tensions and supply-chain disruptions made domestic resource utilization increasingly important. ... Jha said the flexible packaging sector had made significant progress in mechanical recycling but now needed to focus on technologies capable of delivering true circularity, particularly in food-contact applications. “ We have done great work in developing technologies to take recycling forward. So much of mechanical recycling is happening. But what is the next big thing?” he said. “ That is why my intention as a group is that now is the time to push the envelope on technology and innovation to really aim for food circularity.” He said brand owners and manufacturers would need to support emerging technologies before they reached commercial scale, pointing to textile and automotive recycling as examples. “ The recycling breakthroughs needed commercial commitments before the certainty arrived in ... technology,” he said. ... Jha highlighted Ester’s work on RPE (recycled polyethylene) and PCR technologies, saying tougher recycled-content mandates would make reliance on mass-balance solutions increasingly difficult. Ester has vertically integrated its RPE technology and developed a patented process to make RPE suitable for PCR film production. “ We are very proud to say that now we are running around 20,000 tons of RPE capacity directed toward film and we are ready to serve the industry,” Jha said. He highlighted Ester’s ability to produce films containing up to 90% actual PCR content rather than relying on mass balance. The company has developed a patented monomaterial PET technology that can enable thinner films and provide a cost advantage over competing solutions. ... Ester is investing more than Rs1,000 crore in a 70,000-ton-per-year chemical recycling facility in Gujarat. The plant will process polyester-heavy laminates and convert them into virgin-like monomers for recycled PET production. Jha said the technology had been proven at a smaller production unit in Canada and that the Gujarat facility was expected to take around 18 months to become operational. Major brands have already signed commercial offtake agreements, he said. “ Nike has signed up. Another leading global brand has signed up a very large contract. And then there is Staroplast,” Jha said. He urged flexible packaging companies to support the technology and help accelerate its commercialization. Jha said sustainable materials currently carry a premium because technologies are still being scaled, but said the eventual impact on consumers would be limited. “ Innovation is a necessity now for achieving meaningful sustainability goals for all of us,” he said.

headline: Kapoor Industries Expands Biancalani AIRO®24 Fleet to Eight Machines
summary_text: The Indian terry product manufacturer’s repeat investment highlights the role of finishing performance and local technical support in building long-term machinery partnerships. Kapoor Industries Limited has expanded its installed base of Biancalani AIRO®24 finishing machines to eight units across its manufacturing facilities in India. The repeat investment represents a significant milestone for Italian textile machinery manufacturer Biancalani and strengthens its position in the Indian textile finishing market. Kapoor Industries is one of India’s established manufacturers and exporters of premium terry products, including towels, bath mats, rugs and bathrobes. The company operates vertically integrated manufacturing facilities in Panipat and supplies international customers, primarily in the United States and Europe. As Kapoor Industries has expanded its production capacity, it has continued investing in the AIRO®24 platform to support the finishing requirements of its terry product lines. While an initial machine order can demonstrate interest in a particular technology, repeated investment provides a stronger indication of its performance under industrial production conditions. The presence of eight AIRO®24 machines suggests that the technology has delivered consistent results across multiple stages of Kapoor Industries’ expansion. ... Biancalani’s AIRO®24 is designed for continuous, open-width tumble drying, softening and finishing of woven, knitted and nonwoven fabrics. The system uses controlled high-speed airflow to move fabric alternately through a treatment channel and against specially designed stainless-steel grids. This mechanical action can improve fabric softness, volume, drape and dimensional stability. For terry towels, the process is intended to straighten and open the loops while increasing softness and bulk, important quality characteristics for premium bath textiles. Depending on the fabric and required final effect, the machine can also provide mechanical softening with reduced reliance on chemical softeners. According to Biancalani, AIRO®24 can operate at fabric treatment speeds of up to 2,800 meters per minute and provide evaporation capacity of up to 1,400 kilograms per hour, depending on its configuration and operating conditions. The platform is available in Single, Duetto, Tandem and Triplex versions, allowing manufacturers to select a configuration based on production capacity and application requirements. ... Kapoor Industries’ eight-machine installation is particularly relevant because it reflects investment decisions made after extended experience with the technology. Textile finishing machinery must deliver consistent performance beyond installation and commissioning. Factors including output quality, productivity, energy use, maintenance requirements, operating costs and machine availability influence whether a manufacturer returns to the same equipment platform. By adding AIRO®24 machines as its production capabilities expanded, Kapoor Industries has demonstrated continued confidence in the technology’s ability to meet the finishing requirements of its export-oriented terry products. For Biancalani, the installation provides an important reference in a market where textile manufacturers increasingly evaluate equipment based on long-term production economics rather than purchase price alone. ... Biancalani’s development in India has also been supported by its long-standing cooperation with local representative Bakubhai Ambalal. Led by General Manager Sumit K. Chatterjee and Rais Inamdar, the organization supports Biancalani customers through machine installation, commissioning, after-sales service and technical assistance. This local infrastructure is an important part of the machinery supplier’s strategy in India. In continuous textile production, rapid access to technical support and spare parts can directly affect machine availability and factory productivity. The partnership enables Biancalani to combine its Italian engineering and textile finishing expertise with local customer support and market knowledge. For Indian manufacturers, this combination can reduce the risks associated with investing in sophisticated imported machinery, particularly when equipment is expected to operate continuously and maintain consistent export quality. ... India is one of the world’s largest textile manufacturing markets, with extensive capacity in spinning, weaving, knitting, processing, home textiles and garment production. As manufacturers modernize their facilities and target higher-value international markets, demand is increasing for finishing technologies that improve product quality, productivity, and resource efficiency. Kapoor Industries’ eight AIRO®24 machines show how strong equipment performance, combined with dependable local service, can turn an initial purchase into a long-term industrial partnership. For Biancalani, the installation provides both a major customer reference and a foundation for further expansion in India’s growing textile finishing sector.

According to Agarwal, many converters have adequate business but struggle to find skilled operators capable of running sophisticated equipment. Approximately 70% of small-molecule drug candidates exhibit poor aqueous solubility, limiting bioavailability and slowing development. Hovione addresses this persistent formulation challenge by turning poorly soluble drug ingredients into more bioavailable forms using amorphous solid dispersions through its specialised spray-drying platform. The company also draws upon more than 25 years of specialised manufacturing expertise in spray drying featuring formulation science, predictive and model-based development tools, scale-up expertise and drug product manufacturing to help customers address this challenge. The opening of the 89 Twin Rivers facility completes Hovione’s current $100 million US investment cycle and represents the first major milestone in the next phase of evolution of its integrated East Windsor, N.J., campus. Over the coming decade, Hovione’s vision is to continue growing its US operations, further strengthening the site as a next-generation pharmaceutical development and manufacturing hub. It marks the next chapter in Hovione’s legacy of more than two decades in the US,” said Marco Gil and Antonio Almeida, Co-Chief Executive Officers of Hovione. “This investment enables us to meet growing demand while further reinforcing our global leadership in pharmaceutical spray drying. Equally important, this technology sits within an integrated offering that extends from drug substance through drug product, giving customers a more direct and resilient path from early development to commercial. This is how we help them address poor solubility, one of the industry’s most persistent development challenges, and bring complex medicines to patients faster.” The East Windsor campus will continue to expand over the next five to 10 years, with plans to develop approximately 15 acres of adjacent property into a 125,000-square-foot manufacturing facility supporting additional laboratories, commercial-scale spray drying and drug product manufacturing. Customers can co-invest in this planned expansion to gain priority access to proprietary Hovione platforms, engineering know-how and accelerated capital deployment to accelerate their programmes. “89 Twin Rivers is a major step forward for Hovione’s US operations and a clear expression of our long-term commitment to East Windsor and New Jersey,” said David Basile, Vice President of Technical Operations, Americas, at Hovione. “Our growth has been built on sustained investment in scientific expertise, technological innovation, advanced manufacturing capabilities, and talented people. headline: Altria Puts $250 Million Into Kentucky Smokeless Plant - Pouch Insider
summary_text: Altria has broken ground on a $250 million, 270,000-square-foot expansion of its U.S. Smokeless Tobacco Company facility in Hopkinsville, Kentucky, a project the company says will create more than 200 local jobs. Altria Group (NYSE: MO) has broken ground on a $250 million expansion of its U.S. Smokeless Tobacco Company plant in Hopkinsville, Kentucky. The project covers 270,000 square feet and will create more than 200 local jobs, according to the weekly industry roundup published by Tobacco Insider. For a company whose earnings engine has for decades been combustible cigarettes, a quarter-billion-dollar bet on a smokeless production site is a statement about where the volume is going. Factories are the least reversible thing a consumer goods company builds. Marketing budgets can be cut in a quarter; a 270,000-square-foot manufacturing hall is a decade-long commitment to a product category. ... .S. Smokeless Tobacco Company ... Hopkinsville is an existing Altria asset, which makes ... an expansion rather than a greenfield build — faster to permit, faster to staff, and anchored to a workforce that already knows the processes. Adding 270,000 square feet to a working site is the ... -friction way to add capacity when demand ... Timing is the more interesting question. Oral nicotine — the modern pouch category as well as traditional moist snuff — has been the one part of the U.S. nicotine market adding units while cigarette stick volumes decline. Building capacity now suggests Altria expects that divergence to persist rather than flatten. ... Altria's strategic problem has been stated plainly by the company for years: it needs non-combustible revenue to grow faster than combustible revenue shrinks. The arithmetic of that transition is unforgiving, because cigarettes carry margins that oral products have historically struggled to match at scale. Capacity is one of the levers. If you cannot manufacture enough units, you cannot take share from competitors who can. ... - Capital is moving toward the growth end of the portfolio. Money spent on smokeless production lines is money not spent defending a declining cigarette franchise. - Domestic manufacturing is the chosen route. Building in Kentucky rather than importing finished goods reduces exposure to trade policy and shipping disruption, and shortens the distance between a regulatory approval and a product on shelves. - Scale is being built ahead of demand, not behind it. A project of this size takes time to come online. Altria is provisioning for a market it expects to exist several years from now. The oral nicotine category has been the most contested space in American tobacco, with pouch brands reshaping consumer habits and forcing incumbents to defend positions built on cans of moist snuff. Manufacturing depth is how incumbents fight back when they cannot out-innovate on brand alone. ... Any expansion of oral nicotine capacity in the United States sits underneath the Food and Drug Administration's premarket tobacco product application regime. Products need authorization to stay on the market legally, and the agency's decisions have repeatedly reshaped which brands can be sold and in which flavors. A manufacturer committing hundreds of millions of dollars to production lines is implicitly making a bet on the regulatory environment holding steady enough for those lines to run at usable capacity. State-level policy adds a second layer. Excise tax treatment of oral nicotine varies considerably across the country, and several states have moved to tax pouches on different bases than cigarettes. Flavor restrictions have been another live front. None of this prevents a factory from being built, but all of it affects the addressable volume that factory eventually serves. ... - Commissioning timeline. When the new square footage actually starts producing determines when the spending shows up as capacity rather than as capital expenditure drag. - Oral nicotine shipment volumes in Altria's reporting. Capacity only matters if shipments follow. A widening gap between smokeless growth and cigarette decline would validate the spend. - Further capital announcements. One project can be maintenance. A second or third at similar scale would confirm a deliberate reallocation of the capital budget away from combustibles. - FDA authorization activity. Marketing orders — or their absence — for oral nicotine products shape how much of the new capacity is legally sellable. For the pouch category generally, a domestic incumbent adding manufacturing depth is a competitive signal worth noting. The brands that have grown fastest in oral nicotine have often been supply-constrained at some point in their expansion. Altria is making sure it is not the one caught short. ... Altria broke ground on a $250 million expansion of its U.S. Smokeless Tobacco Company facility in Hopkinsville, Kentucky. The project adds 270,000 square feet of space and is expected to create more than 200 local jobs. It is an expansion of an existing site rather than a newly built standalone plant. ... U.S. cigarette stick volumes have been in structural decline, while oral nicotine products — including moist snuff and modern nicotine pouches — have been the growth end of the domestic nicotine market. Committing capital to smokeless manufacturing capacity is a way of provisioning for where volume is expected to be several years out. ... In the United States, oral nicotine products require authorization from the Food and Drug Administration under the premarket tobacco product application process to be legally marketed. State excise tax treatment and flavor restrictions vary widely and also affect addressable volume. Those factors determine how much of any new capacity can actually be sold. ... Key markers include the commissioning timeline for the new square footage, whether Altria's reported oral nicotine shipment volumes grow to fill the added capacity, whether further capital projects of similar scale are announced, and FDA authorization decisions that determine which products can be legally marketed in the US.

headline: Foreign CMOs accelerate US investments in regionalization push: GlobalData | Pharma Manufacturing
summary_text: As pharmaceutical companies continue to prioritize supply chain resilience, regional capacity, and greater control over production, foreign-headquartered contract manufacturing organizations (CMOs) are increasing their investments in the United States, according to an analysis by data and analytics firm GlobalData. Macroeconomic uncertainty is pushing the industry toward regionalization, providing a tailwind for CMOs that have global manufacturing footprints and can support these customers across geographies, GlobalData contends. At the same time, foreign contract manufacturers are responding to the growing pressure to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. “The industry is moving away from a traditional, cost-driven global outsourcing model to a more regionalized and integrated approach to manufacturing,” GlobalData said. “Expanding U.S. capacity can help companies manage tariff and geopolitical risks, while closer partnerships can streamline operations and reduce fragmentation across the manufacturing process.” Geopolitical and trade tensions are driving the regionalization of pharmaceutical manufacturing, which is impacting CMO investment in the U.S. as companies expand capacity and boost global supply chains through an in-region, for-region strategy. The threat of tariffs is pushing the move to regional redundancy and capacity distribution. GlobalData noted that recent CMO site upgrades, acquisitions, and new partnerships “signal a shift from cost-driven outsourcing toward integrated, locally anchored models, giving sponsors broader access to end-to-end capabilities while reducing exposure to geopolitical, tariff and technology-transfer risks.” ... As evidence of accelerating CMO investment in U.S. manufacturing, the firm pointed to Germany-based Evonik’s planned $100 million modernization of its Indiana drug substance site — including new reactors and other production systems — with the goal of improving equipment reliability, increasing automation, and enhancing operational efficiency. GlobalData called out Taiwan-headquartered Bora Pharmaceuticals’ $122.5 million acquisition of the GMP manufacturing operations of MacroGenics in Maryland, securing 20,000 liters of single-use bioreactor drug substance capacity. The firm also noted that South Korea’s Samsung Biologics recently completed its $280 million acquisition of a Maryland biologics site from GSK, adding 60,000 liters of drug substance capacity and establishing the company’s first manufacturing presence in the U.S. “This does not mean the end of European and Asian manufacturing,” Edita Hamzic, healthcare analyst at GlobalData, said in a statement. “Rather, companies are likely to maintain a more diversified global footprint, building capacity in the U.S. while using established overseas expertise. CMOs that can provide local manufacturing capabilities with end-to-end services may be better positioned to support sponsors as they seek greater supply chain resilience and a more efficient route to market.” A recent GlobalData analysis found that biopharmaceutical companies are increasingly moving to outsource the manufacturing of new drugs to Europe, while the gap between the use of European and U.S. facilities continues to grow. “Outsourced dose manufacturing for innovator drugs and biosimilars approved in the U.S. and Europe (the EU and UK) has traditionally oscillated between the two geographies, but there has been a pronounced shift toward European facilities over the last two years,” the firm found. In 2025, 50% of new drugs had dose manufacturing contracts with European-based facilities — almost doubling their share since 2023 — while that proportion for U.S.-based facilities has remained static at 18% since 2024, according to GlobalData. Earlier this year, the firm reported that contract manufacturing deals for drugs marketed in the U.S. are shifting to Europe, with biopharma companies increasingly choosing to outsource manufacturing to European facilities, while U.S. contract manufacturing deals for FDA-approved drugs in 2025 experienced their biggest decline in five years.

headline: The Business of Manufacturing Nicotine Pouches - Tobacco Asia
summary_text: The story has changed dramatically. Nicotine pouches have become one of the sector’s biggest magnets for capital growth, and that capital is driving a familiar set of moves: new plants, increased automation, tighter supply arrangements, and a push to bring production closer to the fastest-growing markets. ... As inputs and methods evolve, the global footprint shifts accordingly. Philip Morris International is investing an estimated US$1.2 billion in its Aurora, CO, campus, scaling up a US$600 million plan to build its largest nicotine pouch manufacturing facility and one of the largest smoke-free business bets in North America. Commercial production began in 2025. Buildout and additional capacity are scheduled to continue through 2028, as more production lines and supporting infrastructure come online. Swisher International, the producer of Rogue tobacco-free nicotine pouches and Mojo caffeine and energy pouches, pledged US$135 million to expand its Jacksonville, FL, complex as it further expands into nicotine pouches and the broader modern oral lineup. Turning Point Brands expects domestic production of its nicotine pouch brands to begin by year-end. Independent players are also moving, including Fully Loaded, which is investing in dedicated US manufacturing to support long-term growth. Outside the US, Imperial Brands is positioning Lithuania as a production base for Zone across Europe. Bangladesh has approved what is expected to be the country’s first nicotine pouch manufacturing operation. Chinese companies continue to expand their role as suppliers, not so much of finished pouches as of the machinery, production know-how, and engineering support that nicotine companies worldwide are buying. On their own, each update reads like another factory-opening story. Side by side, they look like a map being redrawn as everyone watches. “The manufacturing conversation has changed,” said Waqas Khan, c.e.o. of CLEW Pouches. “Companies aren’t simply looking for someone who can produce a pouch anymore. They’re looking for partners who can scale production, maintain consistency, meet regulatory expectations and grow with them as their brands expand.” That’s a larger shift than it first sounds. Manufacturing is no longer treated as a background requirement to be solved and then forgotten. It’s increasingly a source of competitive advantage: lowering unit costs, improving consistency, shortening supply chains, and accelerating expansion. ... Turning Point Brands’ c.f.o. Andrew Flynn tied the timing to regulation. “We’re just being mindful of the process and dedicating ourselves to the US Food and Drug Administration’s premarket tobacco product application process (PMTA) first and foremost,” Flynn said. “As we get positive visibility there, we’ll be able to move quickly.” ... are designed to support automation, export logistics, quality assurance, and scalability. That shift raises expectations across the board. Brand owners want precise dosing, consistent pouch weights, stable flavor profiles, and repeatable moisture control across millions of units. Inspection systems now monitor quality at speeds no manual process can match. Packaging lines are becoming as much about traceability as about speed, as tracking requirements are increasingly embedded in regulatory systems worldwide. For contract manufacturers, that evolution shifts the entire sales pitch. ... No market illustrates that change more clearly than the United States. Nicotine pouch demand has risen quickly in recent years, prompting companies to shift to local production rather than relying primarily on imports from Europe. PMI’s Aurora expansion aligns with that approach. It’s intended to become PMI’s largest pouch site, shorten the supply chain, improve responsiveness, and place production near one of the world’s fastest-growing nicotine pouch markets. Smaller companies are moving in the same direction. Turning Point Brands is preparing to launch domestic manufacturing after building its FRĒ and ALP brands largely through outsourced production. “We remain on track to launch US manufacturing by the end of the year,” Purdy said. The investment isn’t only about increasing output. “Over time, we expect domestic manufacturing to significantly reduce our cost of goods sold,” Purdy told analysts, adding that the facility could eventually support gross margins approaching 70%. Another pattern emerges alongside these plans: regulation. Companies are weighing locations not only for labor pools or incentives but also for how efficiently a site can comply with evolving rules, support market authorization, and adapt to market changes. FDA’s nicotine pouch pilot program, which has increased the number of authorized products and shortened review time-lines, has given firms greater confidence that domestic production investments can be supported by clearer pathways to market. Europe tends to operate differently. Rather than building separate plants for each country, companies are relying on centralized hubs to supply multiple markets simultaneously. Policy uncertainty, import price competition and shortages of skilled workers are limiting the pace of reshoring, however, according to the 2026 USA Reshoring Survey from the Reshoring Initiative® and Regions Recruiting®. The second annual study surveyed 249 manufacturers—118 original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and 131 contract manufacturers (CMs). It found stronger reshoring activity among OEMs, a growing pipeline of reshoring opportunities for domestic suppliers and substantial planned U.S. investment. 2026 USA Reshoring Survey Report. Key findings • 36% of OEMs had reshored or were actively engaged in additional reshoring in 2026, up from 29% in 2025. • 32% of CMs were currently quoting reshoring projects—double the 16% reported in 2025—and 79% said at least some customers had discussed reshoring in the prior year. • 63% of OEMs planned U.S. capital expenditures in 2026 or 2027 to support reshoring or other domestic expansion. • 57% of OEMs named policy uncertainty as their primary challenge in the current U.S. trade-policy environment. Market pricing impact was a distant second at 15%. Geopolitical risk is also becoming a stronger driver. Among CMs, 53% cited geopolitical risk as a reason customers are reshoring to domestic suppliers, up from 24% in 2025. Sixty percent said customers importing from China or Taiwan were at least discussing de-risking, although only 19% reported active transitions. "Manufacturers can adjust to known costs and opportunities. What is much harder to manage is a moving target. The survey shows that reshoring interest and investment are there, but companies need greater predictability to commit capital and develop supply chains for the long term." — Harry Moser, Founder and President, Reshoring Initiative Reshoring is delivering operational benefits beyond tariff and geopolitical risk reduction. The two companies behind ZYN and on! — the largest U.S. nicotine pouch brands — have signed a contract manufacturing deal for cigarettes. It lets U.S. tobacco companies exporting products outside the U.S. claw back federal excise taxes paid on domestically sold products. Altria, which does not sell cigarettes outside the U.S., has been boosting similar partnerships to take advantage of the rebate. headline: Trench Group Opens First HSP Manufacturing Facility in U.S. to Support America's Grid Expansion | Financial Post
summary_text: HSP US celebrates the official opening of its first U.S. manufacturing facility in Charlotte, a $60 million investment in high-voltage transformer bushings for North American power-grid modernization. Business Wire State of the art $60-million manufacturing facility in Charlotte, NC, is expected to become the first domestic producer of high-voltage transformer bushings up to 765 kV, will create up to 140 jobs, and strengthen domestic supply for critical power infrastructure. CHARLOTTE, N.C. — HSP US, a Trench Group company, today announced the official opening of its first U.S. manufacturing facility in Charlotte, a milestone representing a more than $60 million investment in domestic production of 25kV to 765kV high-voltage transformer bushings critical in North American power-grid modernization initiatives. The new 170,000-square-foot HSP facility will create up to 140 manufacturing and engineering jobs in Charlotte through 2030 – nearly twice what was originally planned. There is room to more than double production capacity from the initially planned 3,500 to 10,000 bushings per year, reflecting Trench Group’s commitment to the growing North American market. Built and operational in only one and a half years, the plant brings proven HSP’s dry-type bushing technology closer to North American customers as utilities, transformer manufacturers and large energy users respond to aging grid infrastructure and growing power needs from data centers, industrial expansion and electrification in the transportation sector. ... The HSP opening arrives as the United States enters a new era of unprecedented electricity demand, with a 2026 NEMA Study projecting power demand growth exceeding 55% by 2050. To keep up, investor-owned utilities relied on by most Americans will invest $1.4 trillion by 2030 in strengthening the U.S. power grid, the Edison Electric Institute projects. Building on Trench Group’s longtime presence in Canada, where it operates two factories, the new Charlotte facility reflects rapidly growing demand across North America, which accounted for around 50% of the company’s total order intake in the first half of 2026. Since 2024 the order intake in the North American market increased by almost 400%. As utilities plan larger, more efficient transmission corridors, high-voltage 765 kV infrastructure is emerging as future U.S. grid backbone and important solution for moving larger amounts of power over long distances, while offering reduced line losses and greater support for fast-growing load centers. Recently, the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) enlisted Trench Group to support the state’s first-ever 765kV transmission-line deployment. “As America builds out its 765kV transmission backbone, these projects require proven technology, deep engineering expertise and a partner that understands the complexity of extra-high-voltage transmission,” said Jason Neal, President Hyosung HICO, Senior Executive VP HICO America. “Having a supply partner like HSP manufacturing here on U.S. soil is a real advantage, shorter lead times, a stronger supply chain, and a more reliable grid. HSP’s investment is exactly the kind of commitment our grid needs, and we’re proud to build alongside them.” ... The Charlotte facility is one of the most advanced high-voltage bushing factories in the United States, featuring vertical integration, state-of-the art autoclaves and lathe machines, and full-scale production capabilities for manufacturing dry-type transformer bushings, including resin-impregnated paper (RIP) and resin-impregnated synthetic (RIS) technologies, from 25 kV up to 765 kV. The HSP plant also supports future demand-driven expansion into high-voltage direct current, or HVDC, applications. In addition, the facility houses two high-voltage testing laboratories, with capacity to test bushings up to 2,800kV – one of the biggest and most powerful test fields in North America, giving customers access to domestic testing capabilities for some of the most demanding transmission environments. “Charlotte gives HSP US the talent, scale and proximity to serve the market players reshaping North America’s power infrastructure,” said Nils von Dietman, CEO of HSP US. “With agreements in place with leading transformer OEMs and hyperscalers, we are ready to help our customers accelerate grid modernization, support AI-driven power demand and deliver long-term energy reliability with local expertise, shorter supply lines and closer technical collaboration.” The HSP bushings manufactured in Charlotte also play an important role in Trench Group’s global 765 kV solutions portfolio, which brings together key high-voltage technologies – including bushings, instrument transformers, coils and reactors – to help reduce interface risk and support reliable performance across complex extra-high-voltage systems. With assembly operations already underway, Trench Group expects first deliveries by the end of 2026. Once fully operational, the plant is poised to initially produce up to 3,500 HSP bushings per year. ... Designed for Build America, Buy America (BABA) certification, the Charlotte facility is expected to become the first domestic producer of dry-type bushings at that voltage level, adding a domestic sourcing option for customers, including those with projects subject to domestic-content requirements. ... As the company lays down roots in the region, HSP will also invest in STEM and workforce development programs that offer career pathways while building the skills needed to support long-term grid modernization. Currently, it is partnering with Central Piedmont Community College on an apprenticeship program that combines classroom instruction with hands-on training at the Charlotte facility. ... HSP US, a Trench Group company, manufactures high-voltage transformer bushings for the North American market. The company’s Charlotte, N.C., facility is Trench Group’s first U.S.-based manufacturing plant and is designed to produce advanced dry-type bushings for applications ranging from distribution and transmission systems to extra-high-voltage grid infrastructure. Trench Group is a global technology leader for high-voltage grid components and systems, present in nearly every power transmission grid worldwide. Headquartered in Berlin, with more than 100 years of engineering expertise, Trench Group designs and manufactures high-voltage components that address the core challenges of modern power infrastructure – connecting grids, measuring their performance and ensuring reliability. As electricity demand rises and power grids transform worldwide, Trench Group is a key enabler of the infrastructure the world needs, with a portfolio that includes bushings, cable terminations, instrument transformers, coils and reactors. Since its independence in April 2024, Trench Group has doubled its annual revenue to more than $1.1 billion. The company operates 11 factories across 8 countries on 4 continents, employs more than 3,000 people – with plans to grow to 4,000 by 2030.

headline: America’s Semiconductor Packaging Boom Is Reshaping Domestic Supply Chains – USA Business Times
summary_text: Now, amid record federal investment, renewed geopolitical urgency, and an artificial intelligence boom that is straining global chip supply at every link, the United States is engineering a dramatic reversal. A wave of advanced semiconductor packaging facilities is rising across Arizona, Ohio, Texas, and New York, backed by a combination of CHIPS Act funding, Pentagon contracts, and private capital that industry analysts say could exceed $85 billion in committed investment by the end of 2027. ... For the AI era, this matters enormously. Nvidia’s H100 and its successors, AMD’s MI400 series, and custom silicon from Amazon Web Services and Google all depend on sophisticated packaging to deliver the memory bandwidth and compute density that large language models demand. Without domestic packaging capacity, even chips fabricated at TSMC’s new Arizona fabs would still need to leave the country for final assembly — a vulnerability that Pentagon planners and Commerce Department officials have flagged as unacceptable. ... The roster of companies committing capital to domestic packaging reads like a who’s-who of the global semiconductor industry, with American firms joined by foreign manufacturers eager to capture CHIPS Act incentives and long-term government contracts. Intel remains the most aggressive domestic player. The company’s Chandler, Arizona campus, already home to wafer fabrication, is being expanded to include a dedicated advanced packaging facility the company calls its Integrated Foundry Operations hub. Intel executives say the site will eventually employ more than 3,000 packaging engineers and technicians, with full operational ramp targeted for late 2027. Amkor Technology, the Arizona-headquartered packaging and test specialist, broke ground in Peoria, Arizona in 2024 on what it describes as the largest advanced packaging facility ever built on American soil. The $2 billion plant, partially funded through a $400 million CHIPS Act direct funding award, is expected to reach full capacity by mid-2027 and count Apple and Nvidia among its anchor customers. Meanwhile, Micron Technology is integrating advanced packaging directly into its $100 billion investment plan for its Syracuse, New York fab complex, betting that co-locating fabrication and packaging on a single campus will yield supply chain advantages that offshore competitors cannot match. ... The 2022 CHIPS and Science Act allocated $52.7 billion for domestic semiconductor manufacturing and research, with a significant portion earmarked specifically for back-end manufacturing processes including packaging, assembly, and test — areas that had historically been overlooked in U.S. industrial policy in favor of flashier wafer fabrication investments. As of June 2026, the Commerce Department’s CHIPS Program Office has finalized or preliminarily agreed to more than $34 billion in direct funding awards, with packaging and back-end manufacturing accounting for roughly $6 billion of that total — a share that industry advocates say is still too small but represents a meaningful shift in federal priorities. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has made semiconductor self-sufficiency a signature issue, signaled in May that the administration is preparing a second round of CHIPS-adjacent incentives focused specifically on packaging and advanced substrate manufacturing, two areas where U.S. dependence on Asian suppliers remains acute. On Capitol Hill, the Senate Commerce Committee advanced the Domestic Semiconductor Packaging Investment Act in April, a bipartisan bill that would create an additional $8 billion in tax credits specifically for companies building packaging capacity in economically distressed American communities. The bill’s lead sponsors, Senator Mark Warner of Virginia and Senator John Cornyn of Texas, argue that packaging jobs — which tend to be high-skill, high-wage positions requiring specialized training — are precisely the kind of manufacturing employment that should anchor regional economies. ... Advanced semiconductor packaging requires a category of worker that barely exists in the United States in meaningful numbers: technicians and engineers trained in photolithography, die bonding, flip-chip assembly, and thermal management at the nanoscale. Unlike traditional manufacturing roles, these positions typically require two to four years of specialized post-secondary training, and the pipeline of qualified candidates is thin. Community colleges in Arizona, Ohio, and New York are scrambling to build curriculum in partnership with chipmakers, with mixed results. Maricopa County Community College District, which serves the greater Phoenix area, launched a Semiconductor Manufacturing Technician certificate program in 2024 that has enrolled nearly 1,200 students — but industry recruiters say the program is producing graduates faster than it is producing graduates who are fully job-ready for the most demanding packaging roles. Intel and Amkor have both invested in paid apprenticeship programs designed to bridge the gap, and the Biden-era Good Jobs Initiative — continued under the current administration with modified branding — has channeled Department of Labor workforce grants to semiconductor training programs in eight states. ... If economic logic and federal incentives are the engines of America’s packaging buildout, geopolitical anxiety is the accelerant. The Taiwan Strait remains one of the world’s most consequential flashpoints, and the concentration of global advanced packaging capacity in Taiwan — where companies like ASE Technology Group and TSMC’s own packaging operations handle a disproportionate share of the world’s most critical chip finishing work — has become a source of acute concern for defense planners and corporate risk officers alike. A 2025 RAND Corporation study commissioned by the Department of Defense found that even a temporary disruption to Taiwan’s semiconductor packaging capacity — caused by conflict, natural disaster, or economic coercion — could reduce U.S. military electronics ... That finding has given new urgency to the Pentagon’s own investments in domestic packaging. The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s Electronics Resurgence Initiative has funded packaging research at SkyWater Technology and several university labs, while the Department of Defense’s Microelectronics Commons program — a network of domestic chip research hubs — has explicitly prioritized packaging innovation as a gap-fill strategy. For corporate supply chain executives, the calculus has shifted decisively. Surveys conducted by the Semiconductor Industry Association in early 2026 found that 73 percent of American electronics manufacturers are actively working to reduce their dependence on offshore packaging suppliers, up from 41 percent in 2023. Cost remains a concern — domestic packaging typically runs 15 to 25 percent more expensive than Asian alternatives when fully loaded — but supply chain resilience, customer pressure, and government contract requirements are increasingly overriding pure cost optimization. ... The semiconductor packaging surge is not occurring in isolation. It is catalyzing a broader industrial ecosystem — in substrates, specialty chemicals, precision equipment, and logistics — that is beginning to take root alongside the chip facilities themselves. Arizona has seen more than forty supplier companies open or expand operations in the Phoenix metropolitan area since 2023, drawn by the gravitational pull of Intel’s and TSMC’s fab investments and now Amkor’s packaging campus. Ohio’s Columbus region is experiencing a similar effect around Intel’s planned fab complex in New Albany. Industry economists estimate that each advanced semiconductor manufacturing job supports between four and seven additional jobs in the surrounding regional economy.

summary_text: Specialty Program Group has acquired HCM Unlocked, a technology-enabled managed services provider specialising in human capital management, adding leave-of-absence management, payroll, HR, benefits administration and compliance capability to SPG's employee benefits platform at the moment when the US paid family and medical leave landscape has reached its most complex point to date. HCM Unlocked, founded in 2018 and led by CEO John Wallace, serves mid-market and enterprise clients on HR technology vendor selection, implementation and ongoing management. Its proprietary DELTA platform is an AI-enabled data validation tool built to support accuracy across payroll, time and attendance, HR and benefits systems, operating across multiple technology vendors rather than a single software platform. The company's approximately 200 employees will join SPG following the acquisition, which was announced Thursday. Terms were not disclosed. HCM Unlocked will continue to operate under its current name. ... Thirteen states and Washington DC have now enacted paid family and medical leave programmes providing partially wage-replaced leave, according to analysis by law firm Katz, Marshall and Banks: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Washington, Maine and Maryland. Maine's programme launches in May 2026 and Maryland's in 2028. Several of those programmes took effect or expanded this year. Delaware's Healthy Delaware Families Act made benefits available from January 1, 2026, requiring most employers with ten or more employees to participate. Minnesota's paid leave programme also took effect in January 2026, and Colorado's Family and Medical Leave Insurance Programme was expanded from the same date. The practical compliance challenge for mid-market employers operating across multiple states is not any single programme in isolation. It is the combination: programme details vary substantially by jurisdiction across employer size thresholds, funding mechanisms, job-protection provisions and notice requirements, and employers must monitor and respond to state-specific changes on different timelines throughout the year. For a human resources team without dedicated leave administration support, that is a genuine operational burden. For benefits brokers advising mid-market employers, the compliance gap has become a live renewal conversation. An employer that added employees in Delaware or Minnesota in 2025 may not have adjusted their leave administration systems to reflect the new obligations. An employer in five states faces five different sets of rules. The capability HCM Unlocked brings to SPG is directly relevant to the clients where that problem is most acute. ... HCM Unlocked's DELTA platform is built for employers running multiple HR and benefits technology vendors rather than a single integrated system, a configuration common across mid-market companies that have added software incrementally rather than through a planned architecture. DELTA validates data accuracy across those systems in payroll, time and attendance, HR and benefits, without requiring clients to consolidate onto a single platform. Wallace said HCM Unlocked was built to take ownership of payroll, HR, benefits, compliance and technology as a single body of work rather than as separate challenges, and that joining SPG would provide additional resources while the company continues to serve its existing clients and teams. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed. HCM Unlocked's approximately 200 employees will join SPG and the business will continue to operate under its existing name.

summary_text: Sep 11, 2026 July renewals removed any doubt: The employer stop-loss market has hardened. Medical costs are accelerating. High-dollar claims are becoming more frequent and severe. After several years of unsustainable results, stop-loss carriers are correcting through higher rates, more conservative underwriting and tighter contract terms. The pressure is real. But the answer is not a one-size-fits-all funding strategy. Employers need stronger protection from volatility - and the flexibility to address the cost drivers unique to their health plan. ... According to HM Insurance Group, the stop-loss market recorded a 91% loss ratio in 2025, contributing to rate increases exceeding 20% across the broader market. While first-dollar medical trend may moderate in 2027, leveraged stop-loss trend is expected to remain elevated. The July market reflected that reality: significant price increases, fewer competitive alternatives and greater carrier scrutiny. Traditional renewal shopping produced fewer meaningful options. ... PwC projects commercial medical cost trend will reach 9% in 2027 - the highest level in 17 years. AI is creating a new imbalance: 70% of health plans rank provider tools that capture more revenue as a top-three cost inflator, while WTW found that only 20% of employers have operationalized AI within their benefits programs. Providers are moving faster to optimize reimbursement than employers are to use AI for analytics, claims monitoring and cost control. Hospital costs are also consequential. KFF found that prices paid by private insurers for hospital care increased 30% from April 2019 to April 2026, compared with a 21% increase in Medicare rates. Meanwhile, pharmaceutical and clinical advances are improving outcomes while introducing new multimillion-dollar exposures. These forces are reshaping catastrophic claims. HM reported a 56% increase from 2024 to 2025 in projected per-employee costs for claims exceeding $500,000. The frequency of million-dollar claims increased 50%, while their severity rose 72%. This is the reality employers are carrying into the 1/1 renewal season: The cost of care is rising, and the cost of transferring that risk is rising with it. ### Risk Is Rising. Rigidity Is the Greater Threat. ... There is no single right way to self-fund. Employers need a structure aligned with their workforce, financial tolerance and regional healthcare ecosystem. Every health plan contains three distinct components: access, financial protection and management of claims below stop-loss. Separating them gives employers greater visibility and advisors more freedom to select the right carriers, administrators, networks and cost-management partners. Self-funding does not solve healthcare costs. It creates the platform to manage them—if the employer’s risk is protected appropriately. ### Predictability Starts With Defined Exposure Risk should come first. Employers need realistic aggregate protection, clearly defined maximum exposure and contract provisions that endure beyond one favorable year. Saving on protection can become extraordinarily expensive if it introduces new lasers, excessive corridors, shared liability or renewal uncertainty. This is where VERIS, the independent national consortium model, delivers greater stability. As the broader market experienced significant stop-loss pressure during July renewals, the VERIS block remained comparatively insulated. That outcome reflects disciplined actuarial underwriting, diversified purchasing power, long-term carrier alignment and complete employer protection - including guaranteed renewability, no new lasers at renewal and rate caps. The Pay at Max funding approach adds another layer of budget stability. Employers fund to a defined maximum monthly amount instead of absorbing unpredictable claims fluctuations throughout the year. When claims perform favorably, 100% of available surplus belongs to the employer. The result is defined exposure on the front end without giving up the upside of self- ... ### Financing Creates the Platform - Not the Entire Strategy An independent consortium must remain flexible enough to support each market. That means helping employers evaluate the right carrier, TPA, network, pharmacy strategy and cost-containment partners - not dictating a limited set of solutions. It also means using claims data to identify the interventions that matter: network efficiency, facility steerage, plan design, pharmacy management, clinical navigation and focused support for the conditions driving each population’s costs. Advisors, administrators, carriers and risk partners all have a role. There is no fight to win - only a shared responsibility to do what is right for each employer. The goal is to help more employers simply and safely self-fund: protecting capital today while creating the visibility and flexibility to improve healthcare outcomes over time. In this market, the strongest renewal strategy will not be measured by the lowest initial price, but by the stability it delivers across renewal cycles.

headline: Understanding Maryland’s FAMLI Program: What Employers and Attorneys Need to Know | Maryland State Bar Association
summary_text: The clock is ticking for employers to get ready for the implementation of the Maryland Department of Labor’s (MD DOL) Family and Medical Leave Insurance (FAMLI) program. Enacted via the Time to Care Act (TTCA), the FAMLI program introduces significant changes to employee leave options. While benefit payouts do not begin until January 2028, critical operational milestones, including mandatory state registration, Declaration of Intent (DOI) filings for private plans, and mandatory employer contributions, take effect throughout late 2026 and early 2027. Therefore, employers and attorney advisers need to understand how the new requirements work, how funding functions, and what steps must be taken to remain compliant. ... FAMLI is a state-mandated program that provides eligible Maryland workers up to 12 weeks of paid leave per year. Starting in January 2028, workers can receive up to $1,000 per week to take time away from work to welcome a new child, care for a family member with a serious health condition, manage family needs related to deployment, or tend to a serious health condition. Employers with at least one employee located in Maryland will be required to provide paid family and medical leave. For employees, eligibility does not depend on working for a single employer for years. Instead, any worker who logs at least 680 hours in Maryland across the four most recent calendar quarters prior to taking leave qualifies. This standard includes part-time and seasonal staff. Coverage is tied to work physically performed in Maryland rather than an employee’s residence or company headquarters. ... The total length of leave an employee receives is generally capped at 12 weeks per application year, though the actual duration is determined by comparing 12 weeks against the worker’s remaining balance, their specific request, and the supporting paperwork. Employees must submit proper documentation with their claims. Medical leave requires certification from a licensed health care provider outlining the condition or the expected duration of care. Bonding leave requires birth, adoption, or foster records, while military leave requires proof of relationship and official active-duty orders. ... To finance these benefits, the program uses a contribution rate of 0.90% of wages, up to the Social Security wage cap. For employers with 15 or more workers, this cost is split evenly, meaning the employer pays 0.45% and deducts 0.45% from the employee’s paycheck. Smaller businesses with fewer than 15 workers are exempt from paying the employer portion, though their employees still contribute 0.45%. Crucially, while benefit payments do not begin until 2028, state plan pre-funding starts much earlier on January 1, 2027. ... Employers have three options for handling FAMLI compliance: remain in the state-administered plan, purchase an equivalent private insurance plan, or establish a self-insured plan. Private plans may offer benefits such as faster claims processing, multi-state coordination, and integration with short-term disability programs, without requiring state pre-funding payments in 2027. However, private plans are individually risk-rated, and if a private option ends up costing workers more, the employer must absorb the difference. Self-insured options are generally reserved for businesses with at least 50 Maryland employees that can prove solvency, secure a surety bond, and obtain state approval. ... Choosing a private or self-insured plan requires following strict procedures. All employers must register on the state’s FAMLI portal in fall 2026. Employers that intend to use a private plan may submit a DOI signed by a licensed insurance professional between September 1, 2026, and November 15, 2026. Once approved, these employers must set aside and escrow the required contribution funds starting January 1, 2027, rather than sending them to the state. When the private plan receives final approval in summer 2027, any employee money held in escrow must be returned to workers. Employers should be cautious about switching plans later, as dropping a private plan to re-enter the state program before late 2028 requires paying all exempted pre-funding contributions plus interest out of pocket, with no ability to charge employees retroactively. ... Communication and scheduling also play a major role in managing FAMLI compliance. Employers must notify workers about FAMLI benefits starting in July 2027 (six months before benefits launch), as well as at hire, annually, and 30 days before any major plan changes. For their part, employees must give 30 days’ notice for foreseeable leave and notify employers as soon as practical for unexpected absences. When using intermittent leave, workers must make reasonable efforts to avoid disrupting operations. ... Employers must also determine how FAMLI fits with existing leave benefits. Companies cannot require employees to exhaust their vacation or paid time off before using FAMLI, though they may permit workers to use paid time off to top off their benefits to full regular pay. Standard company leave, such as paid parental time off, can run concurrently with FAMLI if proper written notice is given. Similarly, short-term disability policies run concurrently, with FAMLI paying out first and disability insurance covering any allowable difference. Because FAMLI covers the initial primary portion, commercial short-term disability rates are expected to decrease over time. ... Keeping accurate records is vital because all employers must submit wage and hour reports to the state every quarter starting in April 2027, regardless of the plan option they have selected. Failing to comply carries heavy penalties. After 30 days of late payment, the state assesses all missing contributions, applies a 1.5% monthly interest fee, may impose penalties up to twice the missing amount, and will conduct a mandatory audit the following fiscal year. Maryland is not alone in changing its leave landscape. 13 states, plus the District of Columbia, now operate paid family and medical leave programs. Virginia recently enacted its own paid family leave law, establishing a program set for pre-funding in April 2028 and full benefit launch in December 2028. As these shifts continue, Maryland businesses should audit their current workforce, review payroll systems, evaluate private market alternatives, and ensure their policy language is fully prepared for the upcoming deadlines.

As of the release of the bulletin, authorized insurance carriers are only permitted to provide illustrative private plan quotes to employers. Additionally, MIA states that “insurers must provide clear disclosure that such preliminary illustrative quotes are not actual quotes, and that the final rates are subject to approval by the Administration and may be higher or lower than the illustrated rates.” A common practice for insurance carriers is to require an employer to bundle a PFML private plan with another line of coverage, such as basic life insurance. The MIA’s bulletin announces that insurance carriers are permitted to do this for Maryland PFML private plans as long as the coverages are two distinct contracts. The U.S. middle market represents more than $40 billion in insurance and benefits opportunity and accounts for more than one-third of U.S. commercial property and casualty direct written premium, according to Aon's deal announcement. USI gives Aon a ready-made platform in that segment — one with existing employer relationships, adviser networks, and benefits consulting capabilities that would take years to build organically. ... That ambition matters because it signals intent. Aon is not acquiring USI to manage it quietly — it is acquiring it to compete aggressively in the midmarket. That gives USI clients several months to ask their account teams direct questions about what the integration means for their benefits programs. HR directors at organizations currently working with USI should request clarity on service team continuity, any changes to carrier panels or preferred vendor relationships, and how the combined firm plans to handle conflicts of interest across its expanded book of business. Employee affordability concerns are already adding to the pressure on HR benefits teams— and a change in advisory ownership is not a reason to defer those conversations. It is a reason to accelerate them. Equally, HR leaders who are not current USI clients should watch how the combined firm positions itself in the midmarket: rising benefits costs are forcing HR to get smarter, not leaner, and a more capable midmarket adviser — whatever its ownership — could change the options available to plan sponsors.

headline: Health insurers turn to technology, preventive care to contain rising costs
summary_text: Health insurers turn to technology, preventive care to contain rising costs ... PHOTO/ GETTY IMAGES # Health insurers turn to technology, preventive care to contain rising costs Rochelle Shenk// August 31, 2026// Health insurers are looking beyond traditional plan design to help employers contain rising health care costs, turning to technology, preventive care, mental health programs and new approaches to how members access care. “Employers continue to face increasing cost pressure,” said Ed Shellard, DMD, president and CEO United Concordia Dental. “They know that benefit plans are something that can make them more competitive in attracting employees, but they also want to ensure that they’re offering plans that are not only affordable for the business, but also for employees.” “We hear it across all segments–everybody wants to ensure affordability,” added Joe Haddock, Eastern Pennsylvania Market President Highmark Inc. Preventive care becomes a cost-control tool Shellard said employers are taking a more balanced approach with the health care plans they’re offering. “Rather than continuing to increase the employee share of health care, employers are encouraging preventive care to help manage costs,” he said adding that dental care is a bit ahead of the curve since traditionally, dental is focused on cleanings every six months. “Employers today are looking for more than a health plan,” said Dr. Jeremy Wigginton, Chief Medical Officer at Capital Blue Cross. “They deserve to work with a trusted partner that can help them navigate rising healthcare costs while supporting the health and well-being of their workforce. That’s where Capital is focused. We continually invest in care models, technology, and personalized support that make it easier for employees to access care, stay engaged in their health, and address issues before they become more serious and costly.” Shellard and H ... along with Capital Blue Cross President and CEO Todd Shamash, are among the insurance executives featured in ... Central Penn Business Journal’s 2026 CPBJ 300. ... controlling costs is about engaging consumers and educating ... about the importance of dental health and preventive care so that care is delivered earlier. It may also need to be more frequent for people with ongoing health issues such as diabetes. ... Insurers invest in technology, new plan options Haddock said for Highmark, helping employers contain costs centers on a few areas such as providing great service, adding new options and programs and finding ways to increase engagement with our members. We’ve also invested significantly in technology to enhance our member platform and app,” he said. For Highmark, one of the new options is CopayGo, a co-pay only health plan designed to help businesses control costs. The plan features no deductibles–members pay a flat fee at the time of service; a tiered provider network with providers in Enhanced and Standard tiers based on quality, appropriateness, and cost efficiency; and access to digital tools. Haddock said Highmark has also worked with providers, who meet certain criteria, to streamline the pre-authorization process for medical services. “For providers, there’s less paperwork, and for members, it means they often leave the provider’s office with an appointment for further care,” he said. Wigginton said Capital Blue Cross’s approach combines value-based care arrangements that reward quality and outcomes, digital health solutions, whole-person care programs, and data-driven insights that help connect members to the right care at the right time. “We also recognize that every workforce is different, so we work closely with employers to tailor the right mix of coverage, resources, and support for their employees,” he said. “Ultimately, our goal is to help employers get greater value from their healthcare investment by improving health outcomes, enhancing the member experience, and helping manage costs over the long term.” Virtual health visits such as telehealth are also part of the mix for both Capital Blue Cross and Highmark. Wigginton said virtual health visits have become increasingly important and, in many cases, are now an expectation among employers looking to make healthcare more accessible, convenient, and engaging for their employees. “It’s not just about clinical visits; it’s also about giving people more ways to manage their health between appointments and outside the traditional health care setting,” he said. “That’s why Capital offers a range of digital solutions. The common thread is helping people access care, stay connected to their health, and address concerns earlier, which can lead to better outcomes and lower costs over time.” Mental health gets a bigger role in cost containment Both Highmark and Capital Blue Cross have increased the focus on mental health. Haddock said two years ago Highmark launched its partnership with Spring Health to offer mental health services for members age six and up. “We have a whole suite of programs we launched to try to meet the members where they are,” he said. Highmark’s program covers a variety of issues including substance abuse. Members typically have an appointment in two- to three- days, and there’s 24/7 crisis support through the Highmark app. “ “We know mental health affects not only a person’s health, but often their work, family, and overall quality of life,” Wigginton said. Since early 2025, Capital has expanded its our behavioral health provider network by 40%, making it easier for members to find care and support. He said the insurer has seen promising results, including a 9% decline in behavioral health-related emergency department visits in 2025 compared with 2022 through 2024. “To us, that’s a strong reminder that when people can get help earlier, they often avoid more serious health challenges later, which benefits both employers and employees,” he said. One other component to containing costs is helping to identify and prevent fraud. Haddock said Highmark has invested in technology and training to ensure payment integrity–ensuring that the right level of service is reimbursed at the right amount. Rochelle A. Shen

summary_text: MILWAUKEE, Wis., Aug. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Zywave, the leading technology provider for insurance distribution, today released its four 2026 Midyear Market Outlook reports covering commercial insurance, employee benefits, human resources and wellness. While the four reports reveal the trends that defined the first half of 2026 in their respective markets, together, they deliver a resounding verdict: AI is no longer an exploratory talking point but is actively rewriting how risk and coverage gets priced, how benefits are built, and how the workforce itself is structured. The Commercial Insurance Midyear Market Outlook examines pricing and capacity trends across eight lines of coverage, including cyber, D&O and EPL. The Employee Benefits Midyear Market Outlook covers rising healthcare costs, ERISA fiduciary litigation, AI’s growing role in benefits administration and GLP-1 trends. The Human Resources Midyear Market Outlook explores how AI is reshaping the labor market, alongside the expanding gig economy, employee burnout and labor market confidence. Finally, the Wellness Midyear Market Outlook covers GLP-1 and peptide therapies, financial stress, wearable technology adoption and five mental health trends shaping the workplace. “AI is moving past the point of exploratory discussion. It’s in underwriting questionnaires, insurance pricing models, and actively being diffused into application software – from core insurance systems to worksite and benefits enrollment,” said Eric Rentsch, Chief Product Officer at Zywave. “The employers and brokers leading the market right now are treating AI deployment, adoption, governance, and risk as one connected strategy, not separate challenges.” ... AI is now the default infrastructure: AI has moved from pilot programs to standard infrastructure: it is easing administrative workload for teams, while insurers are tightening underwriting on AI-related exposures across cyber, D&O and EPL, and purpose-built AI mental health platforms are becoming mainstream in employee benefits packages. Meanwhile, AI-driven job anxiety is now a named contributor to workplace burnout. At the same time, “AI-washing” and undisclosed algorithmic bias are fueling new D&O and EPL claims, even as insurers require documented AI governance for favorable underwriting terms, the same governance discipline that helps organizations catch fraud and strengthen their defenses. AI is redrawing the workforce, not shrinking it: The labor market data points to reallocation, not reductions: postings for repetitive, rule-based roles are declining while demand for analytical, technical and creative work is rising. Additionally, across the spectrum of both insurance organizations and HR and benefits teams, AI is absorbing routine administrative tasks, freeing staff to focus on strategy rather than eliminating functional capabilities outright, though entry-level pipelines are thinning as a result. Regulators and insurers are racing to keep pace: New 2026 state AI employment laws in Illinois, Texas and Colorado, in addition to the EU AI Act’s phased rollout, are reshaping compliance, while federal policy remains focused on stimulating market investment and adoption.
