headline: Packaging reform needs a clear destination - PKN Packaging News
summary_text: - As Europe’s PPWR comes into effect, Australia’s packaging sector continues to await clarity on its own reform framework. Image: Getty ... ## As Europe’s PPWR comes into effect this week, Australia’s packaging sector is still waiting for the regulatory certainty needed to turn circularity commitments into investment. On 12 August, the European Union’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation begins to apply across its 27 member states. It is an important milestone, although not the end of the regulatory process. Many of the PPWR’s detailed requirements and targets will be introduced progressively, and businesses are still working through what implementation will mean in practice. Even so, Europe has established a direction. The regulation creates a binding framework covering packaging design, minimisation, recyclability, recycled content, reuse, labelling and producer responsibility across the EU market. ... Australia’s packaging reforms remain under development, following consultation on options that included mandatory packaging requirements, an extended producer responsibility scheme and stronger administration of the existing co-regulatory framework. In the meantime, the current arrangements remain in place, and industry continues to operate without certainty about the final shape, timing or cost of reform. On an alarmingly regular basis, PKN is publishing call after call for clarity, certainty, direction on reform, including recycled content mandates and EPR. I do not pretend to have the answers to how Australia’s future packaging framework should be designed. But through PKN’s sustained coverage of the reform debate, a clear and consistent message has emerged from packaging manufacturers, recyclers, brand owners and industry groups: voluntary ambition cannot deliver circularity without the policy settings and market conditions to support it. It is equally apparent that Australia cannot afford much more delay. ... Industry is not simply asking for more regulation. What businesses need is a coherent, nationally consistent framework that defines responsibilities, creates viable end markets and gives companies confidence to invest. That distinction matters. Packaging businesses make decisions about manufacturing equipment, material development, recycling infrastructure and supply contracts over long timeframes. Investment becomes difficult when policy settings remain uncertain or differ between jurisdictions. This point has been reinforced repeatedly through PKN’s coverage. In March, packaging and recycling businesses joined a coordinated call for national reform, warning that uncertainty around its shape and timing was already stalling investment. Their intervention added to the argument that circularity depends on an aligned national system, rather than disconnected state measures and voluntary initiatives. Australia does not need to replicate PPWR. Our geography, population distribution, collection systems, processing capacity and markets are very different from Europe’s. But the PPWR demonstrates the value of setting a clear regulatory destination, even when the pathway towards full implementation extends over several years. ... The need for certainty is particularly apparent in Australia’s recycled plastics market. Recent pressure on the domestic resin and recycling sector has exposed the gap between building processing capacity and creating reliable demand for its output. Recyclers can invest in plants and packaging companies can develop formats incorporating recycled polymers, but those investments remain vulnerable when locally produced recyclate must compete with low-cost virgin resin and imported material. PKN’s coverage of Australia’s resin crisis has repeatedly identified the same structural problem: recycling capacity cannot remain viable without markets for the material it produces. There was a moment when it seemed the crisis would accelerate reform, as it saw Ministers convene a roundtable discussion. Whether that translates into faster policy action remains to be seen. As industry participants and recycling organisations have repeatedly argued, mandatory minimum recycled-content requirements would create a level of demand that voluntary targets have failed to secure. They would also give recyclers and packaging manufacturers a firmer basis for investment, while reducing the commercial disadvantage faced by businesses already incorporating recycled material. The detail would matter enormously. Mandates would need to account for material availability, food-contact requirements, technical performance and the different challenges associated with individual polymers and packaging formats. But those complexities are an argument for carefully designed regulation, not for indefinite delay. ... Extended producer responsibility is another recurring theme in industry submissions and commentary. Pact Group has argued that a mandatory EPR framework is needed to support domestic recycling, stimulate demand for recycled content and ensure producers take greater responsibility for the packaging they place on the market. For EPR to make a material difference, it will need to do more than collect and redistribute fees. It should reward packaging designed for circularity, impose higher costs on difficult-to-recover formats, and direct funding towards the collection, sorting and reprocessing systems required to keep materials in circulation. It must also help connect the different parts of the system. A recyclable package has limited value if it is not collected. Collected material will not become a resource without sorting and reprocessing capacity. Recyclate will not support a circular economy unless manufacturers have both the incentive and the confidence to use it. The same systems thinking applies to soft plastics, where industry investment, collection models, processing technology and end markets must develop together. ... There is already broad agreement about many of the problems. Australia sends substantial volumes of packaging to landfill, recycled-content uptake remains uneven, and fragmented rules add cost and complexity without necessarily delivering better environmental outcomes. What remains unresolved is how responsibility will be allocated, which requirements will become mandatory and when businesses will be expected to comply. Europe’s PPWR will face its own implementation challenges. Its existence does not guarantee that every target will be met or that collection and recycling systems will operate consistently across all member states. Nor does it provide Australia with a policy template that can simply be imported. ... Australian packaging reform must be designed for Australian conditions, drawing on the expertise of the businesses, recyclers, governments and communities that will have to make it work. What industry can reasonably expect is a clear destination, an implementation timetable and rules strong enough to give businesses the confidence to invest in reaching it.

headline: Supply certainty is reshaping packaging procurement decisions - Inside FMCG
summary_text: Packaging procurement is no longer driven purely by cost. For FMCG manufacturers, supply continuity, lead-time certainty and verified sustainability performance are now core selection criteria alongside price. As supply chains continue to navigate geopolitical uncertainty, freight volatility and evolving customer expectations, businesses are placing greater emphasis on suppliers that can deliver consistency as well as quality. That shift is creating renewed interest in regional manufacturing and prompting many Australian companies to reassess how far their packaging materials really need to travel. Against this backdrop, WML Paperboard exhibited at last week’s FoodPro 2026 in Melbourne, using the event to strengthen relationships with Australian food manufacturers, converters and packaging specialists while highlighting the advantages of having a premium paperboard manufacturer close to market. ... “Businesses are increasingly recognising that local or regional manufacturing provides more than convenience. It delivers greater certainty around supply, shorter lead times and stronger technical support, all of which have become increasingly valuable over the past few years,” he says. As Australasia’s only manufacturer of premium folding box board, WML Paperboard occupies a unique position within the regional packaging market. From its New Zealand manufacturing base, the company produces the Formakote range, supplying customers across food, beverage, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics and retail, while exporting to more than 40 countries worldwide. The company’s message at FoodPro was straightforward: Australian manufacturers have a regional alternative to offshore paperboard sourcing. ... The past several years have highlighted the vulnerabilities that can emerge when packaging supply depends on long international logistics networks. Port congestion, freight disruptions, shipping schedule changes and geopolitical tensions have all demonstrated how quickly global events can interrupt production planning. ... “Covid changed the way businesses think about supply chains. It’s no longer just about lowest cost – it’s about certainty and resilience,” he explains. Long supply chains inevitably introduce more variables. Multiple shipping legs, transhipment points and extended freight times can all increase the likelihood of delays that ultimately affect manufacturing schedules and product availability. By contrast, regional manufacturing offers a more streamlined path from production to customer. WML Paperboard manufactures Formakote in Whakatane, New Zealand, with the majority of its raw materials sourced locally before finished paperboard is shipped directly to Australia. From the nearby Port of Tauranga, shipments typically reach Sydney within five to seven days, while total delivery from production to Australia’s eastern seaboard generally takes between 17 and 21 days. The result is a shorter, less complex supply chain that can help businesses respond more quickly to changing demand, reduce inventory pressures, free up working capital and improve production planning. “One of the biggest challenges with offshore sourcing can be the number of touchpoints involved,” Knight says. “Transhipment alone introduces additional risk, delays, and uncertainty into the supply chain.” ... While supply resilience has become a strategic priority, product performance remains equally important for food packaging applications. Formakote is manufactured specifically for demanding packaging environments, with direct-contact food-grade board designed to meet the performance requirements of FMCG brands, converters and packaging specialists. The board is produced from 100 per cent virgin fibre sourced from responsibly managed forests, carries FSC certification and is fully recyclable. Its manufacturing processes are also supported by internationally recognised ISO accreditations, providing customers with independently verified quality, environmental and food safety systems. For food manufacturers balancing regulatory requirements, sustainability targets and operational performance, those credentials are becoming increasingly significant. ... While the company has supplied packaging markets for decades, the event reinforces its ongoing investment in the Australian market and its commitment to supporting local customers through technical expertise and manufacturing capability. ... Working within the region enables closer collaboration with converters and brand owners throughout packaging development, while local technical support can help customers resolve challenges more quickly than relying on suppliers operating across multiple time zones. That responsiveness is becoming increasingly valuable as product cycles shorten and manufacturers seek greater flexibility from their supply partners. As FMCG businesses continue balancing cost pressures with resilience, sustainability and customer expectations, procurement decisions are becoming more strategic than transactional. For many, the question is no longer simply where packaging can be sourced most cheaply, but which supply model offers the greatest confidence for the years ahead. FoodPro 2026 presented WML Paperboard with an opportunity to demonstrate that regional manufacturing can deliver more than premium paperboard alone. It can provide Australian manufacturers with shorter, more reliable supply chains, technical expertise close to home and the confidence that comes from partnering with a supplier committed to the region for the long term.

headline: PIDA 2026 Winners Highlight Circular Economy and Integrated Sustainability Trends
summary_text: The Australasian Institute of Packaging has announced the winners of the 2026 PIDA awards in Melbourne, recognizing excellence in packaging innovation across Australia and New Zealand. The winning entries reflect a significant shift toward circular economy models, prioritizing reuse, recovery, and closed-loop recycling over simple material substitution. These awards serve as a critical benchmark for the sector, with all category winners now eligible to represent the region in the 2027 WorldStar Packaging Awards. The 2026 PIDA awards showcased a transition where sustainability is no longer a standalone category but a fundamental design requirement across the industry. In the food sector, Primo Foods and Amcor Flexibles secured top honors for a peel-and-reseal sliced meats pack that utilizes a recycle-ready mono-material PET structure while reducing plastic usage by 10 per cent. Similarly, Graphic Packaging International and Asahi Beverages were recognized for replacing plastic shrink wrap on Carlton Dry six-packs with a kerbside recyclable fibre-based alternative. These innovations demonstrate the industry's move toward mono-materials and fibre-based solutions that enhance both environmental performance and consumer convenience. Innovation extended into health, beauty, and household sectors, with Impact International winning for a mono-material HDPE tube and cap range that incorporates Australian-made post-consumer recycled content to streamline the recycling stream. Accessibility also became a central theme, highlighted by ByStorm Beauty’s adaptive tools and packaging developed for people living with disabilities, featuring braille and intuitive opening mechanisms. In the domestic category, Yates Group’s Click & Grow Garden Care System introduced a contact-free refill method to improve safety and controlled dispensing when handling garden chemicals. These entries illustrate how the industry is increasingly integrating safety, inclusivity, and recyclability into primary pack design rather than treating them as secondary objectives. The awards further emphasized "systems thinking" and multi-functional solutions, such as Bonson Packaging’s RePlay Returnables, which combines durable containers with digital traceability and consumer engagement. headline: EU veto reportedly looms over UPM-Sappi paper venture
summary_text: UPM and Sappi may face a European Union antitrust veto of their proposed graphic paper joint venture, according to a Reuters report citing people familiar with the matter. The outcome has not yet been formally decided: the European Commission is due to rule on the transaction by 11 November 2026. Reuters reported that the companies had not offered concessions to address the Commission’s competition concerns and had not persuaded regulators at a closed-door hearing. The agency said difficulties in finding a buyer for potential divestments had complicated a possible remedy. UPM and Sappi declined to comment to Reuters, while the Commission did not immediately respond to its request. The proposed €1.42 billion venture would bring together UPM’s communication paper business in Europe and the United States with Sappi’s communication paper business in Europe, as well as Sappi’s specialty paper business and certain ancillary operations. It would create a major supplier of graphic papers in Europe. The Commission sent the companies a statement of objections in August, expressing its preliminary view that the deal could reduce competition in several graphic paper markets, including products used for magazines and books. Its concerns include the possibility of higher prices for customers. UPM and Sappi signed definitive transaction agreements in May 2026 and have since conditionally nominated a management team for the planned company. Those appointments, like completion of the venture, depend on regulatory approval and other closing conditions. Until any transaction closes, the two businesses continue to operate independently. The reported prospect of a veto is a further development in the review, rather than an official prohibition.

The European Commission (EC) has informed UPM and Sappi that its proposed joint venture may restrict competition in the communication paper market. In May, UPM and Sappi signed a definitive agreement that proposed creating an independent, equal-owned partnership combining UPM’s global communication papers business and Sappi’s European graphic paper business. In a Statement of Objections, the EC explains that it is concerned that the proposed partnership could increase prices and decrease quality. It says that it is “currently unconvinced” that the joint venture would bring “enough benefits” in cost savings, environmental performance, or resilience improvements, to “offset the potential harm” of the merger. "The EC has informed UPM and Sappi of its preliminary view that its proposed joint venture may restrict competition in the markets for different types of communication paper, which is used for printed materials, such as magazines or books," an EC spokesperson tells Packaging Insights. "In particular, EC has made the preliminary finding that the joint venture may have a dominant position in the markets for coated mechanical and wood free coated paper, and that it could exercise its market power to increase prices and reduce choice for customers." ... In April, the EC opened an investigation assessing whether the joint venture could reduce competition for certain communication papers in the European Economic Area (EEA), UK, and Switzerland. The investigation included analysis of internal documents provided by UPM and Sappi, and “views and data” from competitors, outlines the EC. ... Moreover, a UPM spokesperson tells us that the company is “confident that [it] will be able to respond fully to the EC’s preliminary concerns. The planned joint venture is a necessary step to secure reliable supply continuity for graphic paper customers in Europe.” ... UPM and Sappi estimate the enterprise value of the planned business combination to be €1.42 billion (US$1.65 billion). The UPM spokesperson outlines that the joint venture would contribute to the “resilience of the entire European graphic paper industry, in the interest of customers.” UPM and Sappi say that the joint venture would contribute to the “resilience" of the graphic paper industry. One of the EC’s responsibilities is to assess mergers and acquisitions involving companies with a turnover above certain thresholds. It aims to prevent concentrations that would “significantly impede” effective competition in the EEA. The Sappi spokesperson tells us that the rationale for the proposed joint venture “remains strong,” especially in a declining graphic paper market. The joint venture aims to rationalize supply in an industry facing declining demand, structural overcapacity, and high energy costs, according to the companies. ... A Statement of Objections is a formal procedure in any EC investigation into mergers and acquisitions. The EC states that the Statement of Objections “does not prejudge the outcome of the investigation,” but seeks to update the companies in writing of the formal objections against the joint venture. UPM and Sappi can now reply to the EC’s Statement of Objections, consult the case file, and request an oral hearing, as underscored by the EC. The companies will respond “in detail” to the EC’s concerns, says the UPM spokesperson, adding that these are confidential discussions on which it cannot comment further. The Sappi spokesperson tells us that the company’s advisors are also reviewing the Statement of Objections and are focused on responding to concerns raised by the EC. “Sappi and UPM will submit their observations addressing the EC’s preliminary concerns and will continue to engage constructively with the EC to demonstrate the benefits of the transaction,” adds the Sappi spokesperson. ... The EC says the joint venture could increase prices and decrease quality. Alongside amalgamated manufacturing processes, the packaging industry is entering a post-mega merger era, defined by consolidation, a prolonged downturn, and rising geopolitical uncertainty, say experts from Rabobank Packaging and Logistics. In a previous interview with Packaging Insights, Rabobank senior analysts Xinnan Li, Natasha Valeeva, and Jim Owen discussed shifting competitive dynamics, future growth prospects, and the increasing impact of regulation and private equity on the industry. Yet, a year after the merger, it announced plans to split into two regional, publicly traded companies. As part of the separation, its EMEA Packaging business will be spun off to shareholders, while IP intends to retain a meaningful ownership stake in the new company. headline: EU challenges UPM and Sappi’s planned paper venture
summary_text: EU challenges UPM and Sappi’s planned paper venture # UPM-Sappi deal could weaken competition, EU warns Sappi’s Kirkniemi paper mill near Lohja in Finland is due to become part of the planned joint venture with UPM. The European Commission fears the transaction could weaken competition in the printing paper market. Photo: Valmet. Published by Markku Björkman - 3 Sep, 2026 The European Commission has reached the preliminary conclusion that the proposed joint venture between Finland’s UPM and South Africa’s Sappi could restrict competition in the European printing paper market. Brussels fears that the transaction could enable the new company to raise prices or reduce product quality. The Commission has outlined its concerns in a statement of objections sent to the two forest industry groups. The document represents a formal step in the EU’s competition investigation and does not prejudge the final outcome of the case. According to Finnish public service broadcaster Yle, the planned joint venture would become the market leader in several categories of graphic paper across the European Economic Area, or EEA. Printing paper is used in products including magazines, catalogues, advertising material and books. Demand has been declining for years as information, publishing and advertising have increasingly moved to digital channels. The downturn has resulted in mill closures, production cuts and extensive restructuring across the European paper industry. ... The proposed company would combine UPM’s graphic paper operations in Europe and the United States with Sappi’s European business in the same sector. Selected parts of Sappi’s speciality paper activities and related operations would also be included. The European Commission’s concerns focus primarily on the markets for coated mechanical paper and coated woodfree paper. Its preliminary assessment indicates that the joint venture could obtain a sufficiently strong position to reduce competitive pressure. Greater market power could allow the company to raise prices or lower product quality to the detriment of customers. A highly concentrated market could also reduce customers’ choice of suppliers and weaken the incentive for producers to develop their products and services. The assessment is particularly significant because the transaction would combine two of Europe’s largest graphic paper producers. The Commission must now determine whether competition from other manufacturers and alternative products would be sufficient to constrain the new company. The investigation comes as European paper producers are already adjusting to a structurally contracting market. Companies argue that consolidation may be necessary to maintain efficient production, while customers remain concerned about the consequences of having fewer suppliers. ... According to UPM, the joint venture is a necessary step to safeguard long-term supplies of graphic paper to European customers. The company also argues that the transaction would help strengthen a European paper industry facing declining demand, high energy and raw-material costs, and excess production capacity. ... The companies’ case rests largely on the rapid transformation of the market. Structural demand for graphic paper has fallen for many years, making it increasingly difficult to maintain profitable production and sufficient capacity at European mills. The Commission must nevertheless assess whether the claimed industrial benefits outweigh the risk of customers having fewer suppliers from which to choose. ... headline: Valmet delivers the first commercial-scale 3D Fiber line to Metsä Group, enabling high-quality molded fiber packaging production
summary_text: Metsä Group has selected Valmet to deliver a 3D Fiber molded fiber production line for their mill in Äänekoski, Finland. The investment responds to growing demand for alternatives to replace plastics by enabling high-volume industrial production of three-dimensional fiber-based packaging that is competitive with similar plastic solutions. This investment marks a significant milestone as the world's first commercial-scale implementation of the innovation. It follows Valmet's extensive development, piloting, and the successful launch of the 3D Fiber technology in June 2026. The start-up of the line is scheduled for 2028. "After years of fruitful co-development with Valmet, including the start-up of the joint demo plant in 2022, Muoto is now entering an exciting new phase. We are expanding our capabilities, deepening customer collaborations, and building the foundations for future growth. At the same time, demand is growing for packaging solutions that combine performance, circularity, and scalability," says Antti Valtonen, Vice President of the Muoto project, Metsä Spring. "Valmet 3D Fiber technology is the first large-scale molded fiber production technology on the market, and it provides an attractive and competitive end-to-end solution for the growing sustainable packaging market. The investment confirms the market potential of the technology and accelerates the replacement of plastic packaging in high-volume production. Over the years, Metsä Group and Valmet have worked closely together to develop and validate the 3D Fiber technology, creating a strong foundation of trust and shared ambition," says Juho Pyrrö, Head of 3D Fiber at Valmet. Valmet 3D Fiber technology combines high capacity and speed, automation, and resource efficiency to produce high-quality molded fiber packaging. Valmet 3D Fiber technology enables the production of lightweight yet rigid end products, including trays, plates, and food packaging containers, offering alternatives to plastic. The technology uses cellulose fibers to form ready-to-use, three-dimensional products directly from pulp, eliminating the need for intermediate steps. Valmet offers a complete solution from fiber processing to automatic packing of end products along with services. With comprehensive testing and piloting opportunities, customers are able to develop and test new end products together with Valmet. Valmet and Metsä Group have been developing the novel technology together in their demo plant in Äänekoski. The new production line will be located alongside the existing demo plant with a nominal capacity of more than 100 million products per year, demonstrating the scalability of the technology and paving the way for future industrial investments. ... Metsä Group is a Finnish forest industry group whose renewable products serve millions of people every day. Metsä focuses on pulp, paperboards, tissue and greaseproof papers, wood products, and wood supply and forest services. Its parent company, Metsäliitto Cooperative, is owned by more than 90,000 Finnish forest owners. In 2025, Metsä's sales totaled EUR 5.8 billion, and the company employed approximately 8,800 people.

The European Commission has sent UPM and Sappi its preliminary objections to the joint venture the two companies plan to create in the market for paper used in magazines, books and other printed materials. Brussels considers that the transaction could reduce competition because UPM and Sappi are the two largest manufacturers of communication paper in the European Economic Area and their combination would create the regional market leader. UPM and Sappi plan to combine a substantial part of their communication paper activities, a segment covering products used to print magazines, books and promotional material. The joint venture would bring together UPM’s communication paper business in Europe and the United States with Sappi’s European communication paper operations, as well as part of Sappi’s speciality paper business and related activities. The two companies are already the largest manufacturers of these products in the European Economic Area, meaning the transaction would create the regional market leader. The Commission opened an in-depth investigation on 28 April following notification of the transaction in March and focused on the markets for magazine paper and coated wood free paper in the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom and Switzerland. Brussels examined internal company documents and collected data and views from customers and competitors to determine how the combination would affect competitive pressure between the two producers. Following that investigation, the Commission’s preliminary view is that the joint venture could acquire enough market power to increase prices and reduce quality for coated mechanical paper, a type of magazine paper, and coated wood free paper. These products are widely used by the printing industry for magazines, books, catalogues and promotional materials. The Commission’s concern extends beyond prices. A reduction in the number of major suppliers could also affect customers’ ability to negotiate commercial terms, switch suppliers or obtain different levels of quality and service. From Brussels’ perspective, combining the two largest manufacturers could alter competitive conditions in a sector where buyers rely on a limited number of suppliers capable of providing large volumes and products meeting precise specifications. UPM and Sappi have argued that integrating their operations could generate cost savings and other benefits, including environmental and resilience improvements. The Commission says, however, that it is not currently convinced those advantages would be sufficient to offset the potential harm to competition and customers. This assessment remains preliminary and may change after the companies’ responses are examined. UPM, headquartered in Finland, operates across paper, pulp, electricity, label materials, sawn timber, wood panels, biochemicals and other biomass-based solutions. Sappi, headquartered in South Africa, manufactures materials based on wood fibre and supplies both raw materials, including pulp and biomaterials, and finished products such as communication, speciality and packaging paper. ... The Commission has until 11 November to take a final decision. It may conclude that the identified concerns have been resolved, accept commitments proposed by the companies or decide that the transaction cannot be approved in its current form if the competition risks remain. ... The European Commission reviews large mergers and acquisitions to determine whether they could significantly impede competition in ... European Economic Area. Most notified transactions are cleared after an initial review, while in-depth investigations are opened when concerns remain about potential market effects. In the UPM-Sappi case, the assessment focuses on communication paper segments in which the two companies already hold significant positions. A final decision is due by 11 November 2026.

headline: EU raises objections to UPM-Sappi giant joint venture - Timber Industry News
summary_text: UPM says it can address competition concerns raised by the European Commission over its planned €1.42 billion graphic paper joint venture with Sappi, keeping one of the largest restructurings of Europe's paper industry on course despite a deeper regulatory challenge. The European Commission has issued a Statement of Objections to UPM and Sappi over their proposed combination of graphic paper operations, formally setting out concerns identified during its ongoing merger investigation. UPM confirmed receipt of the statement on 26 August and said it would examine the Commission's objections together with Sappi. The Finnish group maintains that the issues can be resolved and continues to argue that combining the businesses is necessary to maintain a viable European graphic paper supply base. The move follows the Commission's decision in April to open a Phase II investigation after its initial review failed to resolve competition concerns. The Statement of Objections does not amount to a prohibition of the transaction. It gives UPM and Sappi an opportunity to respond to the Commission's preliminary findings and potentially propose remedies before a final decision.

headline: Brussels raises formal objections to €1.42bn UPM-Sappi venture - https://eutoday.net
summary_text: #### The European Commission has formally warned UPM and Sappi that their proposed €1.42 billion graphic-paper joint venture may give the combined business power to raise prices or reduce quality in already concentrated European markets. Its statement of objections concerns coated mechanical paper and coated woodfree paper, products used in magazines, books and promotional material. Brussels remains unconvinced that claimed efficiencies, environmental benefits or greater resilience would compensate customers for the loss of competition. ... The transaction would place UPM Communication Papers and Sappi’s European graphic-paper business in a 50-50 company. The parties value UPM’s contribution at €1.1 billion and Sappi’s at €320 million. They argue that consolidation is needed to manage declining demand, improve utilisation of mills and support investment in more efficient production. ... European graphic paper is a shrinking market. Print circulation has fallen, advertising has moved online and mills face high energy, fibre and labour costs. Producers have closed capacity or converted plants to packaging and other products. Those pressures explain the commercial logic of the venture. They do not automatically satisfy EU merger law. In a declining market, removing a major competitor can still increase prices or reduce service, particularly if remaining capacity is difficult to expand and customers have few substitutes. The Commission’s concern appears to be that the proposed company would hold a strong position in two coated-paper segments where mills, grades and delivery networks are not readily interchangeable. Buyers may be able to switch supplier on paper, yet find that the remaining competitors lack the right specification or available capacity at the required time. UPM and Sappi announced the plan as a route to a more resilient European graphic-paper business. UPM has continued to describe the portfolio change as part of its wider strategy in its half-year financial report. The parties now need to show that benefits are specific to the joint venture, verifiable and likely to reach customers. General claims that a larger producer will be more efficient are rarely sufficient when the same scale could also strengthen bargaining power against publishers and printers. ... The Commission can clear the transaction, accept commitments or prohibit it. A remedy package could involve selling mills, production lines, brands or customer contracts to preserve a credible rival. Behavioural promises on pricing or supply are possible, but Brussels generally prefers assets that allow another operator to compete independently. Finding an effective buyer may be difficult in a structurally declining sector. A divested mill is useful only if it has secure inputs, viable costs, the necessary product mix and customers. That can make a superficially simple disposal less convincing to regulators. The case comes as large European companies increasingly present consolidation as a defence against global competition and expensive industrial transition. EU Today recently examined that tension in WSP’s pursuit of Arcadis, although the paper venture raises a more direct horizontal competition question. UPM and Sappi have not lost the case, but the burden has shifted. To secure approval, they must now answer a detailed theory of harm rather than rely on the industrial case for combining two businesses under pressure.

headline: Europe's Paper Industry Warns of Eroding Competitiveness
summary_text: Europe's pulp and paper industry is reducing carbon emissions and increasingly relying on European raw materials. At the same time, the sector's trade association, Cepi, warns that production capacity and investment are gradually shifting outside the European Union. Europe's pulp and paper industry is facing mounting competitive pressure. Despite major progress in climate performance, recycling and the circular economy, production continues to decline while imports from outside the EU have reached record levels. That is the conclusion of Cepi's latest Key Statistics Report 2025, which describes the current trend as a gradual but persistent weakening of Europe's industrial base. According to the report, European paper and board production fell by 1.6 per cent in 2025 to 77.4 million tonnes. Early figures for 2026 indicate that the decline is continuing, with production falling by another 2.4 per cent during the first quarter compared with the same period a year earlier. ... Demand for packaging papers and products linked to e-commerce and logistics has remained relatively stable, although cartonboard production declined by 5.4 per cent during 2025. Graphic papers continued to perform significantly worse, with production falling 7.3 per cent as digitalisation and declining demand for printed media continued to reshape the market. Overall, European production excluding graphic papers remains approximately 7 per cent below the record levels reached in 2021, reflecting intensifying international competition and an increasingly challenging geopolitical environment, according to Cepi. ... At the same time, competition from producers outside Europe continues to intensify. Imports now account for 7.7 per cent of total EU consumption, the highest level ever recorded. Although exports still represent more than 20 per cent of total production, Europe's trade surplus has begun to shrink. Cepi attributes the growing pressure to state-supported competitors outside Europe, as well as unequal market conditions that continue to undermine the competitiveness of European producers. During the past three years, several production facilities have either closed or reduced capacity, raising concerns that Europe could gradually lose industrial capabilities in one of its most strategic manufacturing sectors. ... the industry's ... come at a time when its environmental performance has reached record levels. In 2025, the sector reduced its specific carbon dioxide emissions by 10.2 per cent. At the same time, 92 per cent of all wood raw material originated from European forests, while almost all recovered fibre used in production was sourced within Europe. The industry also operates the world's most advanced paper recycling system, making it one of the cornerstones of Europe's circular bioeconomy. ... The report is particularly significant for the Nordic forest industry. Sweden and Finland are among Europe's largest producers of pulp, paper and paperboard, exporting substantial volumes across Europe and global markets. Leading companies are investing billions of euros in new bio-based materials, sustainable packaging solutions and products designed to replace fossil-based plastics. A continued decline in Europe's industrial competitiveness could therefore have significant consequences for investment, employment and the long-term development of the continent's growing bioeconomy. ... The organisation calls for stronger trade defence measures against unfair competition, a more predictable regulatory framework for industrial investments and increased support for Europe's bio-based value chains. According to Cepi, Europe risks steadily losing industrial capacity in a sector that is essential for food packaging, hygiene products, logistics and the development of bio-based alternatives to fossil-intensive materials. headline: SunSirs: Converging Market Tailwinds Drive Acetic Acid Prices Up over 35% in a Single Month
summary_text: According to data from SunSirs, the price of acetic acid continued to rise throughout September; as of September 23, the average market price stood at 4,603 RMB/ton, marking a 35.39% increase from the 3,400 RMB/ton recorded at the beginning of the month. Acetic acid prices saw a significant rise over the month, driven by a combination of factors: rising costs, tight supply, and solid downstream demand. Specifically: Upstream cost pressures drove the market upward: international oil prices rose during the first half of the month, pushing up the methanol market, after which methanol prices fluctuated at high levels. Acetic acid producers faced significant cost pressures, providing strong cost-side support for acetic acid; market sentiment favored price increases, leading producers to raise their quotes. Low corporate inventory levels: Although the operating rate for acetic acid has hovered around 80% since September—a relatively high level for the industry—overall corporate inventories remain low. Production cutbacks or maintenance shutdowns at facilities such as Tianjin Soda Plant, Shanghai Huayi, and Hualu Hengsheng have tightened spot supplies; meanwhile, a recovery in downstream demand and a healthy order book have continued to push price levels upward. Stable demand support: During the traditional peak season, operating rates for downstream acetic acid sectors remained relatively high, bolstering procurement volumes and maintaining a decent level of market trading activity; this supported acetic acid prices, keeping them firm at high levels. Favorable export trends: Driven by geopolitical conflicts, high production costs led to reduced operating rates or shutdowns at multiple overseas acetic acid plants. As the world's largest producer, China exported a total of 936,500 tonnes of acetic acid from January to August—a 23.68% increase year-on-year. This rise in exports tightened domestic spot supplies, driving prices steadily upward. Market Outlook: In the short term, the acetic acid market is supported by predominantly positive factors, with prices expected to consolidate at high levels leading up to the holiday. From a long-term perspective, although upstream methanol prices have softened slightly, they remain elevated, providing continued cost support. Downstream acceptance of high prices is limited, which may dampen purchasing enthusiasm. On the supply side, volumes are gradually increasing as maintenance-halted units resume operations; however, INEOS's recent announcement to shut down its last remaining world-scale acetyls plant in Europe—including a 500,000-ton-per-year acetic acid unit and downstream acetic acid and ethyl acetate facilities—is expected to further boost acetic acid export volumes. Overall, the acetic acid market is projected to fluctuate at high levels; key factors to monitor include market supply and the extent of downstream demand.

headline: Ineos Hull Pause Idles Europe's Last Acetyls Plants
summary_text: The Ineos Hull operation is being mothballed. All three of the group’s acetyls plants at Saltend Chemicals Park are coming offline, and the company says the reason comes down to one number: gas that costs it 12 times what an American competitor pays. Two of the units have already stopped. The third is due to follow within days, and all three will stay idle “until further notice”, according to the announcement Ineos published on 22 September. The Ineos Hull decision reaches well beyond East Yorkshire. By the company’s own description these are Europe’s last remaining world-scale acetyls units, making building-block chemicals that end up in medicines, food, paint, clothing and military explosives. Ineos says every other acetyls unit in Europe has already closed because of energy costs, so when Saltend stops, there is no neighbouring European plant waiting to pick up the slack. ... Each plant makes a different chemical, and each one ends up somewhere familiar. According to the BBC’s report on the pause, one unit produces acetic acid, which goes into vinegar, paint and glue. A second makes acetic anhydride, a key ingredient of aspirin. The third makes ethyl acetate, which is used as a solvent and to decaffeinate tea and coffee. Ineos lists the downstream markets more broadly: pharmaceuticals, food products, clothing, cosmetics, detergents, construction materials and high-energy military explosives. Its products are sold to customers throughout Europe. The Hull Story, the city’s independent news site, notes that the plants sit on the 370-acre Saltend Chemicals Park in East Yorkshire, and that the site’s owner had invested heavily there only recently. ... over at a site like this. It is burned to produce energy, and it is also a feedstock, a raw material that ends up chemically inside the finished product. ... For now, the people on site are not being laid off. The BBC understands that workers across the sites will be kept on while Ineos tries to buy liquefied natural gas directly from the United States at lower prices, a process that could take up to a year, or waits for gas prices to fall. That makes this a pause with a price trigger rather than a closure with a date. Business Matters reports that Ineos did not set out any timescale for a move to permanent closure. ... The headline claim in the Ineos statement is that gas in Europe now costs 12 times as much as it does in the United States, and that European gas is eight times more expensive than coal-based production in China. Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the group’s chairman, repeated both numbers in his comments on the decision. Market data points to a very wide gap, though a narrower one than the company’s figure. Reuters, citing LSEG and Intercontinental Exchange data on the day of the announcement, reported British front-month gas trading at around $23.51 per million British thermal units, against $2.84 at the US Henry Hub benchmark. On those two contracts the multiple is a little over eight, not twelve. Ineos did not say which prices its own comparison uses, so the two figures are not a like-for-like test of each other. What both agree on is the direction and the scale: a British producer is paying a large multiple of what its American competitor pays for the same fuel and the same feedstock. The recent move has been steep. According to the BBC, the wholesale price of natural gas has almost doubled in the UK and Europe since July, after disruption to oil and gas supplies through the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israel war in Iran. That timing is part of the story. The decision was not taken after a slow drift upward in costs, but after two months in which the price of the plants’ main input nearly doubled. ... Ratcliffe framed the pause as a policy failure rather than a commercial one. “I’m sure people will find it hard to believe that we are being forced to mothball some of the most efficient plants in Europe but with gas prices now 12 times the level in the US and 8 times that of China, we just cannot compete,” he said in the company’s statement. In remarks reported by Business Matters he went further, saying the UK government’s energy policy was leading to “economic vandalism on an industrial scale”, with jobs exported to China and the United States. His environmental argument runs alongside the economic one. Ineos says material made in Hull carries half the carbon footprint of equivalent US production and an eighth of the Chinese equivalent, so replacing it with imports would raise global emissions rather than cut them. The company is asking the governments of the UK and the EU, where most of its output is sold, to put tariff protections in place against Chinese products. According to Business Matters, a spokesman said Ineos also wants anti-dumping measures to stop cheap US and Chinese products being sold into the market below cost. The Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said it would be “a concerning time for workers in Saltend and their families”. A spokesperson pointed to “£350 million for strategically important chemicals producers, which will be available on a co-investment basis”, to trade measures already in place on foreign chemicals imports, and to the Supercharger and British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme, which are aimed at high electricity costs. The GMB union was blunter. “GMB has repeatedly warned UK industry will suffer from the country’s deeply uncompetitive gas prices,” Charlotte Brumpton-Childs, the union’s national secretary, said in comments reported by The Manufacturer. ... The Hull decision lands on a business that has been under strain for some time. Business Matters reports that Ineos closed its synthetic ethanol plant at Grangemouth in January 2025 with the loss of 80 direct jobs, introduced a hiring freeze in October 2025 and, in March this year, reported a $593m loss, suspended its dividend for a second year and disclosed net debt of €11.7bn. A group carrying that much debt has little room to keep running plants it says cannot compete while it waits for gas prices to ease. There is an awkward irony in the timing. The Hull Story notes that Ineos completed a £30m project at Saltend in 2025 that switched part of the operation from natural gas to hydrogen, cutting carbon emissions by 75 per cent. The site was, in other words, recently upgraded for exactly the kind of lower-carbon production that climate policy is meant to encourage. It is now idle because of the cost of the fuel and feedstock it still depends on, and the company argues that its customers will simply buy the same chemicals from higher-emission plants abroad. ... The pause arrived a day before S&P Global’s flash purchasing managers’ survey showed British business activity cooling. The composite index fell to 51.7 in September from 52.5 in August, while the manufacturing index edged up to 52.0, according to the S&P Global release as reported by investingLive. Chris Williamson, chief business economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said growth, confidence and employment “are all being hamstrung by high energy prices, elevated business costs, geopolitical worries, higher market borrowing costs and uncertainty over government policy at home in the run up to the autumn Budget.” ... Three things will decide whether the Ineos Hull pause becomes something more permanent. The first is the gas price itself, which has almost doubled since July. The second is whether Ineos can secure American liquefied natural gas on better terms, a process the BBC says could take up to a year. The third is policy: whether governments in London and Brussels act on the tariff and anti-dumping measures Ineos is asking for, and whether support such as the £350m chemicals fund reaches sites like Saltend in time to matter. Until one of those moves, Europe’s last world-scale acetyls plants will sit quiet on Humberside.

headline: Latin America's Stablecoin Economy Just Hit $594 Billion. Brazil Is About to Test How Much of It Is Real | CoinAligator
summary_text: A new Chainalysis report puts Latin America's 2026 crypto economy at $593.8 billion, with dollar stablecoins now handling 32% of the region's cross-border crypto value — driven less by trading than by households in Venezuela, Argentina and Brazil using USDT as a bank account. That growth collides head-on with Brazil's central bank, which bans stablecoin settlement in cross-border payments starting October 1. ... Latin America's crypto economy grew 9.8% to $593.8 billion in transaction activity over the year to mid-2026, according to Chainalysis's 2026 Geography of Cryptocurrency report published September 23. But the growth wasn't bitcoin traders piling back in. It was dollar stablecoins: USDT and USDC now account for 32% of the region's cross-border crypto value, 22% of domestic peer-to-peer activity and 17.6% of the balances sitting in personal wallets, as households and small merchants in high-inflation economies increasingly use them less like a trading chip and more like a savings account they're not supposed to have. ... Brazil is still the region's biggest single market at $252.5 billion in activity — 47% of the regional total — even though overall Brazilian crypto activity actually contracted 1.6% over the period. What grew inside that shrinking pie was stablecoins specifically: stablecoin activity in Brazil rose 495% year-over-year, and stablecoin inflows onto domestic platforms climbed to 12.5% of the total, up from just 1.5% two years earlier. Mexico's monthly stablecoin cross-border volume has roughly quadrupled since early 2024 to $1.8 billion by June, and 81% of all Mexican crypto activity now runs through a stablecoin. In Argentina, where consumer inflation ran 211% in 2023 and 118% in 2024, the number of wallets holding more than $10,000 in stablecoins grew 82% year-over-year, and exchange Bitso reports stablecoins now make up more than 70% of crypto purchases on its platform. Venezuela is the extreme case: crypto activity there grew 107.2%, cross-border stablecoin outflows surged 891% quarter-over-quarter, and Chainalysis found merchants reporting that 40% of their income now arrives in USDT. ... StraitsX co-founder and CEO Tianwei Liu, whose regional read is cited in the same report, put the driver plainly: stablecoins in Latin America serve "dollar access, remittances and protection against inflation or capital controls" rather than trading appetite. The country data backs that up — the fastest stablecoin growth is concentrated in the economies with the worst currency problems, not the ones with the deepest crypto-trading culture. But that growth is arriving just as Brazil, the region's anchor market, moves to wall off exactly the use case Liu describes. Central bank Resolution BCB 561, effective October 1, bars licensed foreign-exchange providers from settling cross-border payments in stablecoins or any other crypto asset; those payments now have to route through a conventional FX transaction or a real-denominated account instead. Separately, exchanges and brokers face a new minimum capital requirement of 37.2 million reais (roughly $7 million) to keep operating, with lower tiers down to 10.8 million reais (roughly $2 million) for smaller custodial and service providers — firms that don't secure authorization have to shut down their Brazilian operations. Rio Times has reported that four exchanges have already wound down in Brazil this year rather than clear that bar. ... The regional numbers deserve a reality check the Chainalysis data itself supplies: worldwide, genuine point-of-sale stablecoin payments — people actually spending the tokens rather than trading, saving or wiring them across a border — total only about $390 billion against roughly $35 trillion in total stablecoin volume, and Latin America and Africa combined still account for less than $1 billion of that true payment figure. Most of what's showing up in Brazil's, Mexico's and Argentina's totals is dollar-holding and remittance-adjacent transfer, not people buying groceries with USDT. What our own eight-exchange composite can confirm is the more basic question underneath all of this: whether the peg is holding up under the demand. It is. As of this morning, USDC was pricing at $0.9999 across seven tracked venues and USDT at $0.9998 across three, both essentially dead-on their dollar peg with no thin-liquidity flag on either. Bitcoin, for reference, was last at $84,154 on the same composite. A region absorbing this much incremental stablecoin demand without moving the peg is itself informative — it suggests issuers are managing redemptions fine so far, which is exactly the assumption Brazil's regulators are betting they don't need to stress-test with an outright settlement ban. ... Latin America is turning into the clearest live test of what stablecoins are actually for. If Brazil's October rules succeed in shifting settlement back onto bank rails without denting underlying demand, that's evidence the demand is substitutable — just another payment corridor a regulator can route around. If usage keeps climbing anyway, through P2P channels and self-custody wallets a central bank can't easily police, that's evidence the demand is about dollar access itself, not the specific rails carrying it. Either way, the region that adopted stablecoins first — for its own currency problems, not for trading — is about to show the rest of the world what happens when a government tries to put that particular habit back in the bank.

headline: Brazil’s CVM rulemaking shift raises transparency concerns
summary_text: Brazil’s CVM rulemaking shift raises transparency concerns ## Market groups and former officials question governance changes as the securities regulator gains a much larger budget and advances tokenization plans Por Liane Thedim — Rio de Janeiro 25/09/2026 08h57 Atualizado 25/09/2026 08h57 Antônio Carlos Berwanger — Foto: Leo Pinheiro/Valor A change in how the Securities and Exchange Commission of Brazil (CVM) drafts regulations has heightened market concerns after months of negative news that have shaken confidence in the regulator. Under the new arrangement, rules may be drafted under the direct coordination of the CVM’s board, without the involvement of the Market Development Superintendence (SDM), which had traditionally overseen the process. Until now, rulemaking followed clearly defined stages that included regulatory impact assessments and public consultations. Market participants now fear the change could reduce transparency. ... In a joint statement, the Capital Markets Investors Association (Amec) and the Brazilian Institute of Corporate Governance (IBGC) requested clarification and said they were watching “with caution” the broader possibility of drafting new rules outside the area traditionally responsible for the work. The two organizations defended continued participation by the regulator’s technical staff. “The reports raise relevant questions, although they do not yet allow conclusions about possible irregularities. That does not diminish the need for clarification and governance mechanisms that preserve confidence in CVM decisions,” the statement said. ... The change was approved by the CVM board on Sept. 15 and amended CVM Resolution 67 of 2022. Presented by director João Accioly, the proposal allows the board to assign responsibility for coordinating the drafting of new rules to one of its own members or to another superintendence. Accioly voted in favor alongside CVM Chair Otto Lobo and director Igor Muniz. Director Marina Copola voted against the proposal. People familiar with the regulator, who asked not to be identified, told Valor on Thursday (Sept. 24) that concerns about a potential weakening of governance have become even more significant after the Federal Supreme Court ordered the government to transfer 70% of the revenue from the regulatory inspection fee to the CVM. The regulator’s budget, initially projected at R$41 million t his year, is expected to rise to about R$639 million over 12 months. “How will the decision-making process work for the CVM to allocate that money?” a former board member asked. The CVM’s current board is chaired by Lobo and also includes Accioly, Copola and Muniz. ... Lobo, for example, has repeatedly pointed to tokenization as a potential answer to several problems in Brazil’s financial market, including fraud prevention in cases such as Banco Master. Specialists, however, say tokenization requires extensive supervisory training because it could bring many more participants into a market that is now largely concentrated at B3. “Will the CVM know how to supervise it? Will it be able to build the necessary capabilities in time?” another former board member asked. The CVM’s Tokenization Working Grou p, created to prepare proposals on the subject, has itself faced criticism over what some market participants describe as a lack of transparency in its discussions. “Even within the CVM, people don’t know what is happening in this group,” the former director said. ... Contacted by Valor on Thursday, the CVM repeated an official statement issued the previous day saying the group “involves members of the Board and 14 superintendences, with input from members of society, in a transparent process of dialogue.” The regulator said on Sept. 16 that its technical staff had submitted to the board a draft resolution for a distributed ledger technology (DLT) pilot covering experimental securities issuance, distribution, trading, custody and settlement. ... Another issue drawing market attention is the internalization of securities orders, which allows brokerages to execute clients’ trades internally rather than sending them to B3. The debate has been under way in Brazil since 2007, driven in part by pressure from large brokerages. This year, the CVM said it had completed its regulatory impact assessment and recommended only partial flexibility, removing some restrictions rather than fully liberalizing the practice. “Order internalization is a sensitive issue, but one that has been pushed by market participants,” another person familiar with the CVM said. In its official statement, the regulator said the change to its rulemaking process “aims to streamline the regulatory agenda and accelerate development.” Amec and IBGC, however, said that “any gains in procedural speed must preserve both public consultations and the participation of technical teams.” ... The CVM said its board has always held full responsibility for analyzing matters within the regulator’s remit, describing the previous arrangement as a practice that had been “interrupted for a short period” and has now been restored. People familiar with the process gave a different account. “In the past, it was common for directors to take charge of a particular rule to make things easier. It ends up moving faster,” one source said. “Since the SDM already existed, there was generally coordination between the area and the director, including to ensure a public hearing, standardized drafting and so on.” In 2022, the source said, mandatory routing through the SDM was established as a governance safeguard. “It is a slower process, but it is carried out with a high degree of quality and standardization, with accountability to the market as a whole. Removing the SDM’s exclusive role is very bad.” Staff reaction The decision prompted a strong reaction among CVM employees and led the National Union of CVM Employees (SindCVM) to issue a letter also defending the participation of technical departments in drafting regulations. The union also expressed concern about criticism directed at the SDM. The CVM said there were “indications” that the department had “great difficulty” managing the regulatory agenda and “conducting processes satisfactorily,” while also questioning the attention it had given to tokenization. The SDM has been headed since 2015 by Antônio Carlos Berwanger, a career CVM employee who was nominated by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in August for the regulator’s last vacant board seat. Berwanger’s name came from a three-person list organized by SindCVM with participation from the regulator’s staff. Widely regarded within the institution as a highly qualified technical official, Berwanger is described as having good relations with the team and extensive knowledge of innovation and digital assets. His nomination process, however, has stalled and, people interviewed by Valor said, has faced pressure to remain frozen. The proximity of the elections has further complicated the Senate Economic Affairs Committee’s agenda, and no confirmation hearing has been scheduled. Lobo took over as CVM chair in June and is due to serve until July 2027. Accioly’s term runs through December 2026, Muniz’s through December 2029 and Copola’s through December 2028.

headline: Afya, Yduqs merge to create R$9bn education group
summary_text: Afya, Yduqs merge to create R$9bn education group ... Afya and Yduqs agreed to merge in a deal that will create an education company with net revenue of about R$9 billion. The transaction was confirmed in a material fact notice released Wednesday night (Sept. 23). Afya, a medical education company, will control 69% of the combined group. Yduqs, one of Brazil’s largest higher-education companies, will account for the remaining 31%, with its shareholders entitled to receive at least R$750 million in dividends. German media and services group Bertelsmann, Afya’s largest shareholder, will hold 47.3% of the combined company and have seats on its board of directors. The exact number of seats is still being determined. Governance of the combined group will be led by Bertelsmann’s Kay Krafft. ... Private-equity firm Advent and the Zaher family, both Yduqs shareholders for at least a decade, will each own about 5% of the combined company and have one board seat. The board will also include an independent director. “We have always supported a merger. The two companies are very complementary,” said Rossano Marques, Yduqs’s current CEO. In the combined company, Marques will head higher education outside the medical segment. “It is a transaction that delivers the best outcome for all shareholders, on both sides. Yduqs’s medical students will gain access to and strengthen our healthcare platform,” said Afya CEO Virgílio Gibbon, who will lead the new group. Financial profile Based on the 12 months ended June 2026, the combined company had net revenue of R$9.4 billion, adjusted EBITDA of R$3.6 billion and adjusted net income of R$1.3 billion. About 55% of net revenue and 66% of adjusted EBITDA come from the companies’ premium businesses—Afya, Yduqs’s medical education arm Idomed and business school Ibmec. Medical education alone accounts for about 45% of total net revenue. Pro forma leverage is about 1.4 times. If Yduqs generates more than R$750 million in cash, its shareholders may receive additional dividends. For every R$1 distributed above that amount, the agreed adjustment is R$2.226 “in order to preserve the agreed shareholding structure unchanged.” The transaction also establishes a 50% dividend payout ratio. Synergies and listing The companies estimate R$2 billion in synergies from lower general expenses, technology costs and capital expenditures. Afya will delist from Nasdaq, where its shares have low liquidity. The combined group will remain listed on Brazil’s B3 stock exchange, as Yduqs is today, and will retain the Yduqs name. The deadline to complete the transaction is March 31, 2028. If either party fails to meet its obligations, termination fees range from R$325 million to R$625 million. The merger will create a company with 5,900 medical-school seats and about 1.5 million students across all undergraduate programs. The group will also own well-known brands including Ibmec, Estácio and Unigranrio. Sector consolidation The deal marks the first merger between two publicly traded higher-education groups in Brazil and could pave the way for other combinations in an industry where consolidation has been discussed for years. Cogna and Yduqs resumed merger talks in 2024, but negotiations did not advance. Cruzeiro do Sul, Vitru and Ser Educacional have also held discussions about potential transactions, most of them with investment banks already hired. Afya was advised by Bank of America, while Yduqs worked with BTG Pactual. Because scale is particularly important in education, especially in distance learning, the Afya-Yduqs combination is likely to intensify competition for other large groups. Companies also face new rules for distance education, with a transition period ending in 2027 that will require additional investment. The education sector has lost some of its appeal to investors, particularly foreign investors, amid weak enrollment growth. Demand for higher education is closely tied to household income, while Brazilian consumers currently face high debt levels. Until recently, Afya was not widely seen as a likely merger candidate because of its heavy focus on medical degrees, which are considerably more profitable than most other undergraduate programs. That profitability created a large gap in market capitalization between Afya and other education groups. Afya is currently valued at $1.2 billion, while Yduqs has a market capitalization of R$2.4 billion. However, increased competition in medical education, partly driven by legal disputes over the opening of new medical-school slots, has changed that environment and pushed Afya to look for ways to diversify its business. Yduqs combines a large medical education operation with other undergraduate businesses, including Ibmec, a business school focused on higher-income students that tends to be less exposed to economic downturns. Regulatory approval The transaction still requires approval from shareholders at an extraordinary general meeting and clearance from Brazil’s antitrust regulator, Cade. Market participants see relatively little overlap between the two companies, with the main concentration in Rio de Janeiro, Teresina and Ji-Paraná, in the state of Rondônia. Even if regulators require asset sales in some of those cities, such divestitures are not expected to prevent the deal from going ahead.

headline: Tokenized asset market in Brazil reaches R$10bn
summary_text: Tokenized asset market in Brazil reaches R$10bn ## Market grew tenfold in one year and is heavily concentrated in credit, study says ... 26 1 ... 11h ... CVM Chairman Otto Lobo — Foto: Leo Pinheiro/Valor The market for tokenized assets grew approximately tenfold in just one year in Brazil and surpassed R$10 billion in August 2026, compared with just over R$1 billion during the same period last year. The growth, however, is heavily concentrated in credit: 88% of the value of tokenized assets in the country is in private-credit assets. The data are part of the 2026 edition of the Brazil Tokenization Report, produced by Nexa Finance and obtained by Valor Investe. ... tokenized assets - Securitization ... s CVM ... for tokenized debt crowdfunding ... Nexa’s survey shows that, of the more than R$10 billion already tokenized, R$7 billion is spread across seven private-credit classes, another R$2 billion across eight receivables classes, and approximately R$1 billion across three multi-asset fund classes. The entire remainder of the market—another seven asset classes—totals just R$26 million. The concentration becomes even more evident when looking at the products with the highest volumes. Five of the 25 asset classes mapped account for 94% of all tokenized money in the country, and four of them are credit instruments. The pace of expansion also stands out in international comparison. According to the report, the value of tokenized assets in Brazil increased approximately tenfold in the 12 months through August, while the global market grew by about twofold over the same period. Despite this jump, tokenization still represents a small share of Brazil’s financial market. Tokenized private-credit assets account for just 0.3% of the country’s R$2.7 trillion stock of corporate credit. The gap is even wider when considering the technology’s potential market. The report cites the R$11 trillion investment-fund sector, R$9.3 trillion in federal government debt, and R$1.5 trillion in mortgage lending. ... The growth comes at a time when tokenization is also gaining ground in capital-markets regulation. The report highlights CVM Resolution 88, originally created to regulate “crowdfunding” offerings—smaller-scale collective investment platforms—which has become one of the main entry points for tokenized offerings by providing a simpler, lower-cost route. As transactions have grown in size, part of the market has begun using CVM Resolution 160, which governs public offerings of securities. In the first half of this year alone, R$3.1 billion was tokenized through this route, which has already become the leading channel by volume, according to the survey. Given its scale and potential, tokenization has become a priority under Otto Lobo’s leadership of the CVM, Brazil’s Securities and Exchange Commission. The agency’s chairman has been advocating for the creation of a regulatory and supervisory framework capable of overseeing both the traditional market and assets registered on blockchain networks. In July, the CVM created a working group specifically dedicated to the issue, bringing together specialists from 14 areas of the agency. Last week, the group delivered its first proposal: the creation of the CVM DLT Pilot Program, which would allow the testing of transactions involving shares, debentures, receivables certificates, fund units, and other securities on distributed-ledger technology networks. The tests could cover everything from the issuance and offering of assets to trading, custody, and settlement, with the CVM having real-time access to transaction records. The draft still needs to be reviewed by the agency’s collegial board. Commenting on the tokenization agenda, Lobo said the market is already beginning to move beyond the testing phase and into a stage of actual operations. “It is an evolution, not a revolution,” he said, arguing that Brazil’s regulations should be built around the market’s needs and supported by infrastructure that enables the supervision of assets.
