headline: 2026 LATAM Crypto Adoption: Latin America Grew 9.8%
summary_text: in the 2 ... The factors behind crypto growth vary widely across the Americas. In some markets, such as Mexico, crypto is increasingly intersecting with existing financial offerings; in others, such as Venezuela and Argentina, it is providing a crucial alternative to traditional financial services or access to much-needed foreign currency that’s in short supply. This may help explain why the pace — and character — of adoption can differ so sharply across Latin America. ... At the same time, stablecoins took up a larger share of the crypto that individuals held and moved across the region. Stablecoins gained sustained ground across every measure we examined in 2026. By June, they accounted for nearly a third (32.1%) of cross-border value, as well as 22.1% of domestic P2P and 17.6% of personal wallet balances. Although stablecoins’ rising share of total crypto value does not necessarily mean stablecoin activity increased at the same pace — because a decline in other crypto asset value can also affect the measure — the trend nonetheless underscores their increasingly dominant role in Latin America’s crypto economy. ... The way Latin Americans hold crypto is also changing. During the report period, both self-custody and service balances fell across the region, as prices cratered from all-time highs during the crypto market correction that began in October 2025. But, amid this broad-based decline, self-custody balances fell much more sharply, by 66.7%, compared with 28.0% for services. That divergence builds on a longer-term structural shift toward services. The share of Latin American crypto balances held with services has risen steadily in recent years, reaching 71.2% in June 2026 — well above the global share of 68.0%. ... This growing preference for services may point to a new stage in the region’s adoption story. As Latin Americans increasingly use crypto to move money, make payments, convert assets, and access liquidity, they may also be looking for more established services through which to do it. ... Brazil’s crypto economy is becoming more concentrated among domestic, or Brazil-based, platforms — potentially a result of greater regulatory clarity, investment, and stronger local offerings. Domestic exchanges that once accounted for just 1.5% of inflows now receive 12.5%. ... This migration accelerated just as Brazil’s domestic exchange landscape faced a shakeup. In February 2026, Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) introduced new rules for the country’s virtual asset service providers, affecting their governance, risk management, security, and compliance. Crucially, the new rules also introduced substantial minimum capital requirements. While designed to strengthen Brazil’s crypto market, those higher barriers could prove difficult for smaller firms to meet — setting the stage for further consolidation. ... BCB’s higher barriers to entry may end up instilling greater consumer confidence in the firms that survive, says Julia Rosin, president of crypto industry association ABCripto. “When rules arrive, trust follows.” She says stronger regulations are the single most important factor in the long-term growth of Brazil’s retail crypto scene. Rosin describes this transition as “institutional maturation.” The distinction helps explain what is happening beneath Brazil’s slowing topline growth. Clearer regulations give banks, corporates, fintechs, and other established financial institutions greater confidence to engage with crypto counterparties, potentially expanding B2B demand and making it easier to build digital-asset products within existing financial businesses. ... Helping drive this growth are Brazil’s businesses, said ABCripto’s Rosin. “The market’s own view is that stablecoins are for companies first — ahead of financial institutions and consumers.” She said businesses are using stablecoins for liquidity and also to make cross-border transfers. Bitso’s Reid shared a similar view: “In Brazil, stablecoins have been more of a B2B” tool, he said. The success of BCB’s digital payments system — called Pix, which is used by 91% of Brazilians — makes stablecoins less prominent for everyday payments by regular consumers. ... If Brazil represents the scale and maturation of Latin America’s crypto economy, Venezuela represents its most acute case of crypto as financial necessity. Years of inflation, currency depreciation, and limited access to dollars had already pushed households and businesses toward alternative ways to hold and move value. In 2026, political rupture accelerated that shift. ... Those outflows were not enough to derail Venezuela’s broad growth story. The country’s crypto economy reached $39.1 billion in activity in the report period, a 107.2% increase. That growth rate was nearly eight times that of Colombia, the regional market closest to Venezuela’s overall crypto activity. ... Marianella Vanci, senior reporter at CriptoNoticias, describes an “accelerated redollarization” increasingly taking place outside traditional banking channels, through stablecoins such as USDT and USDC. Merchants Vanci interviewed in Venezuela reported receiving close to 40% of their income in USDT, while freelancers, businesses, and remote workers reported also increasingly receiving payments in crypto. For these users, stablecoins offer a way to transact while limiting exposure to bolívar depreciation and some of the frictions associated with traditional financial channels. ... Our analysis finds that Mexico is 11th overall in our grassroots adoption index. It is Latin America’s third-largest crypto economy, with $77.6 billion in activity during the report period. Over $47 billion (61%) of those flows came through stablecoins. Historically much of Mexico’s demand for stablecoins has been for the dollar-denominated variants that dominate the global crypto economy. That’s beginning to shift, says Bitso’s Ben Reid: “We are also seeing strong demand for peso-denominated stablecoins like MXNB as a fiat ramp currency, because companies struggle to find reliable fiat ramp and custody solutions within Mexico.” ... Monthly stablecoin value on corridors with either endpoint in Mexico reached $1.8 billion in June 2026 — roughly four times its early 2024 level — and was still climbing at the end of the period. The U.S.-Mexico corridor is particularly important to this growth. One of the world’s largest remittance corridors, banks and money transfer providers have traditionally dominated it. Stablecoins are becoming a meaningful part of how value moves between the two countries, said Reid. ... This year’s data captures two sides of Latin America’s crypto market. One is about growth from maturation. In Brazil, for instance, a more comprehensive regulatory framework is taking shape, bringing greater certainty and new offerings to the market even as smaller players face pressure. ABCripto’s Rosin describes this certainty as key to unlocking institutional adoption. The other is about growth from necessity. Venezuela is the clearest example of a dynamic we have seen across the region for years: where traditional finance falls short, demand for crypto becomes stronger. While different forces are at play, they are leading to similar outcomes: crypto assets are becoming more deeply embedded in how people and businesses hold, move, and access money across the region. As Bitso’s Reid put it, “crypto, and stablecoins in particular, has evolved beyond early adoption to become an integral part of Latin America’s financial landscape.” The question that remains is how far this integration will go, especially in terms of institutional growth and investment. As Campa puts it, “Until now, much of the industry has concentrated on helping customers buy, sell and hold crypto.” The next step is connecting those assets to the real economy.

headline: Chile, Mexico and Brazil tighten PLD rules — CiberLATAM
summary_text: Between August and September 2026, regulators across Latin America moved data protection, cybersecurity, fraud prevention and virtual asset rules toward stricter regimes for banks, fintechs and other regulated entities. The common pattern is more monitoring, more traceability, more data governance and more demonstrable accountability to supervisors. ... Chile, Mexico, Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Paraguay, Argentina, Uruguay and Bolivia entered the second half of 2026 with overlapping reforms that all point in the same direction: more traceability, more reporting obligations, more automated controls and more direct supervisory or sanctioning power over banks, fintechs and other regulated entities. The shift is staged, but not fragmented. In most countries, the relevant calendar now runs from November 2026 through January 2028, with interim milestones already forcing changes to processes, systems and internal governance. The clearest picture is in Mexico, where Agreement 115/2026 rewrote the General Rules under the LFPIORPI and moved compliance for vulnerable activities away from a file-and-notice model toward documented risk management, automated monitoring, customer classification and annual audits. The research material shows that this is not just a semantic change. The risk-based assessment requirement begins in March 2027 for several operational components, while the general effective date starts on November 30, 2026 and extends through January 2028. At the same time, Brazil closed its authorization framework for virtual asset service providers and later added specific anti-fraud controls that take effect in January 2027. In data protection and identity fraud, Colombia and Chile delivered two particularly relevant regulatory signals for banking and telecom. Colombia put Statutory Law 2573 into force, strengthening identity validation, protecting victims of impersonation and requiring sufficient and reasonable digital security measures. Chile still formally keeps Law 21,719 set for December 2026, although the executive branch has already asked to delay it by one year and reinforce the institutional framework for the future Personal Data Protection Agency. Peru followed a similar tightening path, with the SBS linking cybersecurity, transparency, operational continuity and BaaS. Paraguay deserves separate treatment because it brings three fronts together at once: a new comprehensive personal data law with a specialized agency, an annual reporting duty for cryptoassets and an automated information exchange system between the DNIT and banks. That makes it one of the few countries in the report where privacy, taxation and access to banking information are moving in sync. The practical effect for entities is straightforward: customer data, tax filings, bank transactions and virtual asset activity are starting to converge through formal channels of exchange and verification. Threat conditions also explain why these frameworks are hardening. Casbaneiro kept targeting banks across the region using distributed infrastructure, while actors such as CL-CRI-1163, BREEZE COMET and campaigns assisted by language models added pressure on fraud and security teams. The practical result for banks and fintechs is a 2026 to 2027 calendar in which compliance, cybersecurity, personal data and fraud analytics stop operating as silos and move onto the same operational plane. ... The available material shows that 2026 became a hinge year for compliance frameworks in the region. On one side are laws on personal data protection, identity fraud and incident reporting that are entering into force or nearing it. On the other are transition periods that push full implementation into 2027 or 2028. That combination matters because the market is no longer dealing with a single effective date, but with staged schedules, mandatory appointments, methodology documentation and testing requirements. Chile, for example, has Law No. 21,719, published in December 2024 and scheduled to take effect on December 1, 2026, although the Ministry of Economy said on September 1, 2026 that the government proposed moving that date to December 1, 2027 to buy time for the Personal Data Protection Agency to be set up and for application standards to be defined. According to Anguita & Osorio, the bill would also adjust the agency's institutional design, expand the board from three to five members and allow a written warning as the first sanction during the first 12 months of application. Paraguay arrives with a different but related picture. Law No. 7593/2025 creates the National Personal Data Protection Agency within MITIC, sets a 24-month vacatio legis and adds concrete rules on incident notification, international transfers and sanctioning powers. At the same time, the DNIT published General Resolution No. 47/2026 on cryptoassets, which requires residents and platforms to report annual transactions above US$5,000 through Marangatu, under obligation 959-DJI with an annual filing deadline. The country is also moving toward a data-sharing platform between DNIT and banks, based on web services, which speeds access to financial movements during audits. Peru, meanwhile, shows a more fragmented but still coherent sequence. Supreme Decree No. 016-2024-JUS modernized the regulations for Personal Data Protection Law 29733 and set staggered deadlines for appointing the Personal Data Officer. At the same time, the SBS has been updating its incident and continuity framework, with one cybersecurity resolution and another on operational incidents under public consultation. Resolution SBS No. 01747-2026, meanwhile, sets the operating model for Banking as a Service, with board policies, prior risk assessment, continuous monitoring and minimum contractual terms. Mexico, Brazil and Argentina add another layer that should be read as convergence between fraud prevention, operational risk and beneficial ownership control. In Mexico, the LFPIORPI reform centers on risk, monitoring, auditing and customer classification. In Argentina, the BCRA added a specific section for fraud risk management within operational risk guidelines. headline: Medellin Native David Velez to Invest US$1.58 Billion in Colombia, Calls for End to Usury Cap
summary_text: Nubank will invest $1.58 billion in Colombia by 2030 as David Velez calls for an end to the usury cap. Photo: Nubank / CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons. ... David Velez, the Medellin-born founder and CEO of Nubank, plans to invest approximately US$1.58 billion in Colombia between 2026 and 2030 as the digital bank expands its presence in the country. Velez announced the investment alongside Nu Colombia General Manager Marcela Torres and Colombia Fintech President Gabriel Santos, saying the company intends to remain in Colombia for the long term. Nu entered Colombia in 2021 with a credit card and has since expanded its financial products. The company now holds more than US$3.49 billion in deposits across savings accounts and CDTs, or fixed-term deposit certificates. Velez said Nu grew from zero to five million customers within five years, including customers who previously lacked access to credit, and that the company’s next goal is to become one of Colombia’s leading financial institutions. The planned US$1.58 billion investment will focus on four areas: advanced data and artificial intelligence platforms, new financial services, expansion of strategic teams, and capital to support what Velez described as “responsible, scaled growth.” ... Torres also presented figures on Nu’s position in Colombia’s banking sector, saying the company now has the fourth-largest base of individual deposits nationwide. Nu currently holds roughly 10% of Colombia’s credit card market and about 7% of individual deposits, according to figures presented by the company. It has reached 6 million customers, equivalent to approximately 14% to 15% of Colombia’s adult population. Torres said Nu’s credit card business is growing 60% year over year. She also argued that without the company’s growth, Colombia’s overall credit card market would have contracted. According to Nu, nearly 40% of customers who joined the company over the past year had no previous relationship with Colombia’s financial sector. The company also said it accounted for 25% of people who gained access to credit nationwide during the same period, despite holding about 10% of the credit card market. Women represented 59% of those newly included customers, compared with what Nu described as a sector average of 41%. Torres acknowledged that credit risk could increase as the company expands lending to populations that have historically had less access to the formal financial system. ... ## Why David Velez wants to end Colombia’s usury cap Velez also called for changes to Colombia’s usury rate, the maximum interest rate lenders are legally permitted to charge. He described the cap as “the biggest obstacle to financial inclusion in Colombia,” arguing that it limits regulated financial institutions’ ability to lend to higher-risk customers. According to Velez, only 20% of Colombia’s population has access to credit, leaving many others dependent on informal lenders, including those known as “gota a gota,” or daily-payment lenders. He said interest rates charged by such lenders can range from 500% to 2,000%, while borrowers do not receive the consumer protections available through regulated financial institutions. Velez argued that because regulated banks cannot price loans according to the risk associated with individual borrowers beyond the legal ceiling, lenders may reject higher-risk applicants rather than extend credit. He proposed two possible changes. The first would end the practice of combining different credit products when calculating a single usury ceiling and instead establish separate limits for different types of credit. The second would eliminate the interest rate cap altogether, a measure Velez argues would increase credit availability for consumers and small businesses. Velez said he hopes Colombia’s next administration will address the issue, arguing that changes involving interest rates, reduced dependence on cash and faster implementation of open finance regulations could significantly accelerate financial inclusion.

headline: Latin America accelerates in fintech: inclusion, payments and regulation at the center of the debate
summary_text: - Only 35,6% of Colombian adults have access to formal credit, while 'gota a gota' (loan sharking) charges exorbitant rates. - Bre-B has accumulated more than 1.200 billion transactions and is positioned as the cornerstone of payments modernization. - The fintech industry is calling for regulatory changes to lift Bre-B limits, eliminate the 4x1000 and regulate crypto assets. - Guatemala is emerging as a promising fintech market with artificial intelligence as a lever for growth. ... The fintech sector in Latin America is experiencing a boom. The influx of investment, the digitization of consumer habits, and the emergence of new players are transforming a landscape that still suffers from significant imbalances. While payment infrastructure is advancing rapidly, access to credit remains the major challenge, and this is where financial technology companies have a crucial role to play. Proof of this is the eighth edition of the Latam Fintech Market, held in Barranquilla, which brought together the main players in the ecosystem to discuss the challenges and opportunities of an industry that is growing at an unstoppable pace. Among the hottest topics: the interoperability of payment systems, the rise of artificial intelligence, and the need to adapt the regulatory framework to a reality that is moving faster than the laws. ... The data is striking: over 96% of Colombian adults have a deposit account, but only 35,6% manage to access a formal loan . This gap is the perfect breeding ground for the infamous "gota a gota" (drop by drop) loan sharking to become the number one competitor to traditional banks. According to figures presented at the event, this informal lending system charges interest rates as high as 382% for individuals and up to 666% for businesses, meaning that those who resort to it can end up paying nine times the original amount in just two months. This is no small problem. In 2025, 480.000 people were excluded from the formal credit system, and in the last three years, that number has risen to three million. Behind this situation lie political decisions, but also a model that has failed to adapt to changing risk profiles. Gabriel Santos, CEO of Colombia Fintech, summed it up clearly: people aren't leaving the system because their habits change, but because a political decision has closed the door to credit. In rural areas, penetration drops to as low as 12%, leaving millions of citizens with no viable options beyond predatory lending. Faced with this scenario, fintech companies are emerging as a viable alternative. The sector's global revenue is around $504.000 billion and is growing four times faster than traditional banking. In Colombia, six out of every ten dollars invested in startups go to fintech projects, and across the region, more than 470 million people are underbanked and awaiting solutions. The market is ready: all that's needed is a supportive regulatory framework to ensure that alternative credit, factoring, and revenue-based loans reach those who need them. ... The other major story is that of Bre-B, the Central Bank's instant payment system, which has processed over 1.200 billion transactions and moved nearly 184 trillion pesos since its launch. With 113 million registered keys, 35 million users, and 3,7 million connected businesses, it has become an essential component of the country's financial infrastructure. Even so, it still has enormous room for growth: 80% of daily transactions occur between individuals, and only 4,9% of keys belong to legal entities. The industry is clear on this: for Bre-B to become a true engine of the economy, it's necessary to raise the operating limits and allow its use as a government revenue collection channel. Colombia Fintech has formally requested that government payments, such as subsidies and payroll, be channeled through this system, which could move approximately 8 trillion pesos annually. Furthermore, the arrival of recurring automatic debits, facilitated by fintechs like DRUO, is paving the way for schools, insurance companies, and subscription platforms to migrate from cards to this infrastructure—a step already successfully implemented in Brazil through Pix. ... Artificial intelligence is undoubtedly the great catalyst for change. In Guatemala, for example, the fintech sector has experienced exponential growth thanks to a young and tech-hungry market. Michel Caputi, Strategic Alliances Manager at BI, affirms that the Central American country has the perfect conditions: a dominant regional GDP, low credit penetration, and accelerated technology adoption. AI is enabling fintech companies to offer personalized products, from micro-investments to cross-border payments, and is also allowing large corporations to get on board. Real-world applications are already emerging: autonomous agents capable of trading currencies or executing transactions without human intervention, and algorithms that assess credit risk based on digital signals. AI is also democratizing access to developed markets, which until recently was reserved for the very wealthy. In Guatemala, interest in digital assets, such as stablecoins, is growing strongly, and a regulatory ecosystem that provides security for investors is expected to be consolidated in the coming years. This development isn't just theoretical. The application of AI in wealth management is revolutionizing how users interact with their money. Platforms that analyze markets in real time, answer contextualized questions, and recommend investments tailored to each individual's profile are already a reality in the European market, and Latin America doesn't want to be left behind. The key is for technology to bridge the historical gap between personalized advice, reserved for high-net-worth individuals, and standardized products with little support. ... Without a clear regulatory framework, the sector will be unable to reach its full potential. For this reason, Colombia Fintech has put forward a series of proposals ranging from a review of open finance to a modification of the method for calculating the current bank interest rate. The industry group argues that the current methodology, based on a single average, does not reflect the differences between products and risk profiles, which particularly disadvantages higher-risk consumers. The regulation of cryptocurrencies is another open front. According to industry data, six million Colombians already trade cryptocurrencies, and more than half of the funds are allocated to stablecoins. Despite this massive adoption, the lack of specific regulations creates uncertainty for businesses and investors. The request is clear: recognize the magnitude of this market and establish a framework that provides legal certainty without stifling innovation. The tax chapter is also generating friction. The Bogotá Mayor's proposal to modify the Industry and Commerce Tax (ICA) for financial activities, calculating it on income instead of profits, has raised concerns. For fintech companies in their growth phase, such a tax could represent an insurmountable burden. The industry is calling for predictable rules that don't stifle companies that are still gaining market share and building their business models. Ultimately, what's at stake in the coming months is whether the authorities will listen to the demands of a sector that's already too large to ignore. Latin American fintech has the potential to lead the region's financial inclusion, but it needs policy to catch up. The payments infrastructure is there, the technology is there, and the talent is there too. All that's missing is an environment that fosters competition and innovation, and that protects citizens without tying their hands.

headline: Latinoamérica acelera en fintech: inclusión, pagos y regulación en el centro del debate
summary_text: El sector fintech en América Latina vive un momento dulce. La llegada de inversión, la digitalización de los hábitos de consumo y la aparición de nuevos actores están transformando un panorama que aún arrastra enormes desequilibrios. Mientras las infraestructuras de pago avanzan a buen ritmo, el acceso al crédito sigue siendo la gran asignatura pendiente, y ahí es donde las empresas de tecnología financiera tienen mucho que decir. Prueba de ello es la octava edición del Latam Fintech Market, celebrada en Barranquilla, que ha reunido a los principales actores del ecosistema para debatir sobre los retos y oportunidades de una industria que crece a un ritmo imparable. Entre los temas más candentes: la interoperabilidad de los sistemas de pago, el auge de la inteligencia artificial y la necesidad de ajustar el marco normativo a una realidad que se mueve más rápido que las leyes. ... El dato es contundente: más del 96% de los adultos colombianos tiene una cuenta de depósito, pero solo un 35,6% logra acceder a un préstamo formal. Esta brecha es el caldo de cultivo perfecto para que el famoso ‘gota a gota’ se convierta en el competidor número uno de la banca tradicional. Según las cifras presentadas durante el evento, este sistema de préstamo informal llega a cobrar tasas cercanas al 382% para personas y hasta 666% para empresas, lo que se traduce en que quien recurre a él puede acabar pagando nueve veces el importe original en apenas dos meses. No es un problema menor. En 2025, 480.000 personas fueron expulsadas del sistema crediticio formal, y en los últimos tres años la cifra asciende a tres millones. Detrás de esta situación hay decisiones políticas, pero también un modelo que no ha sabido adaptarse a los perfiles de riesgo. El presidente ejecutivo de Colombia Fintech, Gabriel Santos, lo resumía con claridad: la gente no sale del sistema porque sus hábitos cambien, sino porque una decisión política le cerró la puerta al crédito. En las zonas rurales, la penetración cae hasta el 12%, lo que deja a millones de ciudadanos sin opciones viables más allá de la usura. Frente a este escenario, las fintech aparecen como una alternativa real. Los ingresos globales del sector rondan los 504.000 millones de dólares y crecen a un ritmo cuatro veces superior al de la banca tradicional. En Colombia, seis de cada diez dólares de inversión en startups van a parar a proyectos fintech, y en toda la región hay más de 470 millones de personas en situación de subbancarización esperando soluciones. El mercado está servido: solo falta que el marco normativo acompañe para que el crédito alternativo, el factoring y los préstamos basados en flujos de ingresos lleguen a quien los necesita. ... La otra gran historia es la de Bre-B, el sistema de pagos inmediatos del Banco de la República, que acumula más de 1.200 millones de transacciones y ha movilizado cerca de 184 billones de pesos desde su lanzamiento. Con 113 millones de llaves registradas, 35 millones de usuarios y 3,7 millones de comercios conectados, se ha convertido en un componente esencial de la infraestructura financiera del país. Aun así, todavía tiene un margen enorme para crecer: el 80% de las transacciones diarias se produce entre personas naturales, y solo el 4,9% de las llaves corresponden a personas jurídicas. La industria lo tiene claro: para que Bre-B se convierta en un verdadero motor de la economía, es necesario levantar los topes de operación y permitir su uso como canal de recaudo estatal. Colombia Fintech ha solicitado formalmente que los pagos del Gobierno, como subsidios y nóminas, se canalicen a través de este sistema, lo que podría mover cerca de 8 billones de pesos al año. Además, la llegada de los débitos automáticos recurrentes, de la mano de fintech como DRUO, está allanando el camino para que colegios, aseguradoras y plataformas de suscripción migren desde las tarjetas hacia esta infraestructura, un paso que ya se dio con éxito en Brasil a través de Pix. ... La inteligencia artificial es, sin duda, el gran catalizador del cambio. En Guatemala, por ejemplo, el sector fintech se ha desarrollado de forma multiplicadora gracias a un mercado joven y ávido de tecnología. Michel Caputi, gerente de Alianzas Estratégicas de BI, asegura que el país centroamericano reúne las condiciones perfectas: un PIB regional dominante, una baja penetración del crédito y una adopción tecnológica acelerada. La IA está permitiendo que las fintech ofrezcan productos personalizados, desde microinversiones hasta pagos transfronterizos, y que las grandes corporaciones también se suban al carro. Ya se están viendo usos reales: agentes autónomos capaces de negociar divisas o ejecutar transacciones sin intervención humana, y algoritmos que evalúan el riesgo crediticio a partir de señales digitales. La IA también está democratizando el acceso a los mercados desarrollados, que hasta hace poco estaba reservado a las grandes fortunas. En Guatemala, el interés por los activos digitales, como las stablecoins, está creciendo con fuerza, y se espera que en los próximos años se consolide un ecosistema regulatorio que dé seguridad a los inversores. El desarrollo no se queda en el plano teórico. La aplicación de la IA en la gestión patrimonial está revolucionando la forma en la que los usuarios interactúan con su dinero. Plataformas que analizan en tiempo real los mercados, responden preguntas contextualizadas y recomiendan inversiones a medida de cada perfil son ya una realidad en el mercado europeo, y la región latinoamericana no quiere quedarse atrás. La clave está en que la tecnología permita superar la brecha histórica entre el asesoramiento personalizado, reservado a los patrimonios elevados, y los productos estandarizados con poco acompañamiento. ... Sin un marco regulatorio claro, el sector no podrá desplegar todo su potencial. Por eso, Colombia Fintech ha puesto sobre la mesa una batería de propuestas que van desde la revisión del open finance hasta la modificación del método para calcular la tasa de interés bancario corriente. El gremio defiende que la metodología actual, basada en un promedio único, no refleja las diferencias entre productos y perfiles de riesgo, lo que perjudica especialmente a los consumidores con mayor riesgo. La regulación de los criptoactivos es otro de los frentes abiertos. Según los datos del gremio, seis millones de colombianos ya operan con criptomonedas, y más de la mitad de los fondos se destinan a stablecoins. A pesar de esta adopción masiva, la ausencia de reglas específicas genera incertidumbre para empresas e inversores. La petición es clara: reconocer la magnitud de este mercado y establecer un marco que aporte seguridad jurídica sin frenar la innovación. El capítulo tributario también genera fricción. La propuesta de la Alcaldía de Bogotá de modificar el impuesto de Industria y Comercio (ICA) para las actividades financieras, calculándolo sobre los ingresos en lugar de sobre las ganancias, ha encendido las alarmas. Para las fintech que están en fase de crecimiento, un impuesto de este tipo podría suponer un lastre insoportable. La industria pide reglas previsibles que no ahoguen a las empresas que todavía están ganando cuota de mercado y construyendo sus modelos de negocio. En definitiva, lo que se juega en los próximos meses es si las autoridades van a escuchar las demandas de un sector que ya es demasiado grande como para ignorarlo. El fintech latinoamericano tiene los mimbres para liderar la inclusión financiera de la región, pero necesita que la política se ponga al día. La infraestructura de pagos ya está, la tecnología ya está, y el talento también. Solo falta un entorno que favorezca la competencia y la innovación, y que proteja a los ciudadanos sin atarles de pies y manos.

headline: Gustavo Carmona (EY): “Brazil offers a combination of scale, corporate sophistication, sector diversity and market depth” - Leaders League
summary_text: Gustavo Carmona leads the international tax and transactions services division of EY Brazil. In this interview, he discusses how Brazil’s tax reform will impact M&A in the country, and assesses the attractiveness of the market to foreign investors. Leaders League: Which legal or regulatory developments are currently having the greatest impact on cross-border transactions? Gustavo Carmona: Today’s most relevant regulatory developments are those that affect not only a transaction’s legal structure but also its long-term value creation. In the Brazilian context, tax reform stands out as one of the most significant themes. The implementation of the CBS and IBS is leading investors to reassess supply chains, operating models, cash flows and long-term investment theses. The focus has shifted from mere tax compliance to encompass competitiveness, profitability and operational integration. At the same time, we’re seeing significantly increased scrutiny of international structures, with greater attention paid to economic substance. Topics such as Pillar Two, adopted in Brazil through the CSLL Surtax (Adicional da CSLL), have come to directly influence investment structures, financing models and after-tax return projections. The evolution of transfer pricing rules is also gaining prominence. Brazil’s adoption of the OECD standard has significantly broadened the analysis of transactions involving services, intangibles, financial operations and corporate restructurings. In many cross-border deals, a transaction’s economic viability depends not only on the legal structure adopted but also on the ability to sustain the allocation of functions, risks and profits across different jurisdictions. Finally, antitrust matters, data protection, technology security and compliance have gained strategic relevance. In cross-border deals, these factors now influence valuation, closing timelines and even the decision to invest in the first place. ... Broadly speaking, we are seeing a convergence between strategy, regulation and risk management. In this environment, taxation has ceased to be merely a risk-mitigation topic and has become a relevant element of value creation and competitive differentiation in transactions. How should tax reform (CBS, IBS, Split Payment) impact the structuring of M&A deals in Brazil in the coming years? Tax reform will likely be the main transformative factor in M&A analysis in Brazil during this decade. ... The regulation of the CBS and IBS marks the reform’s transition into its operational phase, requiring the preparation of systems, processes and business models. At the same time, investors will need to analyze how the reform will affect relative prices, the location of operations, credit recoverability and future profitability. In several sectors, the gradual decline in the relevance of traditional tax incentives tends to alter long-standing competitive dynamics. We also expect growing focus on working capital, especially due to split payment mechanisms and new credit rules. These changes could significantly alter cash conversion for certain businesses, influencing valuation, working capital negotiations, earn-outs and other economic clauses in deals. In practice, we believe the reform will transform taxation from a predominantly defensive exercise into a central element of the investment thesis. Companies better prepared to operate in the new tax environment tend to be perceived as more valuable, more resilient and less risky assets. Which sectors of the Brazilian economy do you believe will lead M&A volume in the coming years? I see five major vectors driving the Brazilian M&A market: energy, infrastructure, technology, mining and agribusiness. Energy and the energy transition should continue attracting significant investment. Brazil holds unique competitive advantages in renewable energy, biofuels and infrastructure tied to decarbonization – themes that continue to draw strong interest from both strategic and financial investors. ... In technology, artificial intelligence is accelerating consolidation and the acquisition of digital capabilities. Many companies are using M&A to rapidly acquire AI, technology and digital transformation capabilities rather than building them internally. Beyond technology itself, we expect growth in transactions related to digital infrastructure, including data centers, connectivity and assets needed to support data-processing-intensive applications. ... Finally, agribusiness will continue to be one of the pillars of Brazilian deal activity, now also extending into segments tied to agricultural technology and logistics, in addition to the already traditional bioenergy and export-chain sectors. How have foreign investors been evaluating Brazil compared to other Latin American markets for investments and acquisitions? Foreign investors continue to see Brazil as a complex market, but one that’s hard to ignore. Compared to other Latin American countries, Brazil offers a distinctive combination of scale, corporate sophistication, sector diversity and market depth. These characteristics allow investors to pursue growth strategies that would often not be feasible in smaller markets. It’s true that challenges such as tax complexity, the regulatory environment and macroeconomic volatility remain present. Even so, the size of the market, the quality of available assets, and opportunities related to energy, infrastructure, agribusiness, mining and consumer goods continue to attract global investors. At the same time, many investors see tax reform as a potential factor for reducing the structural complexity of Brazil’s business environment over the coming years. Although the transition period requires preparation, there is an expectation that the new model will contribute to greater predictability and economic efficiency in the long run. ... For these reasons, although Brazil requires greater preparation and execution capability than other markets in the region, it continues to rank among the priority destinations for international investors in Latin America. In your experience, what most distinguishes an M&A negotiation in Brazil from similar international deals? Brazil’s main distinguishing feature is that value creation in a transaction depends, to a large extent, on the ability to navigate local complexity. In many markets, negotiations focus primarily on commercial and strategic aspects. In Brazil, tax, regulatory, labor and corporate matters frequently exert a direct influence on valuation, acquisition structure and contractual protection mechanisms. Another relevant aspect is the importance of structuring. Decisions related to the form of acquisition, pre-closing reorganizations, and liability succession often carry as much economic impact as the price negotiation itself. In addition, many of the factors that determine a transaction’s success in Brazil relate to post-closing execution. Operational integration, corporate reorganizations, synergy capture, regulatory adaptation and tax efficiency frequently determine the actual value generated after the deal closes. There is also a very distinctive feature of the Brazilian market: the need to combine technical sophistication with pragmatism. The best deals are not necessarily those that eliminate all risk, but those that succeed in identifying the relevant risks, pricing them appropriately, and efficiently allocating responsibilities between buyer and seller. In an environment of constant regulatory, technological and economic change, this ability to turn complexity into opportunity remains one of the key differentiators for successful M&A deals in Brazil. In other words, in Brazil, a transaction’s success depends less on signing the contract and more on the ability to execute an efficient, sustainable integration in a complex and constantly evolving environment.

headline: The Digital Frontier: How the Latam Fintech Market is Redefining Colombia’s Financial Landscape
summary_text: The Colombian financial sector is undergoing a profound metamorphosis. If the recent Latam Fintech Market, held this week in Barranquilla, served as a barometer for the industry, the verdict is clear: the era of "digital experimentation" has ended, and the era of "systemic disruption" has begun. Colombia is no longer just observing the fintech revolution; it is actively fueling a multi-billion-peso expansion that challenges the traditional banking hegemony. From massive capital injections into AI-driven infrastructure to the aggressive encroachment into corporate banking, payroll management, and factoring, the nation’s financial ecosystem is pivoting toward a high-growth, high-stakes future. ... For years, the narrative surrounding fintech in Colombia centered on accessibility—the promise of bringing banking services to the underserved via mobile applications. While that mission remains core, the industry has graduated to a more sophisticated phase. The current trend, evidenced by discussions in Barranquilla, shows that fintechs are no longer content with "peripheral" services. They are now encroaching on the core business models of legacy institutions. Credit origination, business treasury management, sophisticated factoring, and payroll services are now the battlegrounds where digital-native firms are fighting for market share. headline: Evolution and Trends of the Insurtech Ecosystem in Latin America
summary_text: - Transition from a distribution-based model to one focused on technological enablers and AI. - Recovery of foreign investment with much stricter criteria and focused on profitability. - The persistence of low insurance penetration in the region opens up opportunities for affordable products. - Sustained leadership of Brazil and Mexico in the volume of startups and attraction of capital. ... The landscape of technology insurers in Latin America has taken a striking turn. After navigating a period of significant adjustment due to the funding crisis that began in 2022, the sector has reached a much more mature phase. Today, we find ourselves in a scenario where strategic rigor is the norm , leaving behind blind euphoria to focus on solutions that truly add value to the insurance business. With 536 active insurtech companies, the market is experiencing a revitalization of investment, although investors are no longer throwing money at the first opportunity. They are only betting on projects that demonstrate a real capacity to solve specific problems and that have a solid business model. It is a time of professionalization where the balance between disruptive innovation and tangible profitability is being sought. ... Looking at the economic forecasts, the region is expected to balance its growth while gradually disinflating. This more stable environment is music to the sector's ears, as economic predictability is essential for designing financial products, scaling business models, and, above all, reaching those markets that are still underinsured. Even so, it's not all rosy, as there's a considerable barrier: the insurance gap. It's surprising that insurance penetration in Latin America hovers around just 3%. This figure makes it abundantly clear that there's a need to create much more accessible products and distribution channels that don't just stay in the capital cities, but reach segments of the population that have been completely overlooked until now. ... Last year was a complete turning point. After a period of contraction, funding has resurfaced, reaching $199 million. While this represents an impressive 117% jump compared to the previous year, we are still far from the investment peaks seen in 2021 or 2022. Now, as expert Carlos Cendra points out, the market has stopped rewarding empty growth and is prioritizing real business impact. This evolution has led to a more rational ecosystem. We've moved from a model where 60% of companies were simply focused on distribution, to one where technology enablers are leading the way , now controlling more than 51% of the market. The focus has shifted towards tools that optimize operations, the intelligent use of data, and the implementation of Artificial Intelligence. ... Startup mortality has fallen to 8%, indicating that the companies that survive are much more resilient. Geographically, diversification is evident, although some countries maintain their dominance: - Brazil remains the giant, concentrating 74% of the investment and having 214 insurtechs. - Mexico ranks second most relevant market by volume of companies. - Chile has consolidated firmly in third position. - Argentina and Colombia They close out the top five, showing their own dynamics of growth and internationalization. This maturity makes it easier for large, traditional insurers to find more reliable technology partners. The goal now is to tackle critical challenges ranging from risk underwriting to claims management , always striving to transform insurance from a luxury into a tool for widespread protection. ... Looking ahead to the coming months, the sector is expected to enter a consolidation phase. Funding will focus on startups that not only innovate but also seamlessly integrate with traditional insurers. A telling statistic is that the internationalization rate is already approaching 19,2% , and almost a third of the insurtechs operating in the region are foreign-owned, demonstrating that Latin America continues to be a magnet for global talent. The biggest challenge is no longer simply creating an eye-catching app, but aligning funding with real business priorities. Only in this way can protection gaps be closed sustainably. The path toward a more professional ecosystem will allow technology to translate into measurable results for both companies and citizens. The technology-driven insurance sector in Latin America has transitioned from a phase of unchecked expansion to a stage of strategic maturity, where AI and data are the main drivers. With recovered but more selective investment and geographic diversification led by Brazil and Mexico, the industry is now focused on reducing low insurance penetration through scalable solutions and strong collaborations between startups and traditional insurers.

headline: LATAM legal market: key trends and insights from the Chambers Latin America Guide 2027
summary_text: The Chambers Latin America Guide 2027 reveals a legal market characterised by growing demand for legal services, increased client expectations, AI-driven transformation and a greater focus on commercially-informed legal advice. ... The LATAM legal market is in good health, enjoying a period of sustained legal demand driven by market change and complexity. 90% of respondents expect demand for external counsel to either increase or remain stable. In fact, 45.2% of those interviewed think it is likely that they will need more legal advice and services over the next 12 months. Confidence is particularly strong in Peru, Mexico, Colombia, Uruguay, Chile and Argentina where demand is being driven by economic, regulatory and general business transformation efforts across the region. From a law firm perspective, the results are particularly positive. Only 5.1% of respondents expect to reduce their use of external counsel, while the overwhelming majority anticipate stable or increased demand. ... Technical excellence is – and always will be – essential. However, clients have expanded their capabilities wish list, selecting firms who demonstrate a clear understanding of business realities. This shift is most clearly seen in what clients say they now highly value. Commercial understanding and strategic advice aligned with corporate goals have become increasingly important. These qualities must be backed by exceptional client services – responsiveness, collaboration and a focus on long-term relationship building will help LATAM law firms stand out from their competitors. The prioritisation of service and commercial understanding is reflected in where LATAM clients believe their law firm partners can improve. Client service (27%) and business understanding/commerciality (26%) were the most frequently mentioned areas of concern. ... Conversations with GCs and law firm representatives consistently highlight the growing importance of artificial intelligence in the LATAM region. Technology has moved from a theoretical discussion to a practical concern for stakeholders on both sides of the legal services divide. Clients now expect their external legal advisors to use technology to deliver faster, more efficient and more cost-effective services, while maintaining the quality and depth of their advice. This is leading to discussions about the service delivery and traditional per hour billing model One counter-intuitive insight we uncovered was that despite virtually everyone talking about AI, just 1% of those surveyed identified it as an area of improvement for law firms. Outlook: Commercial understanding drives success Demand for legal services remains strong across the entire LATAM region, with an overwhelming majority of legal service buyers expecting their need for external counsel to either increase or remain stable over the next 12 months. As business navigates increasingly complex regulatory, commercial and operational challenges, law firms are likely to benefit from sustained demand for sophisticated legal advice. It is also important to realise that client prioritisation of commercial value over purely technical expertise is unlikely to change. Business understanding and commercial awareness are the hallmarks of a firm positioned for LATAM success. Artificial intelligence is a major talking point for both clients and law firms. While AI was rarely identified as an area for improvement, conversations across the region highlight growing expectations around the, use of technology, efficiency and how work is measured and billed too. ... - Demand is growing, confidence is high and the LATAM legal market shows no signs of slowing down. - Commercial awareness has become a key differentiator in the race to win and retain clients. - Currently clients place greater value on service quality and business understanding than they do about firms' AI capabilities. - Increasing market sophistication is driving demand for more specialised legal expertise, reflected in the expansion of several ranking tables across the region. - Women are achieving strong representation among emerging talent, signalling a more balanced future for the region's legal profession.

headline: Key changes introduced by the new CNSP regulation affecting large and complex risks
summary_text: SUSEP publishes CNSP Resolution No. 496/2026 relating to Property and Casualty insurance contracts. CNSP Resolution No. 496 was published on 17 August 2026 ("Resolution 496") in the Federal Official Gazette and provides further clarification on the preparation, structuring, marketing, execution, and operation of all property and casualty insurance contracts. It is important to note that this resolution puts an end to the former regulatory distinction between mass risks and "large risks." ... 1. Single contractual regime: All property and casualty insurance contracts are subject to the same framework for contract formation and execution. 2. Repeal of Resolution 407/21 (affecting previously known as "Large Risks"): Article 53 of Resolution 496 expressly repeals CNSP Resolution No. 407/2021 and ends the distinction relating to the so-called "large risks" in Brazil. 3. Specific risks previously classified as "Large Risks": Chapter III lists the specific risks below. The resolution expressly permits the adoption of a period of up to 120 days for adjusting a claim and settling a covered claim (Articles 28 and 29, paragraph 2). The possibility of applying such extended periods to other insurance products involving greater complexity in claims assessment remains unregulated. | Branch (Chapter III) | Specific risks | | --- | --- | | Petroleum risks | Onshore/offshore prospecting, drilling, production, storage, and refining operations, including liability and financial losses (Arts. 32-33) | | Named and operational risks | Named risks (listed coverages) or operational risks (all risks) with LMG exceeding R$ 15 million (Art. 34) | | Global bankers blanket | Losses of financial institutions involving cash and assets (theft, robbery, destruction, etc.) (Art. 35) | | Aviation risks | Hull and liability coverage for hangars/airport operations and possibly including coverage for defence costs, fees, and fines, with provision for free choice of counsel (Arts. 36-37) | | Maritime risks | Vessel hull coverage and rules for port operators and covered port operations (Arts. 38-40) | | Nuclear risks | Property damage and liability arising from nuclear energy activities; same approach to defence costs/fees as aeronautical insurance (Arts. 41-42) | | Domestic and export credit – legal entities | Coverage for losses arising from insured and unpaid receivables, when the insured is a legal entity (Art. 43) | 4. Claims adjustment and settlement of covered risks: Except for risks governed by Chapter III, the period for adjusting and settling a covered claim is up to 30 days (Articles 28 and 29). Claims adjustment and settlement reports, together with their annexes, constitute documents common to the parties and are subject to supplementary regulation by SUSEP (Article 30). 5. Product Registration: All contractual conditions, including terms and clauses drafted and negotiated on a customised basis to meet the specific needs of the insured or beneficiary, must be registered prior to commercialisation. 6. Notifications through the Broker: Notifications must be made by appropriate means and be capable of proof of receipt. Articles 22 and 45 provide that such notifications may be forwarded to a broker or to a representative of the recipient, within the limits of their respective authority, but do not specify how such authority is to be evidenced or verified. 7. Application of Brazilian Law: CNSP Resolution No. 496 reinforces the trend already observed in CNSP Resolution No. 494 of strengthening the application of Brazilian law to insurance contracts with a substantial connection to the country. Article 3 mandates the exclusive application of Brazilian law and rules issued by the CNSP and SUSEP in the following cases: (a) contracts entered into by an insurer authorised to operate in Brazil; (b) where the insured or proposer is resident or domiciled in the country; and (c) where the assets underlying the insured interests are located in Brazil. 8. Adaptation period: The resolution was published and entered into force on 18 August 2026 (Article 54). In practice, insurers and other market participants must, before 5 January 2027, complete a review of how they intend to adapt to the new resolution and ensure that the required clauses are properly drafted, while also monitoring supplementary regulations issued by SUSEP affecting these risks. CNSP Resolution No. 496/2026, as issued by the local regulator, introduces a new grouping of risks and should provide the reinsurance market with guidance as to how these risks may justify an extended claims adjustment and settlement period of up to 120 days. It remains to be seen what supplementary regulations SUSEP will issue in relation to these risks and how the market will adapt to these changes in Brazil. ### Authors

headline: Latin America Wealth Management Growth Soars
summary_text: In a context where the private wealth management industry is growing at double digits, Latin America stands out. The region is seeing a particularly strong expansion rate according to Boston Consulting Group (BCG), driven by the appreciation of regional currencies and a variety of business-related factors—a momentum that currently shows forward projections. “Latin America stood out for its growth,” emphasizes Federico Muxi, Managing Director & Senior Partner at the consulting firm, in an interview with Funds Society. As part of the firm’s Global Wealth Report, they estimated that the region saw a growth of 17.7% in 2025, measured in dollars. In contrast, the global industry grew by 10.7% during that same period. What explains this? On one hand, there is the currency dynamic. “A good portion of this growth—roughly half—occurred because many of the main Latin American currencies appreciated against the dollar last year,” indicates the executive, who leads BCG’s financial institutions practice in Iberia and South America. This is the case, he explains, for the currencies of several major regional economies, including the Brazilian real, the Mexican peso, the Chilean peso, the Colombian peso, and the Peruvian sol. The other half of last year’s boom comes from the dynamism of the economies, the savings rate they generate, and the evolution of local capital markets. “If you look at market performance over the last year, it was very good. And this year it is being replicated as well,” notes the executive, citing strong gains in stock markets that appreciate wealth. “Despite geopolitical uncertainty and rising inflation in some markets, exacerbated by the increase in oil prices, the markets have still not adjusted and continue to show very good yields,” he adds. ... Muxi highlights Brazil and Mexico as the hubs of greatest growth in terms of absolute volume. Regarding sophistication—including variables such as industry competitiveness and investment firm capabilities—he highlights Brazil and Chile. ... In a context where the trend is moving toward offshore investments—a trend established in the industry globally—these characteristics favor the local development of the business. Macroeconomic stability and legal certainty bring more local investments compared to offshore hubs, comments the BCG executive, which incentivizes the development of a more competitive local advisory offering. At the same time, this sophistication brings more onshore investments. To illustrate, Muxi points out that the percentage of total financial wealth—including pension funds—held offshore reaches only 9% in Chile and 11% in Brazil. In contrast, that figure reaches 70% in cases like Argentina. ... Another trend that has favored the boom in the region’s wealth management business, according to the consulting firm, is the greater variety of wealth the industry is capturing. This focus leaves wealth between 500,000 and 1 million dollars seeking services elsewhere. This presents an opportunity for onshore segment players, who tend to be closer to these clients and can generally better leverage commercial banking—often as part of the same financial groups—as well as for new players, such as B2B2C platforms that channel independent wealth managers. “That is a super relevant phenomenon in the region and one of growing size,” Muxi indicates. Funds are not doing fewer deals out of broad caution; they are doing fewer deals because they are being more selective and committing larger amounts per transaction — precisely the pattern that characterizes buy-and-build strategies, where an initial larger-ticket platform is used as the vehicle for successive bolt-on acquisitions. ... From a financing-structure standpoint, consolidation platforms (roll-ups) face a recurring technical trade-off: financing each bolt-on acquisition individually — which multiplies transaction costs and covenant complexity — or negotiating a revolving acquisition facility (delayed-draw term loan) from the closing of the initial platform, enabling multiple acquisitions under a single credit documentation package. In today’s environment of wider spreads flagged by global private credit managers, the second option gains appeal because it reduces the friction of renegotiating terms with every bolt-on, though it requires sponsors to commit to more conservative consolidated leverage covenants from the outset. ... 1. A force majeure clause is standard boilerplate in large construction contracts - it lets a party pause certain obligations when events genuinely outside its control, such as permitting delays, make performance impossible on schedule. The developer on the other side of the contract is a unit of Blue Owl Capital (NYSE: OWL) , whose Stack Infrastructure business is building the 1,400-acre campus. Crucially, Oracle is not trying to walk away as tenant. Reuters reported the software giant is seeking room to delay payments, not exit the lease, and Blue Owl said the notice "does not change financial commitments" to what it called a multi-year project.

headline: Leading market infrastructure firms form Coalition to advance issuer-sponsored tokenized securities
summary_text: GEORGE TOWN, Cayman Islands, Sept. 24, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) - Bullish (NYSE: BLSH) and Equiniti today announced the formation of the Issuer Sponsored Token Coalition, a multi-stakeholder industry working group bringing together leading firms across brokerage, trading and market infrastructure to advance issuer-sponsored tokenized securities. Alpaca, Apex Fintech Solutions and DriveWealth are among the first market infrastructure participants joining Bullish and Equiniti in the Coalition, which is being established to help develop the technical standards, market infrastructure and operating frameworks necessary for tokenized securities to scale alongside, and interoperate with, the existing capital markets ecosystem. The Coalition is founded on the belief that the next generation of tokenized public securities should preserve the fundamental relationship between an issuer and its shareholders. Under an issuer-sponsored model, tokenized securities can be directly connected to the issuer's authoritative shareholder register, helping preserve ownership rights, corporate-action entitlements and investor protections while enabling the benefits of blockchain - based market infrastructure. The launch follows the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's Sept. 17 Innovation Exemption, which permits limited onchain trading of U.S. - listed equities.

headline: Amid Challenges, Dairy Has All the Right Ingredients to Win - Cheese Reporter
summary_text: There is a number on the minds of all in American dairy processing right now: 11 billion. It’s the number of dollars committed to more than 50 new and expanded dairy production projects through early 2028. That remarkable amount is made still more so by the environment in which these investments are taking place. Dairy companies are navigating trade volatility, rising costs of production – particularly related to milk, fuel, and equipment, workforce shortages, infrastructure constraints, and a dynamic policy and regulatory environment. Capital is being invested in what could be described as a challenging, unpredictable business climate. ... I had the opportunity to explore why this week at the Wisconsin Cheese Makers Association’s Annual Member Meeting, during our keynote panel, “Value-Added Ventures: How Dairy Leaders Are Investing in Dairy’s Strengths.” The discussion featured executives from three companies making significant investments of their own: Jenny Drake, Vice President of Operations at Grande Cheese Company; Brianne Maier, Vice President of Dairy Foods Research and Development at Land O’Lakes; and Derek Miller, Vice President of Communications at Lifeway Foods. ... “Protein demand continues to be one of the strongest trends in food and beverage industry and is creating great opportunity for dairy,” said Maier. “At Land O’Lakes, we are investing in innovation and expanding our new product pipeline to bring new products and ingredients to market. One of these investments is at our Tulare, California manufacturing plant where we are bringing on Ultra-Filtrated 85 (UF-85) capacity this spring.” “People are making a return to natural foods, and dairy is something they know and they trust,” said Miller, highlighting Lifeway’s $50 million project in Waukesha, Wisconsin, which will double the site’s manufacturing capacity and improve packaging efficiency. Lifeway sees significant opportunity at the intersection of cultured dairy, probiotics and protein, including new applications. “We’ve got this new product called Lifeway Muscle Mates, and it has 20 grams of whey protein and probiotics, but also five grams of creatine. All we need to do with dairy is ‘zhuzh’ it up a little to create disruptive, profitable moments on the shelf.” ... Sometimes it means taking something consumers already know and making it more convenient, more functional or more relevant. Sometimes it means investing in automation or process improvements that make a plant more efficient. Sometimes – as is the case for Grande Cheese – it means helping a customer sell more of its own product, or entering a new market or geography. “We have a fantastic sales team that is boots-on-the-ground here, but we’re looking globally. Can we replicate this success in other countries? We’re in Mexico now, and we’re seeing big wins there from the development of its pizza culture,” said Drake, detailing one driving factors behind a major expansion project the award-winning Italian cheese manufacturer recently completed in Chilton, Wisconsin. But the panel also made clear that investment in dairy’s future extends well beyond bricks, mortar and equipment. The industry’s ability to capitalize on its strengths will depend just as much on how we use emerging technologies, improve efficiency and sustainability, and build the workforce needed to operate and innovate within these facilities. “With the Chilton project, we revisited the job descriptions that were traditional in some of our legacy locations and made adjustments,” said Drake. “Instead of turning prospects away who didn’t have technical skills to qualify for a position, we are partnering with a local technical college to give them that knowledge via onboarding.” Maier noted Land O’Lakes’ move to implement artificial intelligence as a practical tool, “AI’s biggest value is helping people make better decisions faster, not replacing people.” “Our new ERP system is great for production planning and forecasting – and for sales, AI is giving us normalized rates and insights on promotions. It can be a great tool, as long as we maintain real, human communication and authenticity,” said Miller. Taken together, these examples point to a broader definition of investment, strengthening every element that goes into dairy production – and to continued strength ahead. Maier put it simply: “We have all the right ingredients to win.”

headline: Terrain | U.S. Milk Checks Face Greater Exposure to Global Dynamics
summary_text: Over the past few years, cheese and butter have overtaken surplus byproducts as the driver of U.S. dairy exports. This newer susceptibility to price competition and international volatility for cheese and butter markets matters for milk checks: When butter and cheese prices move with international prices, so do the more impactful and closely watched butterfat and protein component prices. ... U.S. prices need to remain competitive with prices in Europe and New Zealand to keep product flowing. If we were to return to the export levels of a few years ago, the U.S. market would be flooded in cheese and butter well beyond what could be consumed domestically. ... With U.S. milk output climbing and key global exporters expected to be competitive in the months ahead, we could experience downward pressure on U.S. component and milk prices. ... The U.S. has an abundance of milk. For years, we’ve increased production faster than domestic demand could keep up with. Thanks to investment in new processing capacity, the industry can handle the milk. Exports have been critical to clearing the market of the extra product, but that makes prices more susceptible to global dynamics. As a result, international markets have a more direct path to the U.S. butterfat and protein component values that appear on milk checks. And heavy global supply will weigh on domestic milk prices. ... Several new U.S. processing plants have come on line over the past two years that have enabled an expansion in milk production. As of June 2026, USDA data show there were 354,000 more milk cows in the U.S. than there were in June 2024. On average, each of those cows produces almost 2% more milk than their 2024 counterparts. Those factors combined mean we’re producing an additional 36 million pounds of milk each day, not to mention the higher component levels that mean more butter and cheese can be made from each pound of that milk. Through the first half of 2026, the U.S. has produced 7.5 billion pounds of cheese. That’s 178 million pounds (2.4%) more than last year and 402 million pounds more than two years ago (adjusting for the leap year). Butter output climbed as well, by nearly 150 million pounds versus the same period two years ago. ... Domestic disappearance of cheese (a proxy for domestic demand) in the first half of 2026 was about 6.8 billion pounds, which is about 112 million pounds more than the same period two years ago. That’s excellent demand growth, but it’s still less than a third of the increase in supply over the same period. Thankfully, we’ve seen exports of cheese and butter climb to record highs. But the celebration of repeatedly setting new export records might be masking the importance of how critical these exports have become. ... Historically, U.S. dairy exports focused on clearing the market of surplus byproducts — primarily dry whey powder and nonfat dry milk from the cheese and butter manufacturing process. But exports of those products have been relatively flat or declining over the past few years. Instead, cheese and butter have been the drivers of export growth. The strong export growth is worth celebrating. But beyond just being a good thing, the export growth is now necessary support for the cheese and butter markets that drive milk prices. If we were to return to the export levels of a few years ago, the U.S. market would be flooded in cheese and butter well beyond what could be consumed domestically, and overburdensome inventories would crush prices. Since we have no choice but to export the additional production, U.S. dairy markets are increasingly at the mercy of international prices. U.S. prices need to remain competitive with prices in Europe and New Zealand to keep product flowing. While commodities like nonfat dry milk and whey have always been susceptible to this price competition and international volatility, it’s a newer development for cheese and butter markets that have historically been much more domestically focused. That matters for milk checks. Movements in whey and nonfat dry milk prices lead to changes in the other solids component price and the Class IV skim milk value. When butter and cheese prices move with international prices, so do the more impactful and closely watched butterfat and protein component prices. ... With U.S. milk output climbing and other global exporters like the EU and New Zealand expected to be actively supplying and competitive in global markets in the months ahead, we could experience downward pressure on U.S. component and milk prices. ... Protein demand is certainly a bright spot in U.S. markets, and consumer demand more broadly is nothing to scoff at. But they’re no match for supply-side growth. In this new era where cheese and butter exports are not just nice but necessary, a close eye on global markets will be increasingly important in understanding our domestic component values, and risk management strategies may need to be adjusted accordingly.

headline: Formo scales precision-fermented casein ahead of US debut - AG Life Media
summary_text: German startup Formo expects to receive an FDA no questions letter for its precision fermented casein protein within weeks and is preparing to scale production to a couple of tons a month with co-manufacturers next year as it prepares to make its US debut. The firm, which handles development through to pilot scale in-house in Frankfurt, is working with a network of contract manufacturing organizations (CMOs) and scaling in line with customer demand, cofounder and CEO Raffael Wohlgensinger told AgFunderNews. It has not ruled out integrated manufacturing later but says financial backers would need to see hundreds of tons of sales “that really de-risk that step” before this becomes a viable option. However, Wohlgensinger says working with co-packers still makes sense commercially given the advances the company has made on boosting titer, productivity and yield with its bacterial production host. ... While some other players making casein proteins in fermentation tanks use yeast or filamentous fungus strains, Formo uses E.coli because it has clear advantages if you can optimize the downstream process and get a pure product at the end without breaking the bank, said Wohlgensinger. ... “But for efficiency, volumetric productivity, everybody knows it’s a super-fast [growing] organism and the best if you can solve those two issues above. And we have. We work with a probiotic E. coli strain, which has demonstrated use to make more than 100 compounds for humans, and we have a really easy, cost-efficient downstream process [for extracting and purifying the casein protein from the microbial cells].” ... Like many startups in the animal-free dairy segment, Formo has shifted away from consumer-facing products to prioritize B2B ingredients, closing down its adjacent koji fermentation operation and branded consumer cheese business in order to focus on casein proteins. Rather than competing with commodity milk proteins, it is positioning its alpha-S1 casein as a premium ingredient with a competitive cost in use that can also open up new application opportunities given its superior foaming, emulsification and oil-holding capacity, said Wohlgensinger. Its solubility at low pH also opens up applications currently dominated by whey and precision-fermented beta-lactoglobulin such as clear protein beverages, an application where conventional casein typically performs poorly, he explained. ... Formo is also exploring high-protein yogurts and drinkable yogurts, where protein loading can create grainy textures, he said. “You can push the ceiling of protein content beyond what is currently possible with regular casein.” He added: “If someone is just looking for a commodity protein or the cheapest protein, today, we are not the best option. But we actually perform better than plant-based and dairy benchmarks across a variety of applications. In creamers, for example, it’s an amazing ingredient and even better than sodium caseinate [a milk-derived ingredient commonly used in creamers].” ... While there are early indications that Formo’s single casein protein is digested more rapidly that regular casein (which contains four casein proteins held in a micellular structure), more research is needed before any claims can be made to this effect, added Wohlgensinger. ... In other areas such as cheese analogs, Formo’s alpha-S1 casein can deliver the stretch and melt that consumers expect while eliminating phosphate salts from the formulation and simplifying product labels for consumers, he said. ... With our casein system, we could ... replace these salts [which often come ... -friendly names ... as sodium caseinate].” ... While Formo’s casein has self-affirmed GRAS status in the US, some large multinationals will not launch products until the company can show an FDA “no questions” letter, he said. However, this is expected very soon, he revealed. ... We’re actually expecting the no questions letter ... come within the next couple of weeks ... No US products containing Formo’s casein are currently on shelves, but the company has sampling and co-development projects with customers from SMEs to multinationals, and is working closely with RX Food Ingredients to build its pipeline. Applications drawing interest include ready-to-drink and ready-to-mix protein products, yogurts, creamers, coffee products, powders and protein snacks, with demand reflecting broader nutrition trends including weight management, longevity and GLP-1 drugs. As a result, the pitch has shifted from animal-free dairy, sustainability and ethics, to performance, said Wohlgensinger. “We’re now convincing people who are completely agnostic to all the other arguments. It’s all about the business case, and that is really the narrative shift that is taking place across this industry.”
